defer and async on <script> (HTML 4.0, 1997, and HTML5). Covered in Resolution 1: both are promises not to call document.write, which is the only reason the parser is allowed to keep going.

Web Workers (2009). A genuine second thread. And the crucial design decision: a worker has no access to the DOM. Not restricted access — none. It cannot see document or window, and communicates only by passing messages that are copied, not shared.

// main thread
const w = new Worker("heavy.js");
w.postMessage(data);
w.onmessage = e => render(e.data);

// heavy.js — a separate thread, no DOM
onmessage = e => { postMessage(compute(e.data)); };

Why no DOM? Because the DOM is a large mutable data structure with no locking, built on the assumption that exactly one thread touches it. Making it thread-safe would mean auditing and locking every node operation in the browser, and would reintroduce every concurrency hazard the single-threaded model eliminated. The platform chose to keep the guarantee and hand you an isolated thread instead. So workers are excellent for computation and useless for anything that touches the page — which is why they are far less used than their power suggests.

requestAnimationFrame (2011) — run this immediately before the next paint, so animation work lands in the right phase of the loop instead of fighting it.

requestIdleCallback — run this only if there is time left in a frame.

Task splitting and yielding. The modern discipline is to chop long work into pieces and hand the thread back between them, so input can be processed. The recent primitive for this is scheduler.yield(); the older idiom was setTimeout(fn, 0), which is the same idea with worse ergonomics.

Off-main-thread rendering. Browsers have progressively moved work off the main thread themselves — compositing and many scroll and transform animations now run on a separate compositor thread, which is why a CSS transform animation keeps moving smoothly even while JavaScript is blocking, and a top/left animation does not. That is a genuinely useful practical consequence of this whole section.

What none of these do is remove the underlying property. In 2026, while (true) {} still freezes the tab.

Section 7 — "Never break old pages": you were right, and the card is wrong

You ended with: "you said never break old pages, so that one I still can't understand — how does it relate to running code inside an untrusted browser page?"

It does not, and the objection is correct. Resolution 1's Part 5 conceded this and I will restate it here because you asked it as its own question and it deserves its own answer rather than a cross-reference.

The card groups four constraints as though they were one family. Three of them genuinely are:

  • start instantly, with no install or compile step
  • never touch the user's machine
  • never freeze the page

All three follow from a single premise: this code arrived from a stranger and runs on your computer, right now, without your consent to this particular program. Instant start is required because there was no install step to hide the latency in. No machine access is required because the author is untrusted. Not freezing is required because the user did not choose to run this program and cannot be made to suffer for it.

"Never break old pages" follows from something else entirely, and the something else is not about trust at all. It follows from publish once, abandon forever — the fact that the web has no update path, that a page from 1997 is still served by a machine nobody administers, and that its author cannot be reached. It is a constraint on the evolution of the language, not on the execution of a program. It binds the committee, not the code.

The two even point in different directions. The trust constraints are about what a running script may do to you. Backwards compatibility is about what future browser vendors may do to already-published pages. Different actor, different victim, different timescale — one is measured in milliseconds and the other in decades.

The whole of Resolution 3 is the proper treatment of the fourth one, which is itself an admission that it did not belong in this list.

What this resolves

Is my security reading right?Section 1: yes, and the defence is at the right layer — trusting the server, verifying code, and asking the user were all tried and all failed (ActiveX being the cautionary case). But the threat you named was the wrong one: the valuable target is not your files, it is your logged-in sessions at other sites. The defence is the same-origin policy (Navigator 2.0, 1995), which restricts reading but not sending — hence CSRF, and hence CORS.
Is that sandboxing, and did the idea come from browsers?Section 2: the reverse. The concept is decades older (chroot 1979; the term standardised by the 1993 fault-isolation paper), and the browser's first explicit sandbox was Java's, not JavaScript's. Java's was designed and eventually failed; JavaScript's was enforced by absence and held.
My tab-isolation guessSection 2: right instinct, and now with the full four-stage timeline — same-origin policy 1995, tabs ~2001 (cosmetic), process-per-tab 2008, site isolation 2018 after Spectre made a CPU bug invalidate the previous model
Are "no file access" and "don't crash the machine" the same?Section 3: no, and your mid-sentence correction was right. Confidentiality/integrity versus availability — different threat, different defence, opposite histories. The browser-locker scam is pure availability attack, stealing nothing.
The history of "never freeze the page" — were there incidents?Section 4: not one incident, a permanent condition. The evidence is that every vendor shipped a watchdog — IE counted statements (default 5,000,000, registry key MaxScriptStatements), Firefox used a ten-second dom.max_script_run_time, Chrome killed the renderer process instead. And the card is loose: this was never a design constraint, it was an unachievable property that browsers defended after the fact.
Was it architectural? How can a script affect rendering?Section 5: script and rendering share one main thread, and JavaScript runs to completion and cannot be preempted. A script does not interfere with rendering — it occupies the thread rendering runs on. Tabs are isolated from each other; a script is not isolated from its own page. And the payoff: "nothing can interrupt my code" and "my slow code freezes the page" are the same sentence, which is why JavaScript has no locks and why the whole of Node 9 exists.
The two filesResolution 2, Section 1 — <SCRIPT SRC>, absent from Navigator 2.0, added in Navigator 3.0, August 1996
How does "never break old pages" relate to untrusted code?Section 7: it does not. Three constraints come from "a stranger's code runs on your machine"; the fourth comes from "the web has no update path." Different actor, different victim, one measured in milliseconds and one in decades. Your objection stands, and Resolution 3 is the fourth one's proper treatment.

Seven asks. Two were already answered elsewhere, and one of them was you being right about a flaw in the question.

pieces.title: Resolution 7 — Q8: why these types exist, what types are for, and where null and undefined came from
pieces.content:
The long middle stretch of this follow-up — where you reason from "RAM is just cells of zeros and ones" to "types must be metadata so instructions know how to manipulate data" and then to "if every kind of data had its own dedicated instruction, maybe types would not be needed at all" — is not a guess that needs correcting. It is a description of how machine code actually works. You reasoned your way to the real answer and then apologised for it. Section 3 finishes the thought.

The asks I find:

  1. How were these seven shortlisted? Who decided, and on what basis? Sections 1–2.
  2. How was it decided they were sufficient — that everything else could be derived? Sections 2 and 6.
  3. Was there a way to make custom or composite types at release? Section 6 — yes, and they never become types.
  4. Where are types actually used? You could not name the places. Section 5 — because in JavaScript there almost are none.
  5. Check my theory of what types are for. Sections 3–4. It is righter than you thought.
  6. Why Symbol? Why Boolean? Why undefined as types at all? Sections 7, 8, 9.
  7. Where did undefined come from, and why does it seem JavaScript-specific? Section 10.
  8. Where did null come from — it exists in C++ too? Section 11, and it has a precise birthday and a famous apology.

Section 1 — The correction that reframes the whole question: it was never seven

Your question assumes a moment of selection — a room where someone chose seven types and judged the set complete. There was no such moment, and knowing that dissolves most of the puzzle.

In 1995 there were five primitives. Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null. Plus Object, for six language types in total. That was the entire type system, and it stayed exactly that for twenty years.

1995Number, String, Boolean, Undefined, Null (+ Object)five primitives
June 2015+ Symbolsix
2020+ BigIntseven

So "the seven primitive types" is a fact about 2020, not about 1995. Nobody ever sat down and picked seven. Five were picked in ten days, and two were added a generation later, each for one specific and nameable reason — which are Sections 7 and 8.

That also answers your second ask before it is asked. Nobody decided the set was sufficient. It was not sufficient; it was extended twice, and both extensions were forced by problems that did not exist in 1995. What was decided in 1995 was something weaker and more sensible: that these five plus a general-purpose Object were enough for the kind of program the language was for — validating a form, swapping an image, showing a message.

Section 2 — Why those five, and the one genuinely good decision in the ten days

Four of the five are not choices at all. Number, String and Boolean are the universal floor — present in essentially every programming language ever built, because arithmetic, text and conditions are what programs do. null was borrowed from Java, along with the name JavaScript itself and a good deal of syntax; Section 11 covers where Java got it. Only undefined is genuinely original, and Section 10 covers why it had to be.

But there is a real design decision inside "Number," and it is arguably the best one made in the ten days. Look at what a systems language of the era offered:

// C, 1995
char        short       int        long
unsigned char  unsigned short  unsigned int  unsigned long
float       double      long double

Eleven-ish numeric types, and choosing between them requires knowing your value's range, your platform's word size, and whether you need fractions. JavaScript has one. Every number is an IEEE-754 double-precision float — including the ones that look like integers.

typeof 1        // "number"
typeof 1.5      // "number"
typeof -0       // "number"
typeof Infinity // "number"
typeof NaN      // "number"   ← yes, Not-a-Number is a number

1 / 2           // 0.5, not 0 — there is no integer division to fall into

Why one? Because of the audience, which Resolution 2, Section 5 established: designers, writers and hobbyists, not systems programmers. You cannot ask that person to choose between short and long. And a double represents every integer up to 253 exactly, which is roughly nine quadrillion — vastly more than any quantity a form-validation script will ever count. So one type genuinely covered the use case, and it removed an entire category of decision and an entire category of bug (integer overflow, which JavaScript simply does not have).

It also caused two permanent problems, both of which you will meet:

0.1 + 0.2                  // 0.30000000000000004  — binary floating point
9007199254740992 + 1       // 9007199254740992     — past 2^53, integers stop being exact
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER    // 9007199254740991

The first is not JavaScript's fault — it is IEEE-754, and Python and Java do it too. The second is what eventually forced BigInt in 2020, twenty-five years later. So the best decision in the ten days is also the one that required a whole new primitive type to patch. That is a fair summary of the language generally.

Section 3 — Your theory, finished: the type is the instruction

Your reasoning, restated: memory is undifferentiated bits; RAM cells carry no labels saying "this one is an integer"; therefore there is no way to look at a chunk of memory and know what it holds; therefore types must be metadata attached to data so instructions know how to treat it — and, you added, if each kind of data had its own dedicated instruction instead, maybe types would not be needed.

Every step of that is correct, and the last one is the answer. Let me make it concrete, because seeing it once permanently changes how you read this material.

Take eight bytes of memory. Here they are:

01000000 00001001 00100001 11111011 01010100 01000100 00101101 00011000

What is that? Interpreted as a 64-bit signed integer it is 4,614,256,656,552,045,848. Interpreted as an IEEE-754 double it is 3.14159265358979. Interpreted as eight ASCII characters it is a short piece of gibberish text. Interpreted as x86 machine code it is a sequence of instructions the CPU would happily execute. All four readings are equally valid, and the bits contain nothing that distinguishes them. Your intuition is exactly right and it is worth holding on to, because it is also the reason buffer overflows and code injection are possible — a machine that cannot tell data from code can be persuaded to run data.

Now your final step. How does the CPU know which reading to use? It does not, and it never asks. The instruction decides.

ADD    rax, rbx      ; treat both as 64-bit integers, add them
ADDSD  xmm0, xmm1    ; treat both as IEEE-754 doubles, add them

Two different opcodes. Same bits, potentially in the same registers. The processor has no concept of type at all — it has instructions that impose an interpretation. So your speculation "if for every kind of data there were a different instruction, types might not be needed" is not a hypothesis about an alternative world. It is a description of the actual machine. At the hardware level, there are no types; there are only typed operations.

Which gives the real definition, and it is worth stating as a rule:

A type system is the mechanism by which a language chooses the right instruction for you. Types exist because at some point above the metal, we stopped wanting to pick ADD versus ADDSD by hand.

That is the primary job. The error-catching you also mentioned is a consequence: once the language knows an operand is text, it can notice that you asked for it to be divided, and object. But the noticing comes second. The selection comes first.

To be complete, types do four distinguishable jobs, and it helps to keep them apart:

1. Select the operationWhich machine instruction, or which overload, or which method. The original job.
2. Determine representationHow many bytes, laid out how. int is 4 bytes; a struct's fields are at known offsets.
3. Prevent errorsReject illegal operations before they run.
4. Communicate intentTo other humans, to tooling, to autocomplete.

Hold this table, because JavaScript's position on it is unusual and Section 5 needs it: JavaScript does 1 and 2 at runtime, and deliberately declines to do 3. That declining is what coercion is, and it is the whole of Node 1.

Section 4 — The consequence: who carries the tag, and why V8 spends its life guessing

Given Section 3, there are exactly two arrangements a language can pick, and the choice determines almost everything about its performance.

Arrangement A — the compiler knows (static typing). You write int x, so the compiler knows at compile time that x + y is integer addition and emits ADD. The check happens once, before the program runs. And then — the part that surprises people — the type information is thrown away. The running program contains no tags. Thirty-two bits in memory, nothing marking them as an integer, because nothing needs to: the correct instruction was already chosen. This is why C is fast, and why C has no typeof — at runtime there is nothing left to ask.

Arrangement B — nobody knows until it happens (dynamic typing). JavaScript has no declarations, so at the moment the engine compiles a + b it genuinely cannot know what a is. Therefore every value must carry its own type with it — which is precisely the tagged representation from Resolution 5, Section 1, the tag bits that gave us typeof null === "object". And every operation must, at runtime, read the tags and branch:

// what `a + b` actually means in JavaScript
if      (both are numbers)  →  numeric addition
else if (either is a string) → convert both to strings, concatenate
else if (either is an object) → call its valueOf / toString, then start over
else if (BigInt mixed with Number) → throw TypeError
...

That branch runs on every single addition. It is why the interpreter-only engines of 1995–2008 were slow — Resolution 2, Section 4 — and it is the mechanical reason dynamic languages have historically been an order of magnitude behind static ones.

And here is the payoff that connects your theory to modern reality. V8's entire strategy is to recover Arrangement A at runtime by guessing. It watches your code run, notices that this particular a + b has seen two small integers every one of the last thousand times, and emits specialised machine code — a real ADD — guarded by a cheap check that the tags are still what it expects. That mechanism is called an inline cache, and the object-shape equivalent is a hidden class. When the guess holds, you get near-static-language speed. When it fails — you pass a string to a function that has only ever seen numbers — the engine deoptimises, throws away the specialised code, and falls back to the slow branching version.

Which is why the perennial JavaScript performance advice — keep variables monomorphic, do not change the type of a thing, give objects their properties in the same order — is not superstition. It is advice about not defeating a guess. The engine is trying to do what a C compiler does, without being told anything, and you can either help it or not.

Section 5 — Where types are used in JavaScript: almost nowhere

You said you could not properly name where types would be used, and listed the obvious candidates — declaring a variable, a function's return type. Your difficulty is not ignorance. It is that in JavaScript those places do not exist.

// there is no place in this program where a type is written
function add(a, b) {
  let result = a + b;
  return result;
}

No parameter types, no return type, no variable type, no cast, no generic. JavaScript source code contains no type annotations of any kind. Not "optional ones" — none. There is no syntax for it.

So the complete list of places types are observable in JavaScript is:

On values at runtimeThe tag every value carries (Section 4). Invisible to you, load-bearing for the engine.
typeofThe only operator that reports a type, and it returns a string, not a type — Resolution 5, Section 7.
CoercionThe rules that decide what "5" * 2 or [] + {} means. This is the type system's main observable behaviour.
A handful of errorsTypeError: x is not a function, Cannot read property of null, and BigInt/Number mixing. Almost the only cases where JavaScript refuses rather than coerces.

Look at that table against the four jobs in Section 3. JavaScript does job 1 and job 2 invisibly at runtime, does job 3 barely, and does job 4 not at all. The type system exists entirely inside the engine and surfaces mainly as coercion. That is why the node you are in is called "values, types, and coercion" — in this language, coercion is the type system, seen from the outside.

And it is precisely why TypeScript exists, and why you are studying it as a separate topic. TypeScript's entire contribution is to add jobs 3 and 4 — a place to write the types, and a checker that reads them before the program runs — and then to delete all of it before the code executes. Resolution 5, Section 8 has the framing: TypeScript's types are claims about your program; JavaScript's types are facts about your values.

Section 6 — Can you make custom types? The set is closed

Your third ask: at release, was there a way to make derived or composite types — to cluster values of different types together, or define a custom type?

Yes, from day one — objects and constructor functions. This worked in Navigator 2.0:

function Point(x, y) {
  this.x = x;
  this.y = y;
}
Point.prototype.norm = function () {
  return Math.sqrt(this.x * this.x + this.y * this.y);
};

var p = new Point(3, 4);
p.norm();              // 5

That is composition of values of different types under one name, with behaviour attached — everything you described. So the capability was there.

But it never produces a new type, and this is the firm answer to your question about whether the set could be extended:

typeof p                    // "object"  — not "Point", not ever
typeof new Date()           // "object"
typeof [1, 2, 3]            // "object"
typeof /regex/              // "object"
typeof new Map()            // "object"

The eight language types are a closed set. Nothing you write, and nothing any library writes, can add a ninth. Every user-defined thing, every built-in added since 1995 — Date, Array, Map, Set, Promise, RegExp, every DOM node — is an Object with a different prototype. That is why the answer to "how was it decided these were sufficient" has a second half: the set did not need to be extensible, because Object is the extension point. One general-purpose composite type, plus prototypes, covers everything a user could want to define, without ever touching the built-in list.

Which then forces a second, user-level classification system to sit on top, because typeof is useless for anything you built. That is what these are for:

p instanceof Point                        // true — walks the prototype chain
p.constructor === Point                   // true — but forgeable
Array.isArray(x)                          // the special case for arrays
Object.prototype.toString.call(x)         // "[object Date]", "[object Array]"

class Temperature {
  get [Symbol.toStringTag]() { return "Temperature"; }
}
Object.prototype.toString.call(new Temperature());   // "[object Temperature]"

That last one is as close as JavaScript gets to a user-defined type name — and note it is built out of Symbol, which is Section 7.

One caution on instanceof, since it looks like the answer and has a real flaw: it compares prototype identity, so it fails across realms. An array created inside an <iframe> is not instanceof your window's Array, because the iframe has its own Array with its own prototype object. That is why Array.isArray exists as a separate function — it checks an internal slot rather than a prototype, and works across realms.

Section 7 — Why Symbol was added (2015)

You asked why a symbol would be included as a primitive at all. The answer is unusually clean: Symbol is the only type in the language added purely to solve a backwards-compatibility problem.

Resolution 3, Section 3 has the general shape as Hatch 4; here is the specific case. ES2015 wanted to let any object say how it should be iterated, so that for...of and spread would work on user-defined collections. That requires a hook — a well-known property name the language looks for. The obvious move is a string:

obj.iterator = function () { ... };   // the naive design

And it is unusable, because the string "iterator" is not free. Somewhere on the web is an object with a property called iterator that means something else entirely, and the language would start calling it. Every plausible name — iterator, toPrimitive, hasInstance — has the same problem. Resolution 3, Section 8's SmooshGate is what happens when the committee takes a name that was already occupied.

So the language needed a new kind of property key that could not collide with any existing one. Property keys could only be strings, so a new primitive type was created for the purpose: a value that is unique by construction, cannot be forged, and cannot equal any string.

const a = Symbol("id");
const b = Symbol("id");
a === b              // false — the description is a label, not an identity
typeof a             // "symbol"

const o = {};
o[a] = 1;
o[b] = 2;            // a different key entirely
Object.keys(o)       // []        — symbol keys are skipped
JSON.stringify(o)    // "{}"      — and ignored by serialisation

Then the language's own hooks live at fixed, published symbols:

Symbol.iterator      // how to iterate me
Symbol.asyncIterator // how to iterate me asynchronously
Symbol.toPrimitive   // how to coerce me — directly relevant to Node 1
Symbol.toStringTag   // what to call me (Section 6)
Symbol.hasInstance   // how instanceof should treat me

Two consequences worth noting. Symbol keys being invisible to Object.keys and JSON.stringify was not incidental — it means adding a symbol-keyed property to someone else's object does not change how existing code sees it, which is the same non-collision goal one level up. And new Symbol() throws a TypeError, deliberately, to stop people creating wrapper objects around them: symbols are meant to be used as bare primitive keys and the wrapper would only cause confusion.

Section 8 — Why BigInt was added (2020)

Section 2 set up the problem. Numbers are doubles, so integers stop being exact above 253:

9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993     // true. Two different integers. Equal.

For twenty-five years this did not matter, because nothing on a web page counted that high. Then it did, in several places at once: 64-bit database identifiers (Twitter's snowflake IDs are the famous case, where JavaScript clients were silently corrupting IDs and the API had to also return them as strings), timestamps in nanoseconds, cryptographic values, and financial values in the smallest unit of currency.

Per Resolution 3, Number could not be changed. So a second numeric primitive was added, with its own literal syntax and its own operations:

9007199254740993n === 9007199254740994n   // false — exact
2n ** 64n                                  // exact, arbitrary precision
typeof 10n                                 // "bigint"

And the decision that makes it a good design rather than a trap:

1n + 1        // TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types

It throws rather than silently converting. In a language whose defining characteristic is silent coercion, this is a striking exception, and it is deliberate: any automatic conversion between an exact integer and an approximate double would silently lose the precision the type exists to provide. The one place JavaScript refuses to coerce is the one place coercion would destroy the point. It is also a small window into how the committee thinks now versus in 1995.

Section 9 — Why Boolean is its own type, honestly

You asked this and it deserves a straight answer rather than a justification: it did not have to be, and the argument for it is weaker in JavaScript than almost anywhere else.

Plenty of languages managed without one. C had no boolean type until C99 — you used int, with zero as false. Python has bool, but it is a subclass of int, so True + True is 2. The usual case for a separate type is that it makes intent explicit and lets the compiler reject if (x = 5).

JavaScript takes the separate type and then undercuts it completely, because every value has a boolean interpretation:

if ("")        // falsy
if (0)         // falsy
if (NaN)       // falsy
if (null)      // falsy
if (undefined) // falsy
if (0n)        // falsy
if (document.all)  // falsy — Resolution 3, the [[IsHTMLDDA]] slot

if ("0")       // TRUTHY — a non-empty string
if ([])        // TRUTHY — an object
if ({})        // TRUTHY

Eight falsy values; everything else is truthy. So the Boolean type does not gate the if statement — if accepts anything and coerces. The type's practical value is reduced to being the return type of comparisons and the thing Boolean(x) and !!x produce. It is a real type carrying real information, in a language that will accept any other type in the places you would use it.

Section 10 — Where undefined came from, and why it feels JavaScript-specific

Your instinct is right: most languages have one absence. C and Java have null, Python has None, Ruby has nil, Lisp has nil. JavaScript has two, and that is unusual. (Not unique — Perl has undef and it predates JavaScript, and Perl was a live influence on the era. But two absences as a designed distinction is rare.)

The reason is the design principle from Resolution 2, Section 5: never fail loudly. Count the situations where JavaScript needs a value and none was supplied, and notice that in a stricter language most of these are compile errors:

let a;                          // declared, never assigned
({}).nothing                    // a property that does not exist
function f(x) {}  f();          // a parameter that was not passed
function g() {}   g();          // a function that returns nothing
[1, 2, 3][99]                   // an index past the end
[1, , 3][1]                     // an array hole
// every one of these is `undefined`, and none of them is an error

Because the language refuses to error in any of these cases, it must produce a value. So a value meaning "nothing was ever put here" was structurally required. undefined is the price of permissiveness.

Why not just use null for all of it? Because null already meant something else — it had been imported from Java meaning deliberately no object (Resolution 5, Section 2). Merging them would have destroyed a distinction that turns out to be genuinely useful:

const config = { retries: null };

config.retries        // null      — the key exists; someone set it to nothing
config.timeout        // undefined — there is no such key

"retries" in config   // true
"timeout" in config   // false

"The server explicitly sent no value for this field" and "the server did not send this field" are different facts, and JavaScript can express both. Most languages cannot without extra machinery.

The distinction is load-bearing in real APIs. Default parameters trigger on undefined only:

function f(x = 10) { return x; }
f();            // 10 — nothing passed
f(undefined);   // 10 — explicitly "nothing"
f(null);        // null — null is a value, and defaults do not fire

And ?? and ?. (ES2020) treat exactly these two as "absent," which is why x ?? 5 differs from x || 5: the former only falls through for null and undefined, the latter for all eight falsy values, including 0 and "".

One historical oddity worth knowing, because you will see the workaround in old code. null is a literal — part of the grammar, unforgeable. undefined is not. It is an ordinary property of the global object, and in ES3 it was writable. This was legal and catastrophic:

var undefined = 5;                    // ES3: this worked
if (x === undefined) { ... }          // now comparing against 5

Which is why careful code used void 0 — an expression guaranteed to evaluate to the real undefined — and why the jQuery-era library wrapper looked like this:

(function (window, document, undefined) {
  // `undefined` is a parameter with nothing passed to it,
  // so it is guaranteed to be genuinely undefined in here
})(window, document);

ES5 (2009) made the global undefined non-writable and non-configurable, which closed the global hole. You can still shadow it with a local binding, which is why that idiom worked at all.

And the asymmetry that ties back to Resolution 5: typeof undefined is "undefined", correctly, because undefined's internal representation did not collide with the object tag. typeof null is "object", incorrectly, because null's did. Two absences, one accurate, one not, for reasons of bit patterns.

Section 11 — Where null came from: a precise date and a public apology

You noticed null is not JavaScript's. It is not, and it has one of the best-documented origins in computing.

Tony Hoare introduced the null reference in 1965, in ALGOL W. He has explained why with unusual candour: he was designing a type system meant to guarantee that all reference use was safe, checked by the compiler — and he put in the null reference "simply because it was so easy to implement."

In 2009, at QCon London, he called it his "billion-dollar mistake," and the estimate was conservative — his reasoning being that it has caused "innumerable errors, vulnerabilities, and system crashes, which have probably caused a billion dollars of pain and damage in the last forty years."

Why "easy to implement" is the whole story connects directly to Resolution 5, Section 1. A reference is an address. You need a value meaning "points at nothing." Address zero is never a valid object address, so it is sitting right there, free. No extra storage, no extra check. That is the same fact that produced typeof null === "object": JavaScript's null is a machine null pointer, and its zero bits collided with the object tag. One 1965 convenience produced both the billion-dollar mistake and JavaScript's most notorious wart.

Why it is a mistake, stated precisely. Null makes every reference type secretly a union without saying so. When a function signature says it returns a String, it is lying — it returns "a String, or nothing," and the compiler will not make you handle the second case. So every dereference is a potential crash, and the crash happens at runtime, far from the code that was actually wrong.

What later languages did instead — and this matters for you specifically, because you are studying TypeScript. The modern answer is to make absence part of the type and force you to deal with it:

-- Haskell / ML
Maybe String          -- either Just "x" or Nothing; you must handle both

// Rust
Option<String>        // Some(s) or None; the compiler will not let you skip it

// Swift, Kotlin
String?               // nullable, and dereferencing requires unwrapping

// TypeScript, with strictNullChecks on
let a: string = null;         // error — string does not include null
let b: string | null = null;  // fine, and every use must narrow first

TypeScript's strictNullChecks is Hoare's mistake being retrofitted onto JavaScript from outside, sixty years later. It is one of the highest-value things TypeScript does, and it is worth knowing that this is the problem it is solving.

And C++ specifically, since you raised it. C used a NULL macro that was literally 0, which caused real bugs — f(NULL) could resolve to the int overload rather than the pointer one, because NULL genuinely was an integer. C++11 added nullptr, a value with its own type std::nullptr_t, purely to fix that. Even the fix for null needed a fix.

What null is actually for in JavaScript, since it does have legitimate jobs:

document.getElementById("nope")     // null — I looked, there was nothing
"abc".match(/z/)                    // null — same
this.cache = null;                  // explicitly clearing a reference
Object.create(null)                 // an object with no prototype
Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype) === null   // the end of every chain

That last one is structural rather than conventional: null is what terminates the prototype chain, so it is load-bearing in the object model itself, not just an API convention.

Section 12 — The practical rule

Since the two absences are a real distinction and not merely historical clutter:

  • Let the language produce undefined. It means "nothing was ever here." Do not assign it by hand.
  • Assign null yourself when you mean "I deliberately have no value for this." It is the one that carries intent.
  • Test for either with x == null — the single legitimate use of loose equality, because null == undefined is true and neither equals anything else. This was designed, not accidental.
  • Use ?? and ?. when you want "absent" to mean exactly these two and not 0 or "".
  • Use typeof x === "undefined" only for identifiers that may not be declared at all — Resolution 5, Section 6.

What this resolves

How were the seven shortlisted?Section 1: they were not. There were five in 1995, for twenty years. Symbol arrived in 2015, BigInt in 2020. "Seven" is a fact about 2020.
How was it decided they were sufficient?Sections 1 and 6: it was not decided, and they were not sufficient — the set grew twice. What made five workable was that Object is the extension point, so user-defined structure never needed a new type.
Why one Number type?Section 2: the best decision of the ten days. C offered eleven numeric types; the intended audience could not be asked to choose. A double holds every integer to 2⁵³ exactly. It also caused 0.1 + 0.2 and eventually forced BigInt.
My theory of what types are forSection 3: correct, including the last step you were unsure of. The bits carry nothing; the instruction imposes the interpretation — ADD versus ADDSD. A type system is the mechanism that picks the instruction for you. Error-catching is a consequence, not the purpose.
The consequence of thatSection 4: static languages decide at compile time and erase the types; dynamic languages must tag every value and branch at every operation. V8's inline caches and hidden classes are an attempt to recover the static arrangement by guessing — which is why "don't change a variable's type" is real advice.
Where are types used in JavaScript?Section 5: your difficulty was not ignorance — JavaScript source contains no type annotations at all. Types surface only as runtime tags, typeof, coercion, and a few TypeErrors. Coercion is the type system seen from outside, which is why this node pairs them.
Could you make custom types?Section 6: constructor functions and prototypes worked from day one — but typeof still says "object" forever. The eight types are a closed set, which is why instanceof, Array.isArray and Symbol.toStringTag exist as a second classification layer, and why instanceof fails across iframes.
Why Symbol?Section 7: the only type added purely for backwards compatibility. The language needed hooks like Symbol.iterator that could not collide with any string key anyone had already used.
Why BigInt?Section 8: integers stop being exact above 2⁵³, and Number could not be changed. Note that 1n + 1 throws — the one place this language refuses to coerce, because coercing would destroy the point.
Why Boolean at all?Section 9: honestly, it did not have to be. C managed without one until C99; Python's is a subclass of int. And JavaScript undercuts it with truthiness — eight falsy values, everything else true, and if accepts any type.
Where did undefined come from?Section 10: it is structurally required by a language that refuses to error on unassigned variables, missing properties, absent parameters and empty returns. Kept separate from null because "no such key" and "key set to nothing" are different facts. Plus the ES3 hole where var undefined = 5 worked, and the void 0 and IIFE-parameter workarounds it produced.
Where did null come from?Section 11: Tony Hoare, ALGOL W, 1965, added "simply because it was so easy to implement," and called his billion-dollar mistake at QCon London in 2009. "Easy to implement" means address zero was free — the same fact that gave JavaScript typeof null === "object". Modern answers are Maybe, Option<T>, T?, and TypeScript's strictNullChecks, which is this mistake being retrofitted from outside.
What to actually doSection 12

Eight asks. The fifth one you had already answered yourself.

pieces.title: Resolution 8 — Q9: why primitives cannot be mutated, and why copying them is free
pieces.content:
Resolution 5, Section 5 established what the rule is — primitives are immutable and compared by value, and "atomic" is the wrong criterion because strings have parts. This follow-up asks a different and better question: why. Why can they not be mutated, why does assignment copy, what were the alternatives, and — the framing you keep returning to — was this decided by people who could have decided otherwise?

That last question has a real answer here, and it is not the one you have been assuming. Most of this was not a design decision. It was forced. Section 8 separates the parts that were genuinely chosen from the parts that could not have gone any other way, because telling those apart is a skill worth having generally.

The asks:

  1. What does "no parts" actually mean? You proposed: an object is a cluster of key-value pairs and each pair is a property, whereas a primitive has nothing dividable. Section 1 — you are one word away from the precise version.
  2. Why can primitives not be mutated, and why was that decided? Sections 2 and 3.
  3. Why does copying produce an independent copy, and why was it needed? Sections 4 and 5 — the answer is that it is free, and the reason it is free is ask 2.
  4. What were the other options, and what were the issues with them? Section 6 — all three alternatives are real, shipped languages.

Section 1 — "No parts": the word you are reaching for is slot

Your formulation is right and needs one term to become exact. You said an object is a cluster of key-value pairs, each pair being a property, and that primitives have no equivalent. The precise version is:

An object is a container of addressable, writable locations. A primitive is a value with no locations in it.

The word for such a location is a slot, and the test is not "does this thing have parts" but "can I point at a part and write to it."

const o = { a: 1 };
o.a = 2;         // `o.a` names a slot. This writes to it.

const s = "hello";
s[0] = "H";      // `s[0]` does not name a slot. Nothing happens.
s.length = 2;    // nor does this. Nothing happens.

And here is the distinction that makes Resolution 5's correction and your intuition fit together, which is the thing you were circling. A string's "parts" are computed, not stored.

const s = "hello";
s[0]        // "h" — this does not read a slot out of s.
            // It CONSTRUCTS a new one-character string and returns it.
s.length    // 5   — a derived fact about the value, not a field in a record.

s[0] is a question whose answer is a fresh value. o.a is a place. That is why s[0] = "H" is meaningless while o.a = 2 works: you cannot assign to the answer of a question.

So the card's "no parts" is defensible if read as "no slots," and misleading if read as "indivisible" — which is exactly why Resolution 5 rejected the atomic reading. Your instinct that the object's dividedness is the significant thing was correct; the significant thing is specifically that its divisions are writable.

Section 2 — Why primitives cannot be mutated: there is nothing there to mutate

You framed this as a rule someone imposed. Try to imagine the alternative and it comes apart in your hands.

Suppose you could mutate a number. What would that mean?

let a = 5;
let b = 5;

mutate(a, 6);      // hypothetically: change the number 5 into 6

console.log(b);    // ...6?
console.log(2 + 3) // ...6??

The question is not "would this be a bad idea." The question is: what is being changed? There is no object called "the 5" sitting in memory that a and b both refer to. There is not one 5 that could be edited, nor a distinguishable set of separate 5s. Five is not a thing at a location; it is a value.

The concept that makes this precise is identity. An object has identity — a "which one" that persists independently of its contents:

const p = {};
const q = {};
p === q            // false — identical contents, different objects

const r = p;
r === p            // true — the same object, reached by two names
r.x = 1;
p.x                // 1 — because it is the same thing

A primitive has no identity. There is no "this 5" as distinct from "that 5":

5 === 5                // true, necessarily
"abc" === "abc"        // true, necessarily
// there is no way to construct two distinguishable 5s.

And now the point:

Mutation requires identity. To change something, there must be a something that survives the change — that is the same thing before and after, but different. A value with no identity cannot be changed, because there is nothing that persists through the change to be the subject of it.

So immutability is not a restriction placed on primitives. It is a consequence of them being values rather than things. Nobody decided it for numbers, booleans, symbols, bigints, null or undefined, because there was no decision available. Any language in which 5 is a value rather than an object has immutable numbers automatically.

Which is also, incidentally, why NaN !== NaN is such an odd wart: it is the one primitive value that fails the "compared by value" rule, and it fails it because IEEE-754 says so, not because JavaScript wanted it.

Section 3 — Strings are the case where it genuinely was a choice

Section 2 is airtight for numbers and booleans. It is not airtight for strings, and this is where your instinct that someone decided something is correct.

A string has length. It has indexable positions. It occupies a contiguous run of memory. It looks exactly like the sort of thing you could edit in place — and in several languages, you can.

/* C — a string is literally a mutable array of bytes */
char s[] = "hello";
s[0] = 'H';              /* works. The memory changed. */
# Ruby — strings are mutable OBJECTS
s = "hello"
t = s                    # t and s are the same string object
s << " world"            # mutates in place
puts t                   # "hello world"  ← t changed too

Ruby is the important counter-example, because it is a modern, high-level, garbage-collected language that made the opposite call and shipped it. So mutable strings are possible. The question is what they cost — and Ruby is the evidence, because Ruby has spent years walking it back: String#freeze, the frozen_string_literal magic comment, and a long-running effort to make string literals frozen by default. The language that chose mutability is trying to get back.

Three reasons JavaScript's choice was the right one, and the third is the one that matters most for your third ask.

Reason 1 — shared references become safe. If a string can never change, then handing the same string to ten different places is risk-free. Nobody can pull it out from under anyone. In Ruby, passing a string to a function means the function might modify your string, which is why defensive .dup calls are idiomatic there and unnecessary here.

Reason 2 — property lookup depends on it. Object property keys are strings, and objects are hash tables. A hash table computes a key's hash once and files the entry accordingly. If a string could be mutated after being used as a key, the entry would be filed under a hash that no longer matches the key, and the table would be silently corrupted. Every property access in JavaScript rests on string immutability. Engines also intern strings — storing one copy of each distinct string and comparing by pointer — which is only sound if strings cannot change.

Reason 3 — it makes copying free. That is Section 4.

Section 4 — Why assignment produces an independent copy, and why it costs nothing

Your third ask, and the answer has a twist: the copy is a guarantee, not an operation. Most of the time nothing is copied at all.

Start with the easy case:

let a = 5;
let b = a;
b = 6;
a;            // 5

Here the engine really does copy — one tagged machine word, eight bytes, a single instruction. There is no cheaper way to do anything, so "copy by value" for numbers is not a policy with a cost; it is the cheapest possible implementation.

Now the case that looks expensive:

let s = "a very long string, perhaps a megabyte of text...";
let t = s;

Does the engine duplicate a megabyte? No. It copies a pointer. s and t refer to the same bytes in memory.

And you can never tell. There is no experiment you can run that distinguishes "these are two independent copies" from "these are two names for the same immutable buffer" — because the only way to tell would be to modify one and see whether the other changed, and modification is impossible. So:

When a value cannot change, copy-by-value and copy-by-reference are indistinguishable. The language can promise the semantics of copying and implement the efficiency of sharing.

That is the real answer to "why was this needed." It was not needed in the sense of being paid for. Value semantics for primitives are free, and immutability is what makes them free. Engines go further and use ropes or slices for concatenation and slice, so even building strings often avoids copying — all legitimate because nothing observable depends on where the bytes live.

Objects cannot have this. An object's whole purpose is that its slots can change, so two names must be able to see each other's writes, so the reference has to be shared, and the sharing is observable. There is no free lunch available on that side.

Section 5 — The three properties in the card are one property

The card lists three things — no parts, cannot be mutated, copying produces an independent copy — as though they were three separate facts to memorise. They are not. They are one fact, stated at three levels, and each implies the next:

A primitive is a value, not a thing.
        ↓  (a value has no location, so nothing can point at a part of it)
It has no writable slots.                          ← "no parts"
        ↓  (mutation requires an identity to be the subject of the change)
It cannot be mutated.                              ← immutability
        ↓  (if it cannot change, sharing is unobservable)
Copying and sharing are indistinguishable.         ← value semantics

Read it upward and it works too: value semantics are safe because of immutability; immutability is inevitable because there are no slots; there are no slots because a value is not a container. One property, three faces — the same shape as Resolution 6's "nothing can interrupt my code" and "my slow code freezes the page."

Section 6 — The alternatives, all of which are real languages

You asked what the other options were and what their issues are. There are exactly three, and each is shipped and in wide use, so we can look at what actually happened rather than speculate.

Alternative A — make everything an object, including numbers

Smalltalk did this, Ruby does it, and Python does it: in CPython, the integer 5 is a heap-allocated PyLongObject with a reference count and a type pointer. It is a real object with a real address.

The cost is performance, and it is severe. Every integer is a heap allocation. Every arithmetic operation dereferences pointers, allocates a result object, and adjusts reference counts. This is a large part of why CPython arithmetic is roughly an order of magnitude slower than JavaScript's, and why numeric Python is really NumPy — a C library that stores unboxed machine numbers precisely to escape this.

And it leaks the abstraction in a way that is worth seeing, because it is the exact failure JavaScript avoided. CPython mitigates the cost by preallocating and sharing small integers — the range −5 to 256 — so they are not reallocated constantly. Which produces this:

# CPython
a = 256; b = 256
a is b        # True   — both names point at the shared cached object

a = 257; b = 257
a is b        # False  — two separately allocated objects

a == b        # True   — equal in value, either way

Identity of an integer becomes an implementation detail of the interpreter's caching strategy, observable from the language. That is what happens when you give values identity: you now have to answer "is this the same 257 as that 257," and there is no good answer. JavaScript never has to, because === on numbers compares values and there is no is.

Alternative B — make everything a value, including objects

The opposite extreme: assignment always copies, so there is no aliasing anywhere. C structs work this way, C++ classes do by default, and Swift's structs are a modern, deliberate version of it.

// Swift — a struct has value semantics
struct Point { var x: Int; var y: Int }
var a = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
var b = a          // a full copy
b.x = 99
a.x                // still 1

Two problems for JavaScript specifically.

Cost. Passing an object to a function would copy it, every time, however large. Swift makes this bearable with copy-on-write — share until someone writes — which is sophisticated machinery, and note that it is the same trick as Section 4 running in reverse. Not something available in ten days in 1995.

And it makes the DOM impossible. This is the decisive one. Consider:

const el = document.getElementById("title");
el.textContent = "Changed";

Under value semantics, getElementById would hand you a copy of the element, and writing to it would change your copy while the page sat there unaltered. Everything the language was built to do — reach into the page the browser has already built and change it, per Resolution 2, Section 3 — requires that you get the element, not a picture of it. Reference semantics for objects is not a preference; it is what makes the DOM work at all.

Alternative C — primitives by value, but mutable

Ruby's strings, from Section 3. The issues are the three reasons in that section, and the evidence against it is Ruby's own retreat toward frozen literals.

What JavaScript picked

The pragmatic split that almost every mainstream language has converged on: small, identity-less values by value; large, identity-bearing containers by reference. Java has exactly this (primitives versus objects, with String immutable and StringBuilder for building). C# has it. Python has the immutability half but not the unboxed half. The convergence is a decent sign the split is right rather than arbitrary.

Section 7 — What this actually does to your code

Four consequences you will meet constantly.

1. The pass-by-reference confusion, resolved. People say "JavaScript passes objects by reference." That is not quite right, and the precise version explains a bug everyone hits:

function mutate(o) { o.a = 1; }      // mutates YOUR object — visible outside
function rebind(o) { o = { a: 1 }; } // reassigns the parameter — invisible outside

const x = {};
mutate(x);  x.a;   // 1
rebind(x);  x.a;   // 1 — unchanged; rebind did nothing to x

If JavaScript were truly pass-by-reference, rebind would replace your object. It does not. JavaScript is always pass-by-value — it is just that for objects, the value being passed is a reference. The parameter is a fresh variable holding a copy of that reference; you can follow it to the shared object, but reassigning it only repoints your copy. The name for this in the literature is call-by-sharing, from Barbara Liskov's work on CLU, and it is what Python, Java and Ruby all do too.

2. Why const does not freeze objects. Resolution 4, Section 2 stated this; now the reason is visible. const protects the binding — the slot the variable name refers to. The object's own slots are a different set of locations entirely, and nothing about the variable declaration reaches them.

const a = { n: 1 };
a.n = 2;              // fine — a different slot
a = { n: 3 };         // TypeError — the binding is const
Object.freeze(a);     // now a.n = 4 does nothing (throws in strict mode)
                      // and it is SHALLOW — a.nested is still mutable

3. Comparing and copying.

[1, 2] === [1, 2]              // false — two objects, different identities
{ a: 1 } === { a: 1 }          // false

const shallow = { ...o };            // top level copied, nested still shared
const shallow2 = Object.assign({}, o);
const deep = structuredClone(o);     // a real deep copy — ES2021 / browsers 2022

JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(o))        // the old deep-copy hack; loses Dates,
                                     // undefined, functions, Map/Set, and
                                     // throws on cycles. structuredClone does not.

4. The default-parameter trap, which is this section in miniature:

function add(item, list = []) { list.push(item); return list; }
add(1);   // [1]
add(2);   // [2] — a NEW array each call, because the default expression re-evaluates

const shared = [];
function bad(item, list = shared) { list.push(item); return list; }
bad(1); bad(2);   // [1, 2] — one array, shared across calls

Section 8 — Your real question: what was decided, and what was forced?

You have now asked some version of this four times across these follow-ups — ultimately everything was in the hands of the people designing the language, so why was it done this way? It is a good habit and it deserves a direct answer, because here the honest reply is that most of this was not available to be decided.

Primitives have no identityForced. It follows from being a value rather than a thing. No language can give 5 an identity without making it an object — and if it does, it gets Python's 256 is 256 problem.
Numbers, booleans, symbols cannot be mutatedForced. Mutation needs a subject that persists through the change. There is none.
Primitives copy on assignmentForced, and free. Given immutability, copying and sharing are indistinguishable, so the semantics cost nothing to promise.
Strings are immutableChosen. Ruby and C chose otherwise. The reasons were safe sharing, hash-key integrity and interning — and Ruby's ongoing move to frozen literals suggests the choice was right.
Objects are by referenceChosen — but with no real alternative. Value semantics for objects would have made the DOM impossible, which was the entire point of the language.

So of five properties, three were consequences and two were choices, and one of the two had only one workable answer. That is a genuinely different situation from, say, the three declaration forms in Resolution 4, every one of which was a decision that could have gone otherwise.

The general skill is worth naming, because it will make the rest of this landscape faster to read: when something in a language looks arbitrary, first ask whether it could have been different. Some things — var's hoisting, typeof null, =='s rules, three ways to declare a variable — are historical accidents that a different Tuesday would have changed. Others — value semantics, run-to-completion, immutable primitives — are load-bearing consequences that any language making the same initial commitments would arrive at independently. The first kind you memorise. The second kind you can derive, and once derived, never need to memorise again.

What this resolves

What does "no parts" mean?Section 1: not "indivisible" (Resolution 5 rejected that — strings have parts) but no writable slots. o.a names a place; s[0] asks a question and gets a fresh value back. Your key-value-pair intuition was right; the operative word is that the divisions are addressable and writable.
Why can primitives not be mutated?Section 2: because there is nothing there to mutate. Mutation requires identity — a subject that persists through the change — and primitives have none. There is no "the 5." This was not decided; it is what "value" means.
Why was it decided that way?Section 3: for numbers and booleans it was not decided at all. For strings it genuinely was, and C and Ruby show the other path — safe sharing, hash-key integrity for every property lookup, and string interning are the three reasons, and Ruby's move toward frozen literals is the evidence.
Why does copying produce an independent copy?Section 4: because it is free. For numbers it is one machine word. For strings nothing is copied at all — the engine shares the buffer, and you cannot tell, because telling would require mutating. When a value cannot change, copy-by-value and copy-by-reference are indistinguishable.
Are these three separate rules?Section 5: no — one property with three faces. Value, therefore no slots, therefore immutable, therefore copying is unobservable.
What were the alternatives?Section 6: all three are shipped languages. Everything an object (Python — heap-allocated integers, and a is b being True at 256 and False at 257). Everything a value (C, Swift structs — and it would have made the DOM impossible, since getElementById would hand you a copy). Mutable primitives (Ruby, retreating).
What it does to my codeSection 7: JavaScript is always pass-by-value — for objects the value is a reference, which is why o.a = 1 inside a function is visible and o = {} is not. The term is call-by-sharing. Plus why const does not freeze, and structuredClone versus the JSON hack.
Was this in the designers' hands?Section 8: three of the five properties were forced, two were chosen, and one of those two had only one workable answer. And the general skill — distinguishing accidents you must memorise from consequences you can derive.

Four asks. The answer to the biggest one is that nobody decided it.

pieces.title: Resolution 9 — Q10: why there is no separate integer type
pieces.content:
This follow-up does something the earlier ones did not: you supplied a candidate answer and asked me to check it. Your candidate is that the language was written in a hurry, nobody expected it to matter, and by the time anyone cared it was frozen by deployed code. That explanation is correct about a great many things in JavaScript — Resolution 3 spent 41,000 characters on them. It is wrong about this one, and the fact that it is wrong here is the most useful thing in this piece.

The single number type was not an accident that got stuck. It was a decision, it was made for reasons that were articulated at the time, it was ratified by a standards committee two years later with full freedom to change it, and when a second numeric type was finally added in 2020 — by a committee, with 25 years of hindsight and no deadline — they deliberately built it so that it will not mix with the first one. That last fact is the strongest evidence available that the 1995 choice was principled rather than rushed.

The asks:

  1. Is the "ten days plus backwards compatibility" explanation the reason here? Section 1 — no, and Section 11 shows how to tell this class of thing apart from the accidents.
  2. Why is there no separate integer type? Sections 2, 3 and 4 — three independent reasons, any one of which would have been sufficient on its own.
  3. Why no char, float, long, double — the whole ladder other languages have? Section 5, one type at a time, including the one whose absence genuinely hurts.
  4. Why a single number type only — what did it buy, and what did it cost? Sections 6 through 9: the engine secretly has integers anyway, the language leaks int32 in exactly one place, here is the honest bill, and here is the repair that finally shipped.

Section 1 — Your candidate answer, tested

Let me state your candidate precisely, because it deserves to be taken seriously rather than waved at:

Brendan Eich wrote the prototype in ten days in May 1995. Nobody expected the language to become universal. Once it shipped and pages depended on it, changing anything would break deployed content — so the shortcuts of the first fortnight became permanent.

Every clause of that is factually true. The prototype — internally called Mocha — was written in roughly ten days in May 1995. It shipped as LiveScript in the Netscape Navigator 2.0 beta in September 1995, and was renamed JavaScript on 4 December 1995 in a joint Netscape/Sun press release, for marketing reasons that had nothing to do with the language. And the don't-break-the-web constraint is real and permanent; it is why typeof null === "object" survived a formal proposal to fix it, and why var's hoisting could only be routed around with let rather than repaired.

So why does it not explain the number type? Three tests, and it fails all three.

Test 1 — did it get a second chance with the constraint lifted? Yes. In November 1996 Netscape submitted JavaScript to Ecma International for standardisation. TC39 — with Microsoft, Netscape, Sun, Borland and others in the room — produced ECMA-262 1st edition in June 1997. The committee was not writing a browser; it was writing a specification, and it argued about a great many things. The single number type was not one of the fights. Section 8.5 of ECMA-262 1st edition simply states that the Number type consists of the IEEE 754 double-precision 64-bit values, and moves on. When people have to live with an accident, you can hear it in the spec text — the typeof null table entry reads like an apology. This one does not.

Test 2 — was an escape hatch added later? This is the reliable tell. When something in JavaScript really is a frozen mistake, the language grows a parallel mechanism beside it and tells you to use the new one: var got let and const; == got ===; sloppy mode got "use strict"; the mutable-arguments mess got rest parameters. In thirty years, nothing was ever added as an alternative to Number for ordinary arithmetic. BigInt (Section 9) is not that — it is an extension for a range doubles genuinely cannot reach, and it is deliberately not usable as a general replacement.

Test 3 — was it an unusual choice at the time? No, and this is the part your candidate answer cannot accommodate at all. A rushed decision looks idiosyncratic. This one was the conventional choice for the category of language Eich was writing:

  • AWK (1977): every number is a double. No integer type at all.
  • Perl (1987): one scalar numeric notion presented to the programmer; the interpreter keeps an integer slot internally as an optimisation, and you are not supposed to notice.
  • Lua (1993): every number is a double, for versions 1.0 through 5.2 — twenty-two years. Section 10 covers what happened when they changed their minds.
  • Tcl (1988): everything is nominally a string, converted on use.
  • HyperTalk (1987), Apple's HyperCard language and an explicit influence on the "scripting for page authors" brief: values are untyped text, coerced to numbers when arithmetic asks for it.

Eich was hired to put Scheme in the browser and then told, after the Sun deal, to make it look like Java. Scheme has a numeric tower — exact integers, rationals, reals — and he did not take it. Java has eight primitive types, and he did not take those either. He took the scripting-language convention, which by 1995 was well-established and had a body of experience behind it.

Verdict: ten days explains the bugs. It does not explain the architecture. The number type is architecture. Now the actual reasons.

Section 2 — Multiple numeric types are a feature of declarations, and JavaScript has no declarations

This is the structural reason, and it is the one that is almost never stated, so start here.

Ask why C and Java have byte, short, int, long, float, double. The answer is not "because programmers want variety." It is that in a statically typed language, you have to tell the compiler how many bytes to reserve before the program runs. The type is not decoration on the variable; it is the allocation instruction.

// Java, 1995
int    count = 0;      // reserve 4 bytes, integer layout
long   id    = 0L;     // reserve 8 bytes, integer layout
double ratio = 0.0;    // reserve 8 bytes, IEEE 754 layout
char   c     = 'x';    // reserve 2 bytes, UTF-16 code unit

Each declaration is a promise: this location will hold that shape forever. The compiler can then emit iadd for one and dadd for another, because it knows statically which is which.

Now write the same thing in JavaScript, and notice there is nowhere to put the information:

var count = 0;
var ratio = 0.0;

There is no declared type. var says "a binding exists"; it says nothing about shape. So if the language had both an integer type and a double type, the type of a variable would have to be inferred from whatever literal happened to be assigned to it — and then silently changed by arithmetic:

var x = 10;      // integer, presumably, because the literal has no point
var y = x / 4;   // ...and now what? 2, or 2.5?
x = x / 4;       // does x change type mid-life? does it truncate?
var z = 10.0;    // a different type from 10? in a language with no declarations?

Every one of those questions has an answer in C, and the answer is written at the declaration site. In a language with no declaration sites, the answers have to be invented as implicit conversion rules — which means the language grows a promotion lattice that fires invisibly on every arithmetic operator.

C's version of that lattice is called the usual arithmetic conversions, and it is one of the most notorious sources of quiet bugs in the language: integer promotion turns char and short into int; signed meeting unsigned converts the signed one, which is why -1 < 1u is false in C. That is a language where the programmer wrote the types down explicitly and it still surprises people. Handing that machinery to someone writing a fifteen-line form validator in 1996, with no type annotations anywhere to make the conversion visible, would have been indefensible.

So the structural claim, which is stronger than a preference: a dynamically typed language with no declarations cannot afford more than one numeric type without paying for it in implicit conversions at every operator. Section 9 is the proof — when JavaScript finally did add a second numeric type, the committee's solution to the promotion problem was to refuse to have one.

Section 3 — Integer division, which would have decided it on its own

Now the pedestrian reason, which is probably the one that actually settled it in Eich's head in May 1995, because it is about the audience.

In C and Java, / on two integers is integer division. It truncates.

// Java
int a = 10, b = 4;
System.out.println(a / b);        // 2
System.out.println(1 / 2);        // 0
System.out.println(3 * (1 / 2));  // 0

double pct = 45 / 100;            // 0.0  — the division happened
                                  // in integer-land BEFORE the assignment
System.out.println(pct * 100);    // 0.0

That last one is the classic. It is not a beginner's confusion you grow out of; experienced Java programmers still write it. The type of the expression is decided by the operands, not by what the result is being stored into, so the precision is destroyed before the assignment ever happens.

Now recall who JavaScript was for. Not systems programmers — that was Java's job in the Netscape strategy, and JavaScript's stated role in the December 1995 press release was the complementary one: a scripting language for page authors and designers, people wiring up forms and rollovers, many of whom had never compiled anything. For that audience:

// The 1996 reality: a form validator
var price = 45;
var total = 100;
var percentage = price / total * 100;   // 45 — and it had better be 45

If 45 / 100 had evaluated to 0 because both literals were written without a decimal point, the language would have been unusable by the people it was written for. And the fix in a typed language — "write 45.0" — requires the author to already understand a type system that JavaScript deliberately does not expose.

With one number type, division is division:

10 / 4        // 2.5
1 / 2         // 0.5
45 / 100      // 0.45
7 / 7         // 1     — and it is exactly 1, not 0.9999...

The cost is that you must ask for truncation when you want it, which is the trade the language made:

Math.floor(10 / 4)   // 2   — rounds toward -Infinity
Math.trunc(10 / 4)   // 2   — rounds toward zero (ES2015)
(10 / 4) | 0         // 2   — the int32 seam, Section 7
~~(10 / 4)           // 2   — same thing, older idiom

This is a good trade in exactly the way that matters: the mistake it prevents is silent, and the inconvenience it introduces is loud. Forgetting Math.floor gives you 2.5 where you wanted 2, and you see it immediately. Forgetting 45.0 in Java gives you 0 and a report that looks plausible.

The strength of this argument is best measured by who else came to agree with it. Python changed / to always produce a float in Python 3 — PEP 238, written in 2001, shipped in Python 3.0 in December 2008 — and added // for the truncating case. That was a deliberately breaking change to the most-used operator in the language, accepted because integer division was judged to surprise people more than it helped them. JavaScript simply never had the problem.

Section 4 — Why a double is the right single type: it contains the integers

Granting one numeric type, why this one? If you must pick one, why not integers, which are what most programs count with?

Because a double is not an approximation of an integer. Within its range, a double represents integers exactly — and the fact that people believe otherwise is the single most common misconception about JavaScript numbers.

A 64-bit IEEE 754 double is laid out as 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, and 52 stored fraction bits. Because normalised numbers have an implicit leading 1, the significand carries 53 bits of precision. Any integer that fits in 53 bits is stored with zero error — not "very close," not "usually fine," exactly. Q11's follow-up is about this layout and I will do it properly there; what matters here is the consequence:

Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER        // 9007199254740991   === 2**53 - 1
Number.isInteger(42)           // true
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3              // false  — fractions are lossy
1 + 2 === 3                    // true   — integers are not
999999999999 * 2 === 1999999999998   // true, exactly

Nine quadrillion. To see what that buys, price the things a program actually counts:

  • Milliseconds since 1970: about 1.7 × 1012 — roughly five thousand times inside the safe range. Date is defined in the spec as a double holding whole milliseconds, and its range is ±8.64 × 1015 ms, about ±273,790 years around 1970.
  • Array indices: the spec caps array length at 232 − 1, about 4.3 × 109 — five thousand times inside the range.
  • Pixels, bytes in a file, rows in a table, characters in a document, money in cents: all far below 253. Nine quadrillion cents is ninety trillion dollars.

So the double is a superset. It gives you every integer any web-facing program was going to count with, exactly, and it gives you fractions, which the web needs constantly — percentages, opacities, positions, ratios, durations, coordinates. Choosing integers as the single type would have meant the language could not express 0.5. Choosing doubles meant the language could express both. There was no third candidate that dominated it.

And one more property that mattered specifically for a language whose source code is shipped to unknown machines: IEEE 754-1985 is bit-exact and portable. By 1995 hardware floating point was universal — the Intel 486DX (1989) integrated the FPU on-die, and the Pentium (1993) made it standard — so double arithmetic was both fast and identical everywhere. The specification can state exactly what 0.1 + 0.2 produces on every conforming implementation, because IEEE 754 pins the result down to the last bit. Had the language exposed a machine-dependent int — as C does, where int is 16, 32, or 64 bits depending on the platform — the same script would have computed different answers on a Mac and a PC. Java solved that by legislating exact widths; JavaScript solved it by having one width, already legislated by an international standard.

Section 5 — The rest of the ladder, one rung at a time

You listed char, float, double, long. Each is absent for its own reason, and they are not equally defensible.

char — absent because strings absorbed it. Resolution 7 covered this ground: JavaScript has no character type, and "a" is simply a string of length 1. This is not a JavaScript quirk — Python and Ruby have no character type either. A separate char only earns its place when you need a fixed-size scalar for array layout, which is a compilation concern. Its absence costs you nothing except that "abc"[0] allocates, which Resolution 8 Section 1 covered: s[0] constructs a fresh one-character string rather than reading a slot.

float (32-bit) — absent because its only advantage is memory. A float is not faster than a double on any FPU of the era; it is smaller, and less precise (24 bits of significand rather than 53). The only reason to want one is when you have a million of them. In 1995, a script manipulating a million numbers in a browser was not a scenario. When it became one — WebGL, audio, image processing — the language did not add a float type. It added typed arrays (Float32Array, Int32Array, Uint8Array; specified for WebGL in 2011, folded into the language in ES2015), which give you the storage layout without adding a scalar type. Read an element out of a Float32Array and you get an ordinary Number — the 32-bit-ness lives in the buffer, not in the value system. That is a genuinely elegant resolution: the memory-layout problem was solved with a memory-layout feature, not with a new number type.

double — present. It is the only one. The type is spelled number, and it is a double.

long / 64-bit integer — this is the real gap, and it hurt. A 64-bit integer needs 64 bits of precision; a double has 53. There is no encoding trick that fixes this, so integers above 253 cannot be represented, and — worse than being rejected — they are silently rounded:

9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993      // true. Both are 2**53.
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1 === Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2   // true

JSON.parse('{"id": 10765432100123456789}').id
// 10765432100123458000   — the ID is now a different ID

The famous casualty is Twitter. In 2010 Twitter moved to 64-bit Snowflake identifiers, and JavaScript clients started corrupting them: an ID would round to a nearby value and the tweet would not be found. The fix was not on the client side — it could not be — so the API began returning every ID twice, once as a JSON number and once as a string, in a field named id_str, with documentation telling JavaScript consumers to use the string. That pattern is now standard practice across the industry: if your database uses bigint primary keys, serialise them as strings, because JSON numbers are read as doubles by the most common consumer on earth.

The same limit is why nanosecond timestamps do not fit (nanoseconds since 1970 is about 1.7 × 1018, roughly 200 times past the safe range), which is why Node exposes process.hrtime.bigint() and why performance.now() returns fractional milliseconds instead of integer nanoseconds. Section 9 is the eventual fix.

decimal — never present in any mainstream dynamic language, and the reason money is hard. A base-2 float cannot represent 0.10 exactly, for the same reason base-10 cannot represent one third. That is Q11's territory and I will not spend it here. The practical rule, which follows directly from Section 4: store money as an integer number of the smallest unit — cents, paise — and you are exact up to 253 of them, which is ninety trillion dollars. The bug is not that JavaScript is bad at money; it is that binary floating point is bad at money, in every language that uses it, and JavaScript merely has no alternative type to reach for.

Section 6 — Underneath, the engine has integers anyway

Here is the part that resolves the performance objection before you raise it, and it is the most satisfying fact in this piece.

You might reasonably assume that if the language only has doubles, then for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) is doing floating-point arithmetic three million times and paying for it. It is not. Every production engine has integers internally; they are simply not observable.
