V8's mechanism is called a Smi — "SMall Integer" — and it works by pointer tagging. Every value in a V8 register or field is one machine word. Heap pointers are aligned, so their low bits are always zero, which leaves a bit free to carry meaning:

a 64-bit word in V8:

  ...xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx1     low bit 1  ->  a pointer to a heap object
  ...nnnnnnnnnnnnnnnnnnn0     low bit 0  ->  a Smi; the payload IS the integer

    +--------------------------------+---+
    |     integer payload            | 0 |     no allocation, no indirection
    +--------------------------------+---+

A Smi is not a heap object. It is not allocated, not garbage collected, not dereferenced — the number lives directly in the word. Its width depends on the build (31 bits with pointer compression, 32 bits on a classic 64-bit build), and any integer that fits is stored and added with ordinary hardware integer instructions. Only when a value escapes that range or acquires a fraction does the engine box it as a HeapNumber — a small heap object containing an actual 64-bit double.

SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore use a different trick to the same end, called NaN-boxing. IEEE 754 reserves an enormous space of bit patterns that all mean "not a number" — far more patterns than anyone needs — so those spare payloads are used to encode integers, pointers, null, undefined and booleans inside a 64-bit slot that is otherwise a double. A real double is stored as itself; everything else hides in the NaN space.

On top of that, optimising compilers do representation selection: V8's TurboFan will observe that a variable has only ever held small integers, compile the loop with raw machine integers and no tagging at all, and insert a guard that bails back to generic code if a double ever shows up.

Now, why is this legal? Because of Section 4. Since a double represents every integer under 253 exactly, the engine can compute with machine integers and produce bit-identical results to what double arithmetic would have produced. The optimisation is invisible because there is nothing to observe — which is the same argument, structurally, that Resolution 8 Section 4 made about string copying: the engine shares the buffer instead of copying it, and you cannot tell, because telling would require mutation.

So the answer to "did the single number type cost performance" is: the specification has one number type; the implementation has several; and the exactness of doubles over the integer range is precisely what lets the implementation hide them. Two decades of engine work went into this, and the language never had to grow a type to get it.

Section 7 — The one seam where int32 shows through

There is exactly one place where the language admits an integer exists, and it has been there since 1995: the bitwise operators.

&, |, ^, ~, <<, >> and >>> do not operate on doubles. The specification defines them to convert their operands with an abstract operation called ToInt32 (or ToUint32 for >>>), perform the operation on 32 bits, and convert the result back to a Number:

5.7  | 0        // 5           — truncates toward zero
-5.7 | 0        // -5
2147483647 | 0  // 2147483647  — 2**31 - 1, the top of int32
2147483648 | 0  // -2147483648 — wraps. This is signed 32-bit overflow.
4294967296 | 0  // 0           — 2**32 wraps to zero
NaN | 0         // 0
1e21 | 0        // 559939584    — meaningless, but specified exactly

-1 >>> 0        // 4294967295   — reinterpreted as unsigned 32-bit

Two things follow. First, | 0 and ~~ became the idiomatic truncation-to-integer, and that idiom was later formalised: asm.js (Mozilla, 2013) used x | 0 and +x as explicit type annotations, so that a whole subset of JavaScript became statically typed by convention and could be compiled ahead of time. The language's one integer seam was turned into an entire compilation target — and that lineage runs directly into WebAssembly, which does have i32 and i64 as real types, and which is where JavaScript ultimately put the numeric types it declined to have.

Second, note the wraparound above. Ordinary JavaScript arithmetic never wraps around. In C, INT_MAX + 1 is signed overflow — undefined behaviour, in practice a large negative number, and a whole category of security vulnerabilities. In JavaScript, exceeding the safe range costs you precision gradually and then gives you Infinity; it never silently becomes negative. That is a real safety property bought with the single type, and it is rarely credited.

Section 8 — The honest bill

Reasons are not a defence unless you also price the damage. Here is what the single number type actually costs, in order of how often it bites:

Fractional arithmetic is inexact0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. Not a JavaScript defect — every IEEE 754 language has it — but JavaScript has no Decimal to escape to. Q11.
Integers above 253 silently corruptThe Twitter class of bug. 64-bit database IDs, Snowflake IDs, nanosecond timestamps. Silent, and it survives a round trip through JSON. Fixed in 2020, Section 9.
No integer divisionMath.floor / Math.trunc / | 0 everywhere. Noisy but harmless.
Money needs a disciplineStore minor units as integers; never accumulate floats. Section 5.
Large-array memoryA naive array of a million numbers is boxed and pointer-chased. Answered by typed arrays rather than by a type.
No overflowThe one entry on the credit side. C's signed overflow is undefined behaviour and a vulnerability class; JavaScript's degradation is gradual and then Infinity.

One of those six is serious. The rest are inconveniences or non-JavaScript-specific. That is a defensible ledger for a decision made in ten days — and it is defensible precisely because it was not invented in ten days; it was borrowed from twenty years of scripting-language practice.

Section 9 — BigInt, and the fact that it refuses to mix

The 253 gap was eventually closed. BigInt reached Stage 4 at TC39 and shipped in Chrome 67 (May 2018), Node 10.4, Firefox 68 (July 2019) and Safari 14 (September 2020), and was standardised in ES2020. It is arbitrary-precision — no width limit, bounded only by memory — and it is a genuinely new primitive type, the eighth, which is why Resolution 5's type list has eight entries rather than seven:

const big = 9007199254740993n;   // the n suffix is the literal form
typeof big                        // "bigint"
big + 1n                          // 9007199254740994n — exact, no rounding
2n ** 128n                        // 340282366920938463463374607431768211456n

BigInt("10765432100123456789")    // exact from a string

Now the part that matters for your question. Watch what happens when you mix it with a Number:

1n + 1
// TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions

1n === 1     // false — different types
1n == 1      // true  — loose equality does convert
1n < 2       // true  — relational comparison is allowed, mathematically
Math.max(1n, 2n)                  // TypeError — Math is Number-only
JSON.stringify({ id: 1n })        // TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt

1n + 1 throwing is not an oversight. It is the entire design, and it was argued at length. The committee had every option available: they could have defined promotion rules, made BigInt the wider type, converted Numbers up automatically. They refused, because every possible automatic rule loses something silently. Convert the BigInt down to a Number and you lose precision — which is the exact bug BigInt exists to fix. Convert the Number up to a BigInt and you must decide what 1.5 becomes, and you lose the fraction. There is no promotion rule that is not a trap, so the language declines to have one and makes you write BigInt(x) or Number(x) and take responsibility for which loss you are accepting.

Which brings the whole question full circle. In 2020, a standards committee with twenty-five years of hindsight, no shipping deadline, and the freedom to design a numeric tower from scratch, looked at the problem of having two numeric types in a language without declarations — and concluded that they must not interoperate. That is Section 2's argument, independently rediscovered and ratified. It is very hard to look at that and still believe the 1995 single-type decision was merely a shortcut nobody had time to think about.

Section 10 — Everyone else who tried it the other way

Two natural experiments, both worth knowing, because they are the closest thing available to a controlled test of your question.

Lua added integers, and paid for it. Lua shipped with doubles only from 1993 through version 5.2. In Lua 5.3 (January 2015) the authors added an integer subtype — 64-bit — for exactly the reasons you would expect: bigger exact range, faster loops on embedded hardware. The consequences arrived immediately. Values now print differently (1 versus 1.0) even when mathematically equal. A new floor-division operator // had to be introduced alongside /, which now always produces a float. Integer overflow wraps around while float overflow goes to infinity, so the same expression has different failure modes depending on a subtype you cannot see. Conversion rules for table keys had to be written down: t[1] and t[1.0] must be the same key, so float keys with integral values are normalised to integers on insertion. None of that is fatal, and Lua 5.3 is a fine language — but the whole list is exactly the complexity budget Section 2 predicted, and JavaScript never spent any of it.

Python spent thirty years removing numeric distinctions. The traffic is all in one direction. Python 2 had int and long as separate types; PEP 237 merged them and Python 3 has only int, arbitrary precision, with the machine-word optimisation hidden inside the interpreter — the same hide-it-underneath move as V8's Smi. Then PEP 238 changed / to always return a float, a deliberately breaking change to the most-used operator in the language, because integer division was judged to cause more errors than it prevented. Python 3 is closer to JavaScript's 1995 numeric model than Python 2 was.

So: the one language that added integer types accumulated the complexity, and the one language that removed them moved toward JavaScript. That is not proof, but it is the best evidence a language design argument ever gets.

Section 11 — Forced or chosen? And what the card left out

Resolution 8 ended by separating the properties that were forced — no designer could have chosen otherwise — from the ones that were genuinely chosen. Same treatment here, because your question was explicitly about whether this was in the designers' hands.

That the language would use IEEE 754 doublesNear-forced. By 1995 it was the only portable, hardware-accelerated, internationally standardised, bit-exact real-number format. Any other choice means either machine-dependent results or software arithmetic.
That there would be exactly one numeric typeChosen — but heavily constrained by Section 2. A second type in a declaration-free language forces implicit promotion rules, and there is no set of those that does not silently lose data. ES2020 reached the same conclusion and refused to write them.
That the one type would be the double rather than an integerForced, given one type. The double contains the integers exactly up to 253; the integer does not contain 0.5. It strictly dominates.
That / would be true divisionA consequence of the above, and the thing Python later broke compatibility to acquire.
That bitwise operators would use int32Chosen — inherited from C and Java for familiarity. This one is the ten-days answer: it is a borrowed convenience, and it is why 2147483648 | 0 is negative.
That there would be no charChosen, and universal among dynamic languages. Costs nothing.
That 64-bit integers would be unreachableNot chosen at all — not foreseen. In 1995 nothing a browser touched had IDs above 253. This is the one place where "nobody expected it to blow up" is genuinely the right explanation, and it took until 2020 to fix.

So your candidate answer was not wrong — it was right about one row of seven, and it happens to be the row that hurt most. That is worth more than a flat yes or no: the ten-days story is a real explanatory tool, and the skill is knowing which parts of the language it actually reaches.

And a correction to our own card, since the format asks for these. Q10's answer says "There is a single number type." That was true when it was written in the sense everyone means it, and it is how the language is taught — but strictly, since ES2020 JavaScript has two numeric types, number and bigint, and Resolution 5 already listed eight primitives including BigInt. The precise statement is: JavaScript has a single number type for arithmetic — a 64-bit IEEE 754 double used for all values including whole numbers — plus a separate, deliberately non-interoperating arbitrary-precision integer type for the range doubles cannot represent. The card's phrasing is ES5-era shorthand and I should keep the distinction visible now that you have asked why the single type exists, because the exception is the best evidence for the rule.

What this resolves

Is it the "ten days + can't change it" answer?Section 1: no, and here are three tests it fails — TC39 ratified it unchanged in June 1997 with full freedom; no escape hatch was ever added beside it, unlike var→let or ==→===; and it was the conventional choice in 1995, matching AWK, Perl, Lua, Tcl and HyperTalk. Eich declined both Scheme's numeric tower and Java's eight primitives. Section 11 shows the one row where your candidate is the right answer.
Why no separate integer type?Three independent reasons. Section 2: multiple numeric types are a feature of declarations, and JavaScript has no declaration sites to hang them on — so a second type forces implicit promotion rules at every operator, the thing that makes C's usual arithmetic conversions notorious. Section 3: integer division. 45 / 100 === 0 in Java would have been fatal for the audience the language was written for. Section 4: a double already contains every integer up to 253 exactly, so integers were not given up.
Why the double specifically?Section 4: it strictly dominates. Exact integers to 9,007,199,254,740,991 and fractions, which the web needs constantly. Plus IEEE 754-1985 was bit-exact and portable, so a script computes the same answer on every machine — critical when the source is shipped to unknown hardware. C's int is machine-dependent; Java had to legislate widths.
Why no char, float, long?Section 5. char: absorbed by strings, as in Python and Ruby; costs nothing. float32: its only advantage is memory, and that was later solved by typed arrays rather than a scalar type — the layout problem got a layout feature. long: the real gap, and it caused the Twitter id_str class of bug — 64-bit IDs silently rounding. decimal: absent everywhere; store money as integer minor units.
Did one type cost performance?Section 6: no, because the engines have integers anyway. V8 tags Smis in the low bit of a machine word — unallocated, uncollected, added with hardware integer instructions; SpiderMonkey and JSC use NaN-boxing; TurboFan does representation selection with bail-out guards. This is only legal because doubles are exact over the integer range. The spec has one type; the implementation has several; you cannot tell.
Does an integer ever show through?Section 7: in exactly one place. Bitwise operators are specified via ToInt32, which is why 2147483648 | 0 is -2147483648 and -1 >>> 0 is 4294967295. That seam became x | 0 as a truncation idiom, then asm.js type annotations (2013), then WebAssembly's real i32/i64. Also: ordinary arithmetic never wraps around, unlike C's undefined signed overflow.
What did it cost?Section 8, itemised. One entry is serious (the 253 silent corruption), one is a credit (no overflow), the rest are inconveniences or are IEEE 754's fault rather than JavaScript's.
Was it ever fixed?Section 9: BigInt, ES2020 — Chrome 67 in May 2018, Safari 14 in September 2020. And the decisive detail: 1n + 1 throws, on purpose, because every possible promotion rule loses precision or range silently. A committee with 25 years of hindsight re-derived Section 2's argument and refused to write the conversion rules.
Did anyone try it the other way?Section 10. Lua 5.3 (2015) added integers and immediately needed a // operator, dual printing of 1 vs 1.0, two different overflow behaviours, and table-key normalisation. Python went the opposite way — PEP 237 merged int/long, PEP 238 made / always float, a deliberately breaking change. Python 3's numeric model is closer to JavaScript 1995 than Python 2's was.
Correction to the cardSection 11: "a single number type" is ES5-era shorthand. Since ES2020 there are two numeric types; the precise claim is one type for arithmetic, plus a deliberately non-interoperating BigInt for the range doubles cannot reach.

Your candidate answer was right about exactly one thing: nobody in 1995 imagined an ID larger than nine quadrillion. Everything else on this page was decided on purpose, and then decided the same way again in 1997 and in 2020.

pieces.title: Resolution 10 — Q11: floating point, from the bits up
pieces.content:
You said plainly that you have never properly understood floating point, and that this is not really a JavaScript question — it is a gap you have carried for a long time. So this piece does not start at 0.1 + 0.2. It starts at the bit level with the model you already have, checks it, corrects the one thing in it that is wrong, and builds up until the answer to 0.1 + 0.2 falls out with nothing left over.

You also proposed a specific design of your own — some bits for the part before the point, some for the part after, maybe a bit marking the point itself. That design is real, shipped, and named. Doom ran on it. Section 2 takes it seriously and then shows exactly what it cannot do, because understanding why fixed point fails is the only way to understand why floating point exists.

And there is a surprise at the end of the derivation that I did not expect when I started checking the arithmetic. 0.1 + 0.2 lands on a perfect tie — exactly halfway between two representable doubles — and which way it falls is decided by a tie-breaking rule from the 1985 standard. Under a different, equally reasonable rule, 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 would be true and this would not be the famous example that it is. Section 6.

The asks:

  1. Is my model of integers right? Bit combinations positionally define a number; for signed integers the most significant bit holds the sign and the rest hold the value. Section 1 — the first half is exactly right, the second half is a real scheme that hardware does not use, and the correction pays off twice later.
  2. Is floating point the same idea — some bits before the point, some after, maybe a bit for the point? Section 2 — that is fixed point, it is real, and here is precisely what kills it.
  3. Something about scientific notation — I half-remember it and do not understand it. Sections 3 and 4 — that memory is correct, and here is the whole layout, bit by bit, with a number encoded by hand.
  4. Why 0.1 + 0.2 specifically? Sections 5, 6 and 7 — three separate causes, and most explanations only give you the first.
  5. I have never truly understood precision generally. Sections 8 through 11 — the shape of the number line, the special values, what to actually do, and where the standard came from.

Section 1 — Your integer model, checked. One correction, and it matters.

The first half is exactly right. Binary is positional in the same way decimal is. In decimal each column is a power of ten; in binary each column is a power of two:

   1     0     1     1        (binary)
   |     |     |     |
   8     4     2     1        (column weights: 2^3 2^2 2^1 2^0)
   |           |     |
   8     +     2  +  1   =  11 (decimal)

Eight bits therefore give 28 = 256 distinct patterns, and if you read them all as unsigned you get 0 through 255. Nothing to correct there.

The second half is where the correction is. You said: for signed integers, the most significant bit is reserved to indicate positive or negative, and the remaining bits hold the value. That scheme has a name — it is called sign-magnitude — and it is a perfectly sensible design that people did build. But essentially no modern processor uses it for integers. Hardware uses two's complement, and the difference is not cosmetic.

In sign-magnitude, the top bit is a flag sitting outside the arithmetic. Two problems follow immediately:

sign-magnitude, 8 bits:

  0 0000000  =  +0
  1 0000000  =  -0        <- two different zeros. Are they equal?
                             does 0 == 0 need a special case in the CPU?

  0 0000101  =  +5
  1 0000101  =  -5

  now add +5 and -3. The adder cannot just add the bit patterns:
  it must compare magnitudes, decide which is larger, subtract the
  smaller from the larger, and then work out the sign of the result.

Two's complement solves both by removing the flag entirely. The top bit is not a sign marker; it is an ordinary positional column whose weight is negative:

two's complement, 8 bits — the column weights are:

  -128    64    32    16     8     4     2     1
    |
    +-- note the minus. This is a value column, not a flag.

  0 0000101 =        4+1        =    5
  1 1111011 = -128 +64+32+16+8+2+1 =  -5
  1 1111111 = -128 +64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = -1
  1 0000000 = -128                    = -128   <- no positive counterpart
  0 0000000 = 0                       <- exactly one zero

Now addition is just addition. 5 + (-5) is 00000101 + 11111011 = 100000000; the ninth bit falls off the end of the register and you are left with 00000000. The processor needs one adder circuit, and subtraction is addition of the complement. That is the whole reason the scheme won: it makes signed arithmetic free. The asymmetry is the visible fingerprint — the range is −128 to +127, one more negative than positive, because the single zero sits on the positive side.

You can see two's complement in JavaScript directly, in the one seam Resolution 9 Section 7 identified. Bitwise operators convert to signed 32-bit, so the top bit's negative weight is observable:

(-1 >>> 0).toString(2)
// "11111111111111111111111111111111"  — all ones is -1, not "negative 2^31-1"

2147483647 | 0     //  2147483647   (0111...111, the largest positive)
2147483648 | 0     // -2147483648   (1000...000, weight -2^31 exactly)
~5                 // -6            — flip every bit; that is -(x+1)

~5 === -6 is the identity ~x === -(x+1), and it is a direct consequence of the negative top column, not a quirk.

Here is why the correction pays off. You applied sign-magnitude to integers, where it is wrong — but IEEE 754 floating point genuinely does use sign-magnitude. A double has a real sign bit, a flag standing outside the value. Your intuition was not wrong about computers in general; it was attached to the wrong type. And the consequence you predicted is exactly the one that exists:

-0 === 0            // true  — the spec makes == and === ignore the sign of zero
Object.is(-0, 0)    // false — but the bit patterns ARE different
1 / 0               //  Infinity
1 / -0              // -Infinity   — the sign survived, and it changes the answer

(-0).toString()     // "0"   — printing hides it
Math.sign(-0)       // -0

JavaScript has a negative zero, and it has one for precisely the reason you sketched: the sign of a float is a separate bit, so flipping it on a zero gives you a second, distinct zero. That is your model, correct, applied to the type that actually uses it.

Section 2 — Your design has a name, it shipped, and here is what kills it

Your proposal: reserve some bits for the digits before the point and some for the digits after. This is fixed-point arithmetic, and it is not a naive guess — it is how an enormous amount of real software did arithmetic before floating-point hardware was cheap.

The format is usually written Qm.n. Take 32 bits and split them 16.16:

  Q16.16 — one 32-bit word

   iiiiiiiiiiiiiiii . ffffffffffffffff
   |                  |
   16 integer bits    16 fraction bits
   weights 2^15..2^0  weights 2^-1 .. 2^-16

  the column weights after the point are:
     1/2   1/4   1/8   1/16  1/32 ...  down to 1/65536

  12.5 in Q16.16:
     00000000 00001100 . 10000000 00000000
     = 8+4  .  1/2  =  12.5     exactly.

And now the answer to the specific sub-question you asked: no, there is no bit for the point. That is the entire meaning of the word fixed. The point does not need to be stored, because it is in the same place in every single value of the format — it is a fact about the type, not about the value. The hardware never sees a point at all; it stores the plain 32-bit integer 819200 and the programmer knows to interpret it as 819200/65536 = 12.5. Fixed point is just integers with an agreed-upon scale factor.

This was everywhere:

  • Doom (id Software, December 1993) did all of its geometry in 16.16 fixed point. The target machine was a 386, which had no floating-point unit unless you bought a separate 387 chip. The renderer's fixed_t type is a 32-bit integer.
  • TrueType font hinting uses F26Dot6 — 26 integer bits, 6 fraction bits, giving 1/64-pixel resolution.
  • Digital audio and DSP work in fixed point constantly, because it is exact, cheap, and has predictable timing.
  • Financial systems use it under a different name: storing money as an integer number of cents is Qn.0 with a scale of 100. Resolution 9 Section 5 recommended exactly this, and this is what it is.

So why is JavaScript not built on it? Because of a single fatal property:

In fixed point, the gap between neighbouring values is the same everywhere. Range and precision are welded together, and you must trade one against the other at compile time, for the whole program.

In Q16.16 the smallest representable step is 1/65536 ≈ 0.0000153 — at 12.5, and also at 30000, and also at 0.0001. Which means:

Q16.16 cannot represent:
   70000          — the integer part maxes out at 32767
   0.000001       — smaller than the smallest step; it becomes 0

Widen the integer half to reach 70000, and you lose fraction bits.
Widen the fraction half to reach 0.000001, and you lose range.
32 bits is 32 bits.

Now price what a general-purpose language must handle. The radius of a hydrogen atom is about 5 × 10−11 metres. The distance to the sun is about 1.5 × 1011 metres. That is twenty-two orders of magnitude, and a fixed-point format that could hold both ends with any useful precision would need something like 150 bits for every number in the program, almost all of them zeros almost all of the time.

And here is the observation that unlocks the whole subject. Nobody actually wants uniform absolute precision. They want uniform relative precision. When measuring the distance to the sun, being off by a metre is irrelevant. When measuring an atom, being off by a metre is absurd. What you want, at every scale, is roughly the same number of significant digits — not the same number of decimal places.

Fixed point gives uniform decimal places. Floating point gives uniform significant digits. That is the whole difference, and everything else follows from it.

Section 3 — Scientific notation, which is the thing you half-remember

Your recollection was right, and it is the correct mental model, so let me make it exact.

In decimal, scientific notation writes a number as a fixed number of significant digits plus a scale:

  Avogadro's number     6.022 × 10^23
  electron mass         9.109 × 10^-31

  three parts:  sign  ·  significand (6.022)  ·  exponent (23)

The significand carries the digits; the exponent says where the point goes. Four significant digits cost the same to store whether the number is 1023 or 10−31 — which is exactly the uniform-relative-precision property Section 2 said we wanted. The point is not stored; it floats, and its position is recorded in the exponent. That word is not decoration: it is literally the name of the mechanism.

Notice one more convention: scientific notation is normalised — exactly one nonzero digit sits before the point. You write 6.022 × 1023, not 60.22 × 1022 or 0.6022 × 1024, even though all three are equal. Normalisation makes the representation unique, and in binary it does something better than that, in a moment.

Now do the same thing in base 2. A binary float is:

  (-1)^sign  ×  1.fffffffff...  ×  2^exponent

and here is the payoff for normalising. In decimal, the leading digit could be any of 1 through 9, so you must store it. In binary, the only nonzero digit is 1. So a normalised binary significand always begins 1. — always, with no exceptions — which means storing that bit would be storing a constant. So it is not stored. It is called the hidden bit or implicit leading one, and it is a free bit of precision: 52 stored fraction bits give you 53 bits of significand. This is where the 53 in Resolution 9 came from.

The 64-bit double layout, then:

  bit:  63 | 62 ............ 52 | 51 ......................................... 0
       +---+--------------------+---------------------------------------------+
       | s |     exponent       |               fraction                      |
       +---+--------------------+---------------------------------------------+
         1          11 bits                       52 bits

  value = (-1)^s  ×  1.fraction  ×  2^(exponent - 1023)

Two details in that formula are worth stopping on.

Why subtract 1023? The exponent must be able to go negative — 2−4 for small numbers, 2+300 for large ones. Eleven bits give 0 through 2047, so the standard stores the exponent biased: subtract 1023 from the stored value to get the real one. Real exponent 0 is stored as 1023; real exponent −4 is stored as 1019. The usable range is −1022 to +1023, with the two extremes (all-zeros and all-ones) reserved for the special cases in Section 9.

But why bias, rather than two's complement, when Section 1 just established two's complement is how you store signed numbers? This is a genuinely elegant piece of engineering and almost nobody is told it. Because the exponent is biased and sits immediately below the sign bit, the bit pattern of a positive float compares correctly as if it were a plain unsigned integer. Bigger exponent → numerically bigger pattern → bigger number; equal exponents → the fraction bits break the tie in the right order. So hardware can sort or compare positive floats with integer instructions, and a sorted array of positive doubles is byte-identical to a sorted array of their bit patterns. Two's complement in the exponent field would have broken that ordering. The choice was made to make comparison free.

Section 4 — Encoding a number by hand: 12.5

Take a value that is exactly representable, so the machinery is visible with no rounding to distract.

Step 1 — write 12.5 in binary.
        12 = 1100
       0.5 = .1          (the first column after the point is 1/2)
      12.5 = 1100.1

Step 2 — normalise: move the point so one 1 sits before it.
      1100.1  =  1.1001 × 2^3        (moved left 3 places -> exponent 3)

Step 3 — the parts.
      sign      = 0                  (positive)
      exponent  = 3 + 1023 = 1026    = 10000000010
      fraction  = 1001 then zeros    (the leading 1 is NOT stored)

Step 4 — assemble.
      0 10000000010 1001000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000

That is byte-for-byte what a machine stores for 12.5; I checked the pattern against a real encoder rather than deriving it on paper. And 12.5 is exact because 0.5 is 1/2 — a power of two. Which is the entire clue to what goes wrong with 0.1.

Section 5 — Why 0.1 cannot be written, and the rule that decides which fractions can

The columns after a binary point are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32 … So a fraction can be written exactly in binary if and only if it is a sum of distinct powers of one-half. 0.5, 0.25, 0.75, 0.125, 12.5, 3.375 — all fine. What about 0.1?

Convert it the standard way, by repeatedly doubling and taking the bit that crosses 1:

  0.1 × 2 = 0.2   -> 0
  0.2 × 2 = 0.4   -> 0
  0.4 × 2 = 0.8   -> 0
  0.8 × 2 = 1.6   -> 1   (keep 0.6)
  0.6 × 2 = 1.2   -> 1   (keep 0.2)
  0.2 × 2 = 0.4   -> 0   <-- 0.2 again. We were here at step 2.
  0.4 × 2 = 0.8   -> 0
  0.8 × 2 = 1.6   -> 1
  0.6 × 2 = 1.2   -> 1
  ...

  0.1 = 0.0001100110011001100110011001100110011...  (1100 forever)

It never terminates. The remainder cycled back to a value it had already produced, so the digits repeat forever, exactly as 1/3 = 0.3333… does in decimal. The card's comparison to one-third was the right one; here is the rule underneath it:

A fraction p/q in lowest terms terminates in base b if and only if every prime factor of q also divides b.

Decimal is base 10 = 2 × 5, so decimal handles halves and fifths and anything built from them — 1/2, 1/4, 1/5, 1/20 all terminate; 1/3 and 1/7 do not. Binary is base 2, whose only prime factor is 2, so binary handles only denominators that are powers of two. And 0.1 is 1/10, and 10 = 2 × 5, and that 5 is fatal. There is no clever encoding that fixes this; it is a fact about the numbers, not about the format.

So the machine stores the closest double it can. Normalise the repeating expansion:

  0.0001100110011...  =  1.100110011001100... × 2^-4

  sign     = 0
  exponent = -4 + 1023 = 1019 = 01111111011
  fraction = 52 bits of 1001100110011001... , then ROUNDED

  actual stored bits:
  0 01111111011 1001100110011001100110011001100110011001100110011010
                                                                 ^^
                             note the tail: ...11010, not ...11001.
                             The last group was rounded UP.

And the number that is actually in the variable when you type 0.1 is:

0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625

  which is exactly the fraction   3602879701896397 / 2^55

Every double is an exact rational number with a power-of-two denominator. Nothing is fuzzy or approximate inside the machine — the value is precise. It is simply a precise value that is not one-tenth. Similarly:

0.2 is really 0.200000000000000011102230246251565404236316680908203125
              = 3602879701896397 / 2^54    (the same numerator, one
                                            exponent up — 0.2 is 0.1 doubled,
                                            and doubling is exact)

0.3 is really 0.299999999999999988897769753748434595763683319091796875
              = 5404319552844595 / 2^54    (note: this one rounded DOWN)

There is the setup for everything. 0.1 rounded up. 0.2 rounded up. 0.3 rounded down. Two errors pointing one way, one pointing the other.

Section 6 — The addition, and the tie I did not expect

Now add. The processor does not add "0.1 and 0.2"; it adds the two exact rationals it actually holds. Put both over 255:

  stored 0.1  =   3602879701896397 / 2^55
  stored 0.2  =   7205759403792794 / 2^55     (= 3602879701896397 × 2)
                 -------------------
  exact sum   =  10808639105689191 / 2^55

  = 0.3000000000000000166533453693773481063544750213623046875

That sum is mathematically exact — no error has occurred yet. But the result has to be squeezed back into 53 bits of significand, and 10808639105689191 needs 54. So it must be rounded to a neighbour. The two candidate doubles are:

  below:  10808639105689190 / 2^55  = 0.29999999999999998889776975374843...
                                       (this is exactly the double for 0.3)
  above:  10808639105689192 / 2^55  = 0.30000000000000004440892098500626...

  our exact sum:
          10808639105689191 / 2^55

10808639105689191 sits precisely halfway between 10808639105689190 and 10808639105689192. This is a perfect tie — not "closer to one," not "slightly nearer." Exactly the midpoint. I did not expect this when I sat down to verify the arithmetic, and it changes the story that is usually told about this example.

So which way does it go? IEEE 754's default rounding mode is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even: when a value falls exactly between two representable neighbours, take the one whose last significand bit is 0. Check the two candidates:

  below: significand ...0011  -> last bit 1, odd
  above: significand ...0100  -> last bit 0, EVEN   <- ties-to-even picks this

The tie-break sends it upward, away from 0.3, and you get 0.30000000000000004. Which means:

If IEEE 754 had specified round-toward-zero, or round-down, 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 would be true, and the most famous example in the whole subject would not exist.

That is not an argument that the standard is wrong — it is an argument that the example is a coincidence of one particular tie-break, and that people who have learned "floating point means 0.1 + 0.2 is broken" have learned a slogan rather than a mechanism.

Why ties-to-even, rather than the ties-away-from-zero you were taught in school? Because "always round halves up" has a systematic bias: over a long run of sums, every tie nudges the result in the same direction and the errors accumulate instead of cancelling. Ties-to-even sends roughly half the ties up and half down, so the error is unbiased and long summations do not drift. It costs one extra bit of logic in the rounder and it is the reason accountants call the same rule "banker's rounding."

Hardware implements this with three extra bits kept during the operation — guard, round and sticky. The guard and round bits hold the two digits just past the significand; the sticky bit records whether anything nonzero was shifted out beyond them. Those three bits are exactly enough to distinguish "below half," "exactly half," and "above half," which is all the information ties-to-even needs. Every IEEE operation is defined as: compute the infinitely precise result, then round once. That single-rounding guarantee is what makes floating-point arithmetic reproducible across machines.

Section 7 — The third cause: why 0.1 looks fine but 0.1 + 0.2 does not

Here is a question that most explanations skip, and it is the one that makes the whole thing feel arbitrary until you have the answer.

If 0.1 is really 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827…, why does typing 0.1 into a console print 0.1? And why does 0.1 + 0.3 print a clean 0.4, when both operands are inexact?

0.1                 // 0.1                    — inexact, prints clean
0.1 + 0.3           // 0.4                    — inexact, prints clean
0.5 + 0.25          // 0.75                   — exact
0.1 + 0.2           // 0.30000000000000004    — the ugly one
0.1 * 3             // 0.30000000000000004
1.005 * 100         // 100.49999999999999

The reason is a rule in the specification about printing, and it is genuinely clever. ECMA-262 defines Number::toString to produce the shortest decimal string that converts back to exactly this double. Not the true value; not a fixed number of digits. The shortest string that round-trips.

So when the double 0.1000000000000000055511… is printed, the engine asks: is "0.1" enough? It converts "0.1" back, gets the same bit pattern, and stops. "0.1" is a faithful name for that double, because no other double is closer to one-tenth. The representation error is real, and the printer hides it — deliberately, because showing you 55 digits every time would be useless.

But 0.1 + 0.2 produced a different double from the one named "0.3". The shortest string that round-trips to that pattern is "0.30000000000000004", so that is what you see. The extra digits are not the error being displayed; they are the minimum needed to distinguish this double from its neighbour.

This has real history. Getting shortest-round-trip conversion correct and fast is a famously hard problem: Steele and White's "How to Print Floating-Point Numbers Accurately" (1990) and David Gay's dtoa from the same era were the standard answers for two decades; Grisu (2010) and then Ryū (2018) made it fast enough to be free, and modern engines use these. The reason every JavaScript engine agrees on the digits 0.30000000000000004, down to the last one, is that this algorithm is specified rather than left to the C library.

So 0.1 + 0.2 is visible because of three things stacking, and the card's answer only gives the first:

1. Representation0.1 and 0.2 are not exactly representable, because 10 has a prime factor of 5. This is the card's answer, and it is necessary but not sufficient — 0.1 and 0.3 are equally unrepresentable and their sum still prints as 0.4.
2. The direction of the errors0.1 and 0.2 both rounded up, while 0.3 rounded down. The errors reinforce instead of cancelling. In 0.1 + 0.3 they cancel, and you see nothing.
3. The tie-breakThe sum lands exactly halfway between two doubles, and ties-to-even pushes it away from 0.3 rather than onto it. A different rounding mode gives the "right" answer.

Section 8 — The shape of the number line, which is the real answer to "precision"

You said the general concept of precision has never clicked. This section is that, and it is one picture.

Doubles are not evenly spaced. That single sentence is most of the subject. Because the exponent scales the whole significand, the gap between neighbouring representable values doubles every time you cross a power of two. The gap has a name: ULP, the unit in the last place.

  range              spacing between neighbours
  -------------      --------------------------
  [1, 2)             2^-52  = 0.00000000000000022...   (Number.EPSILON)
  [2, 4)             2^-51                             (twice as coarse)
  [4, 8)             2^-50
  ...
  [2^52, 2^53)       1          <- neighbours are whole numbers apart
  [2^53, 2^54)       2          <- odd numbers no longer exist
  [2^54, 2^55)       4

  and going the other way:
  [0.5, 1)           2^-53                             (twice as fine)
  [0.25, 0.5)        2^-54     <- this is where 0.1+0.2 was rounded

Read that table and several things you already know stop being separate facts.

Resolution 9's 253 limit is now mechanical. At 253 the spacing becomes 2, so the odd integers are simply not in the format — there is no bit pattern for them. That is why:

9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993     // true — 2^53 and 2^53+1
                                          // are the same double
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER                   // 9007199254740991 = 2^53 - 1
                                          // "safe" = below where integers
                                          // start disappearing

The Twitter id_str disaster from Resolution 9 was not a mysterious rounding bug. It was IDs landing in a region of the number line where the neighbours are 2 or 4 or 8 apart.

Number.EPSILON is not "the smallest number." It is 2−52 ≈ 2.22 × 10−16, the spacing of doubles between 1 and 2, and it is meaningless as an error bound anywhere else — which is the trap in Section 10.

And this is exactly the uniform-relative-precision that Section 2 said we wanted. The spacing scales with the magnitude, so everywhere in the normal range you have about 15–17 significant decimal digits — near 10−300 and near 10+300 alike. Fixed point gives constant absolute precision; floating point gives constant relative precision. That was the trade, and this table is what it bought.

Section 9 — The reserved patterns: infinities, NaN, subnormals, and where NaN-boxing lives

The 11-bit exponent field has 2048 values, and two are reserved. This is where the strange values in JavaScript come from — none of them are JavaScript inventions.

Exponent all ones (2047), fraction all zeros → Infinity.

0 11111111111 0000...0000    =  Infinity
1 11111111111 0000...0000    = -Infinity

1e308 * 10        //  Infinity   — overflow saturates, it does not wrap
1 / 0             //  Infinity   — no exception; IEEE says keep going

Resolution 9 Section 7 noted that JavaScript arithmetic never wraps around the way C's signed integers do. This is the mechanism: overflow goes to infinity, and infinity propagates sensibly through further arithmetic.

Exponent all ones, fraction nonzero → NaN. And note what that means: any nonzero fraction qualifies, so there are roughly 252 distinct bit patterns that all mean NaN — about four and a half quadrillion of them. That enormous unused space is precisely the space that NaN-boxing from Resolution 9 Section 6 moves into: SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore hide pointers, integers, null, undefined and booleans inside those spare NaN payloads. The engine trick you met one resolution ago is a consequence of this table.

NaN === NaN            // false — mandated by IEEE 754, not a JS quirk.
                       // NaN means "the answer is not a number",
                       // and two unknowns are not equal.
[NaN].includes(NaN)    // true  — includes uses SameValueZero, not ===
Object.is(NaN, NaN)    // true
Number.isNaN(NaN)      // true  (the global isNaN coerces first — avoid it)

Exponent all zeros → subnormals. Here the implicit leading 1 becomes an implicit leading 0, which trades precision for the ability to get closer to zero. This is called gradual underflow, and it was one of the hardest-fought features of the 1985 standard — without it, there are pairs of distinct numbers whose difference rounds to zero, so a !== b but a - b === 0, which breaks a great deal of numerical code.

Number.MIN_VALUE      // 5e-324 — a subnormal; its bit pattern is
                      // 0 00000000000 0000...0001, a single 1 bit.
                      // NOT the smallest normal number (that's ~2.2e-308).

0 00000000000 0000...0000   =  +0
1 00000000000 0000...0000   =  -0     <- Section 1's negative zero

Section 10 — What to actually do about it

Everything above is mechanism. Here is the practice, which is short.

Never compare floats with ===. The naive fix is an epsilon, and the naive epsilon is a trap:

// wrong — Number.EPSILON is the spacing near 1, not everywhere
Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON

// at large magnitudes this is stricter than equality; the gap
// between neighbouring doubles near 1e10 is about 1.9e-6, which
// is enormously larger than 2.2e-16.

// better — scale the tolerance to the magnitude
function close(a, b, rel = 1e-9) {
  return Math.abs(a - b) <= rel * Math.max(Math.abs(a), Math.abs(b), 1);
}

Money: integers of the smallest unit. Resolution 9 said this; Section 2 explains what it is — fixed point with a scale of 100. Exact up to 253 minor units.

toFixed has the same disease, and this one catches people out:

(1.005).toFixed(2)    // "1.00"  — not "1.01"

// because 1.005 is really 1.00499999999999989341858963598497211933...
// It was already below the midpoint before toFixed was ever called.
(1.005 * 100)         // 100.49999999999999

That is not a bug in toFixed. The literal you typed was never 1.005.

Long sums drift, and there is a classic fix. Adding a million small numbers accumulates rounding error; Kahan summation (1965) keeps a running compensation term for the low-order bits that were lost at each step and adds them back, recovering most of the lost precision for the cost of three extra operations per element.

And the thing worth internalising: this is not a JavaScript defect. The card said so and it is worth demonstrating, because the belief that JavaScript is uniquely bad at arithmetic is widespread and wrong:

Python:  >>> 0.1 + 0.2
         0.30000000000000004

Java:    System.out.println(0.1 + 0.2);
         0.30000000000000004

C:       printf("%.17f\n", 0.1 + 0.2);
         0.30000000000000004

C#, Go, Ruby, Swift, Rust — all identical.

Every one of these is producing the same 64 bits, because they are all obeying IEEE 754-1985. The only thing that ever differs is how many digits the default printer shows: C's printf("%f") defaults to six decimal places and prints 0.300000, which hides it. JavaScript's shortest-round-trip rule (Section 7) shows it. JavaScript has a reputation for bad arithmetic largely because it has an unusually honest printer.

Section 11 — Where the standard came from, and why it mattered for JavaScript

One piece of history, because it connects back to Resolution 9.

Before 1985 there was no standard. Every manufacturer had its own floating-point format — IBM 360 used base 16, DEC's VAX had its own, Cray had another — with different widths, different rounding, different behaviour on overflow, and no agreement on whether division by zero should stop the machine. The same program produced different numbers on different hardware, and porting numerical code was a research project.

IEEE 754-1985 ended that. Its principal architect was William Kahan at Berkeley, who designed the arithmetic for Intel's 8087 floating-point coprocessor and then drove the standardisation; he received the Turing Award in 1989 for it. The standard fixed the layouts you have just read, mandated round-to-nearest-ties-to-even as the default, insisted on gradual underflow against significant industry resistance, and specified that every basic operation must be correctly rounded — computed as if to infinite precision, then rounded exactly once.

That last requirement is what makes it reproducible. And reproducibility is the reason this matters for your original question. Resolution 9 Section 4 argued that JavaScript needed a numeric type whose results were identical on every machine, because a script's source is shipped across the network to hardware the author has never seen. By 1995 that type existed, was standardised internationally, and was implemented in silicon on every desktop machine. Eich did not have to design arithmetic. He had to choose it, and there was one correct choice.

Section 12 — The model to keep

You said you have never truly ticked in on this. Here is the whole thing compressed to something you can hold:

A double is binary scientific notation in 64 bits: one sign bit, an 11-bit exponent, and 52 stored fraction bits that behave as 53 because the leading 1 of a normalised binary number is always 1 and therefore never written down.

It stores about 16 significant digits, at any scale — which means the spacing between representable numbers grows with their magnitude. That is the point of it: fixed point gives you the same number of decimal places everywhere, floating point gives you the same number of significant digits everywhere, and the second is what physical and financial quantities actually need.

A fraction is exact only when its denominator is a power of two. One-tenth is not, so 0.1 is a very precise number that is not one-tenth — and the console prints 0.1 anyway, because the printing rule shows the shortest string that names that exact double.

Nothing here is approximate or fuzzy. Every double is an exact rational number. The error is not in the arithmetic; it is in the gap between the number you wrote and the nearest one that exists.

What this resolves

Is my integer model right?Section 1: positional binary — exactly right. The sign bit — you described sign-magnitude, which is real but is not what hardware uses for integers. Two's complement makes the top bit a column of weight −2n−1, giving one zero instead of two and letting one adder circuit do both addition and subtraction. Visible in JS through the int32 seam: ~5 === -6, 2147483648 | 0 === -2147483648.
…and the payoff for that correctionSection 1: IEEE 754 floats do use sign-magnitude. Your intuition was attached to the wrong type. That is why -0 exists in JavaScript, why Object.is(-0, 0) is false, and why 1 / -0 is -Infinity.
Is it bits-before-the-point and bits-after?Section 2: that is fixed point, written Qm.n, and it shipped — Doom (1993) rendered entirely in 16.16 because the 386 had no FPU; TrueType hinting uses F26Dot6; storing money in cents is the same idea. Not a naive guess.
Is there a bit for the point itself?Section 2: no — and that is what "fixed" means. The point is a property of the type, not of the value, so it costs nothing to store. The hardware sees a plain integer; the scale is a convention.
So why not use it?Section 2: because the gap between neighbours is the same everywhere, welding range to precision. Atomic radius to solar distance is 22 orders of magnitude; a fixed-point format spanning it needs ~150 bits per number. The insight: nobody wants uniform absolute precision, they want uniform relative precision — the same significant digits at every scale.
The scientific notation thing I half-rememberSections 3–4: correct, and it is the whole design. (-1)^s × 1.fraction × 2^(exp−1023). In binary the leading digit of a normalised number is always 1, so it is not stored — the hidden bit, which is where 52 stored bits become 53 bits of precision, and where Resolution 9's 253 came from. Plus why the exponent is biased rather than two's complement: so positive floats sort correctly when compared as plain integers.
Why can't 0.1 be stored?Section 5: the general rule — p/q terminates in base b iff every prime factor of q divides b. Base 2 admits only powers of two; 10 = 2 × 5 and the 5 is fatal. Long division shown, repeating 1100 forever. What is really stored is 3602879701896397 / 2^55 = 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827…
Why 0.1 + 0.2 specifically?Sections 5–7: three stacked causes, and the card gives only the first. (1) Representation error — necessary but not sufficient, since 0.1 + 0.3 prints a clean 0.4. (2) 0.1 and 0.2 both rounded up while 0.3 rounded down, so the errors reinforce rather than cancel. (3) The sum lands on an exact tie.
The tie — the thing I did not expectSection 6: the exact sum is 10808639105689191 / 2^55, precisely midway between the double for 0.3 and its neighbour. Round-to-nearest-ties-to-even picks the even significand, which is the one away from 0.3. Under round-toward-zero, 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 would be true and this example would not be famous. Ties-to-even exists because always-round-up biases long summations.
Why does 0.1 print as "0.1" then?Section 7: ECMA-262 specifies Number::toString as the shortest decimal string that round-trips to the same double. "0.1" is a faithful name for that bit pattern; "0.30000000000000004" is the shortest name for a different pattern. Steele & White (1990), Gay's dtoa, then Ryū (2018). JavaScript looks bad at arithmetic mainly because it has an unusually honest printer — C's %f shows 0.300000.
Precision, generallySection 8: doubles are not evenly spaced. The gap doubles at every power of two — 2−52 in [1,2), and exactly 1 in [252, 253), and 2 above 253, which is mechanically why MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 253−1 and why Twitter's IDs corrupted. Number.EPSILON is the spacing near 1, not a universal error bound.
The weird valuesSection 9: exponent all-ones + zero fraction is Infinity (why overflow saturates instead of wrapping); all-ones + nonzero fraction is NaN — about 252 spare patterns, which is exactly the space Resolution 9's NaN-boxing hides pointers in. NaN !== NaN is IEEE-mandated. Exponent all-zeros gives subnormals and gradual underflow — Number.MIN_VALUE is 5e-324, a single set bit.
What do I do about itSection 10: relative-tolerance comparison, never bare Number.EPSILON; money as integer minor units; (1.005).toFixed(2) === "1.00" because 1.005 was never 1.005; Kahan summation for long sums. And Python, Java, C, Go, Rust all print 0.30000000000000004 too.
Where it came fromSection 11: before 1985 every vendor had its own format and the same program gave different answers on different machines. IEEE 754-1985, architected by William Kahan (Turing Award, 1989) for Intel's 8087, fixed the layout, the default rounding and correct rounding of every operation. That is what made a portable, bit-reproducible number type available to Eich in 1995 — Resolution 9 Section 4's portability argument, from the other end.

Nothing in a double is approximate. Every one is an exact rational with a power-of-two denominator. The error you see is not the machine being imprecise — it is the distance between the number you asked for and the nearest one that exists.

pieces.title: Resolution 11 — Q12: where the 53 bits come from, and where the other 11 went
pieces.content:
This follow-up is the direct continuation of Q11, and you got most of the way there yourself. Your reasoning was: the number type is a 64-bit double, a double's structure reserves some bits for the fractional side, therefore even when you store a pure integer you are only allowed the bits that the format sets aside for integers — 53 of them — while the rest sit there holding zeros or garbage. The conclusion is right and the mechanism is not. There is no field in a double that holds "the integer part," and the other 11 bits are neither garbage nor zero; they are doing the single most important job in the format.

Getting this exactly right is worth the space, because once the 64 bits are accounted for individually, MAX_SAFE_INTEGER stops being a number to memorise and becomes something you can derive on paper in thirty seconds — and so does the answer to a question you have not asked yet: what happens to integers above the limit, which turns out not to be "they stop working."

The asks:

  1. If the type is 64 bits, why are only 53 available for the integer? Sections 1 and 2 — and the missing 11 are not lost, they are spent on something you would not give up.
  2. Is it because some bits are reserved for the places after the decimal point? Section 1 — no, and the name of the field is actively misleading here. This is the one real correction.
  3. Are the leftover bits garbage or zeros when the value is a whole number? Section 3 — neither; every bit is carrying information for 12 exactly as much as for 12.5.
  4. How does it come out to exactly 53? Section 4 — 52 + 1, and the +1 is free.
  5. (Not asked, but it is the next thing you would hit) Why 253 − 1 rather than 253, and what actually happens past the boundary. Sections 5 and 6 — integers do not stop; they thin out.

Section 1 — The correction: the "fraction" field does not hold the fractional part

Your model imagines the 64 bits divided like the fixed-point format from Resolution 10 Section 2 — a stretch of bits for what is left of the point, a stretch for what is right of it:

what you pictured (this is FIXED point, and it is not what a double is):

   iiiiiiiiiiiiiiii . ffffffffffffffff
   |                  |
   "the integer part" "the decimal places"

A double is not laid out that way. It is:

   s | eeeeeeeeeee | ffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffff
   |       |                              |
   1 bit   11 bits                        52 bits
   sign    EXPONENT                       FRACTION

   value = (-1)^s  ×  1.fraction  ×  2^(exponent - 1023)

The 52-bit field is conventionally called the "fraction" (or "mantissa," or "significand field"), and that name is the trap you fell into. It is not the fractional part of the number. It is the digits after the point of the normalised significand — the .022 in 6.022 × 10^23 — which is a completely different thing.

Watch it hold digits that are unambiguously on the integer side of the value. Take 12, which has no fractional part at all:

  12  =  1100 in binary
      =  1.100 × 2^3      (normalised)

  sign     = 0
  exponent = 3 + 1023 = 1026 = 10000000010
  fraction = 100 followed by 49 zeros
             ^^^
             these three bits are the "100" of 1100 — the tail of
             an INTEGER. They are sitting in the field named "fraction."

So the field does not partition the number into a whole side and a decimal side. It holds significant digits, and it does not know or care where the point is — that is the exponent's entire job, and it is why the point is called floating.

Here is the cleanest demonstration. These three numbers have identical fraction fields and differ only in the exponent:

  1.5     =  1.1 × 2^0     fraction: 1000...0   exponent: 1023
  3       =  1.1 × 2^1     fraction: 1000...0   exponent: 1024
  6       =  1.1 × 2^2     fraction: 1000...0   exponent: 1025
  0.75    =  1.1 × 2^-1    fraction: 1000...0   exponent: 1022
  12582912 = 1.1 × 2^23    fraction: 1000...0   exponent: 1046

One of those is a fraction, three are integers, one is over twelve million — and the "fraction" field is the same in all five. It stores the shape of the number; the exponent stores the scale. If the field really held decimal places, 3 and 0.75 could not possibly share it.

Section 2 — Where the other 11 bits went, and what they bought

So: 1 + 11 + 52 = 64, and your question becomes precise. Why spend 11 bits on an exponent instead of putting them into the significand and getting exact integers up to 264?

Because that is the trade Resolution 10 Section 2 described, and it is a trade you would not want to reverse. Price both sides exactly:

All 64 bits as magnitude
(i.e. a uint64)		Exact integers from 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 (≈1.8 × 1019). And nothing else. No 0.5. No 1020. No 10−9. Above the top it wraps around or overflows.
1 + 11 + 52 as a doubleExact integers from 0 to 9,007,199,254,740,991 (≈9 × 1015) — about 2,000× smaller. In exchange: every value from roughly 5 × 10−324 to 1.8 × 10308, with ~16 significant digits everywhere in between, and fractions.

You gave up 11 bits of precision — a factor of 2,048 in exact-integer range — and bought about 630 orders of magnitude of reach. That is what an exponent is: a multiplier on range that costs you linearly in bits and pays you exponentially in span. Eleven bits give 2,048 distinct scale factors, each a power of two, so the reachable range is squared-and-then-some rather than merely doubled.

And the sacrificed range was chosen to be the part nobody uses. Resolution 9 Section 4 priced this: milliseconds since 1970 is 1.7 × 1012, array indices cap at 4.3 × 109, pixels and bytes and rows are all far below 9 × 1015. The 2,000× that was given up sits in a band — between 9 × 1015 and 1.8 × 1019 — that ordinary programs simply do not visit. What lives there is 64-bit database IDs, which is exactly the gap Q13 is about.

So the answer to "why only 53" is: because 11 bits were spent on range, deliberately, and the format that spends zero bits on range is called an integer and it cannot represent 0.5.

Section 3 — Are the leftover bits garbage? No. Here is 12, bit by bit.

You asked whether, when the value is a pure integer, the rest of the bits are zeros or garbage. Neither. Let me lay out all 64 bits for 12 and name what each one is doing:

  the double for 12:

  0 10000000010 1000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000
  ^ ^           ^
  | |           |
  | |           fraction: the "100" of 1.100, then 49 real zeros.
  | |           Those zeros are MEANINGFUL — they say the significand
  | |           is exactly 1.1 and not 1.1000000000000001.
  | |
  | exponent 1026, meaning 2^(1026-1023) = 2^3 = 8.
  | This field is doing ACTIVE WORK. Change it and you get 6, or 24.
  |
  sign 0.

  reconstruct:  1.100b × 2^3  =  1.5 × 8  =  12

Every bit is load-bearing. There is no region of the word that is ignored for integers and consulted for fractions. The exponent field for 12 holds 1026, and it is the reason the value is 12 rather than 1.5.

That said, there is a real sense in which the encoding is wasteful for small integers — 49 zeros in a row is not information-dense — and Resolution 9 Section 6 is the industry's answer to it. V8's Smi exists precisely because most numbers in real programs are small integers, and spending 64 bits and a heap allocation on the number 3 is absurd. So the engine keeps small integers as tagged machine words and only builds an actual IEEE double — a HeapNumber — when the value needs one. Your instinct that "the rest of the bits are not really being used" is a correct engineering observation about the typical case; it is just not a fact about the format, and the engines act on it rather than the specification.

Section 4 — Where exactly 53 comes from

52 stored bits + 1 bit that is never stored = 53. Resolution 10 Section 3 introduced the hidden bit; here is why it is exactly worth one bit and never more or less.

A normalised binary significand is written 1.ffff…. In decimal scientific notation the leading digit could be anything from 1 to 9, so you must store it. In binary there is only one nonzero digit, so a normalised significand's leading digit is always 1 — 100% of the time, with no exceptions in the normal range. Storing a value that is always the same is storing nothing. So the standard omits it and the hardware puts it back on the way in:

  stored in the word:   1000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000   (52 bits)
  what arithmetic uses:  1.1000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000  (53 bits)
                         ^
                         the implicit leading 1 — free, because it is never anything else

Now the derivation you asked for. An integer is exactly representable as a double if and only if it can be written in 53 significant bits or fewer — that is, if everything from its leading 1 down to its lowest set bit fits in a 53-bit window.

  2^53 - 1 = 11111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111111
             |                                                   |
             +--------------------- 53 ones ---------------------+
             every bit is significant, and it fits exactly. Representable.

  2^53     = 100000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000
             54 bits wide — BUT only one is significant (1.0 × 2^53),
             so it fits. Representable.

  2^53 + 1 = 100000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000001
             ^                                                   ^
             leading 1 and lowest 1 are 54 bits apart.
             You would need 54 significant bits. NOT representable.

So 253 − 1 = 9,007,199,254,740,991 is the last integer with the property that it, and every integer below it, is exactly representable. Add one to it and you land on 253, which is fine; add one more and you fall into a hole.

Section 5 — Why the constant is 253 − 1 and not 253

Section 4 just showed that 253 is exactly representable. So why is MAX_SAFE_INTEGER one below it? Because "safe" in the specification means something stricter than "representable," and it has two clauses:

An integer n is safe if n can be represented exactly as a double, and no other integer rounds to the same double as n.

253 passes the first clause and fails the second, and you can watch it fail:

2 ** 53                          // 9007199254740992
2 ** 53 === 2 ** 53 + 1          // true   <-- 2^53+1 rounded ONTO 2^53
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53)    // false
Number.isSafeInteger(2 ** 53 - 1)// true

Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER          // 9007199254740991

That second clause is the one that matters in practice, and it is worth seeing why the weaker definition would have been useless. If MAX_SAFE_INTEGER were 253, then a value that passed your bounds check could still be a different number from the one that was sent to you — because 9007199254740993 arrived over the wire, rounded down to 9007199254740992 on parse, and now sits inside your "safe" range looking perfectly legitimate. The constant is there to answer "can I trust this value to be the value I was given," and for that, being representable is not enough; you also need nothing else to have collapsed onto you.

Both Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and Number.isSafeInteger were added in ES2015. Before that the check was written as a bare literal, or with Math.abs(n) <= 9007199254740991, and a great deal of code simply did not check at all — which is the setting for the Twitter incident in Resolution 9 Section 5.

Section 6 — What actually happens past the boundary: integers thin out, they do not stop

The card says that beyond the limit "consecutive integers can collide onto the same float value," which is true but easy to read as "integers stop working above 9 quadrillion." They do not. The number line above 253 is populated — just sparsely, and the sparsity follows the exact ULP table from Resolution 10 Section 8:

  range                spacing    which integers survive
  ------------------    -------    ----------------------------
  [0, 2^53)                  1     all of them
  [2^53, 2^54)               2     the even ones only
  [2^54, 2^55)               4     multiples of 4
  [2^55, 2^56)               8     multiples of 8
  ...                              ...
  [2^63, 2^64)            1024     multiples of 1024
  ...
  up to ~1.8e308                   still exact powers of two, and
                                   multiples of enormous strides

Watch it directly:

2**53 + 1     // 9007199254740992   — the odd one vanished
2**53 + 2     // 9007199254740994   — the even one is exact and correct
2**53 + 3     // 9007199254740996   — rounded up to the next even
2**53 * 2     // 18014398509481984  — exact; powers of two always are

1e21 + 1 === 1e21    // true — up here the stride is 131072

So the failure mode is not an error and not an overflow. It is silence. The arithmetic proceeds, returns a plausible number of the right magnitude, and is quietly wrong in the low digits. Compare it to the two alternatives:

  • A C int32 overflowing is undefined behaviour — in practice it wraps to a large negative number, which is at least conspicuous.
  • A BigInt overflowing does not happen; it grows.
  • A double "overflowing" the safe range keeps returning something that looks fine.

This is why the boundary needed a named constant and a predicate in the standard library rather than a footnote — the language cannot warn you, so the check has to be yours. And it is why the industry convention Resolution 9 described exists: serialise 64-bit identifiers as strings, because the corruption happens inside JSON.parse, before any code of yours has seen the value.

Section 7 — The whole thing on one page

  64 bits                     1 sign  +  11 exponent  +  52 fraction

  the 52-bit "fraction" field holds SIGNIFICANT DIGITS,
  not decimal places.  For 12 it holds the "100" of 1.100 x 2^3.

  + 1 hidden leading bit (always 1, so never stored)
  ---------------------------------------------------------------
  = 53 bits of significand  =  53 significant binary digits, at ANY scale

  an integer is exact  <=>  it needs <= 53 significant bits
  the last integer with every predecessor exact  =  2^53 - 1
                                                =  9,007,199,254,740,991

  the 11 exponent bits are not lost — they buy the range
  5e-324 .. 1.8e308, which is what "floating" means.

What this resolves

Is it because bits are reserved for the places after the decimal point?Section 1: no — this is the one real correction. That is the fixed-point layout from Resolution 10 Section 2. A double has no "integer part" field. The 52-bit field is confusingly named fraction, but it holds the digits of the normalised significand — the .022 of 6.022 × 10^23. Proof: 1.5, 3, 6, 0.75 and 12582912 all have identical fraction fields and differ only in the exponent.
Why can only 53 of the 64 bits hold the integer?Section 2: because 11 bits were spent on the exponent, deliberately. A plain uint64 would give exact integers to 1.8 × 1019 and nothing else — no 0.5, no 1020, no 10−9. The double gives up a factor of 2,048 in exact-integer range and buys roughly 630 orders of magnitude of reach. The band that was surrendered (9 × 1015 to 1.8 × 1019) is one ordinary programs never visit — except for 64-bit database IDs, which is Q13.
Are the leftover bits garbage or zeros?Section 3: neither. For 12, the exponent field holds 1026 and is the reason the value is 12 rather than 1.5; the 49 trailing zeros assert that the significand is exactly 1.1. Every bit is load-bearing. But your instinct is right about the typical case — which is exactly why V8 has Smis (Resolution 9 Section 6) and never builds a real double for the number 3.
How does it come out to exactly 53?Section 4: 52 stored + 1 hidden. A normalised binary significand always begins with 1 — there is no other nonzero digit in base 2 — so that bit is a constant and is not written down. Then the rule you can derive from: an integer is exact iff its leading 1 and its lowest 1 fit inside a 53-bit window. 2^53 - 1 is 53 ones and fits; 2^53 + 1 spans 54 and does not.
Why 253 − 1 and not 253?Section 5: 253 is representable — it fails the second clause of the spec's definition of "safe": no other integer may round onto it. 2**53 === 2**53 + 1 is true. The weaker definition would be useless, because a corrupted value could sit inside the "safe" range looking legitimate. MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and isSafeInteger both arrived in ES2015.
What happens above the limit?Section 6: integers thin out; they do not stop. [253, 254) keeps the even ones, the next octave keeps multiples of 4, and so on to 1.8 × 10308. The failure mode is not an error or a wrap-around — it is silence: a plausible number of the right magnitude, quietly wrong in the low digits. That is why the boundary needed a named constant, and why 64-bit IDs must cross the wire as strings.

You had the conclusion before you had the mechanism. The mechanism is: no bits are reserved for decimals, 11 bits were sold for range, and the 53rd bit is free because in binary the leading digit of a normalised number is never anything but 1.

pieces.title: Resolution 12 — Q13: what a BigInt is, and why the language has only seven primitives
pieces.content:
This is the longest set of asks in the follow-ups so far, and they split cleanly into two halves. The first half is what BigInt actually is — you want it given the same bit-by-bit treatment the double got, and you are right to ask, because the honest answer breaks the frame of the question. The second half is much bigger than BigInt: you noticed that the language went from six primitive types to seven, drew the correct inference that types can be added, and asked how seven has been enough, whether anything is missing, and whether anyone has proposed more. That last question has a rich answer, including one proposal that got most of the way and then stalled for reasons that explain the whole design economy.

You also said plainly that you do not understand what "currency in minor units" means. Section 4 starts from nothing on that, and it turns out to be the use case with the most interesting failure — because for ordinary shop prices the technique works fine with plain Numbers, and it is only when the minor unit gets very small that it explodes. The example where it explodes is Ethereum.

The asks:

  1. What is a BigInt? How many bits, what is the bit layout, is it a signed 64-bit integer, an unsigned one, or still a float underneath? Sections 1 and 2 — the answer to "how many bits" is that the question does not apply, and that is the whole point.
  2. The use cases, properly understood — database IDs, nanosecond timestamps, and currency in minor units, which you singled out as the one you do not follow. Sections 3, 4 and 5.
  3. Any other examples that suffered from the boundary? Section 6 — six more, including one where BigInt is the wrong tool and you should not use it.
  4. Fact-check: before 2020 there were six primitives — number, boolean, string, null, undefined, symbol. Section 7 — correct for that window; the full history is 5 → 6 → 7 over thirty years.
  5. So types can be added. How were six or seven enough for every use case? Section 8 — because primitives are not where use cases are met, and adding one is far more expensive than it looks.
  6. Is anything missing, and has anyone discussed adding more — past or future? Sections 9 and 10 — yes, one thing is genuinely missing, and there is a proposal graveyard worth reading.

Section 1 — "How many bits?" does not have an answer, and that is the design

Your question assumes BigInt is like Number: a fixed-width format with a bit layout you can draw. It is not, and the contrast is the cleanest way to see what it is.

  Number — a FIXED layout. Every Number is exactly 64 bits.

      s | eeeeeeeeeee | ffffff...ffff
      1      11             52
      The size is a property of the TYPE.

  BigInt — no layout. There is no width.

      3n                     small
      (2n ** 1000n)          1001 bits
      (2n ** 100000n)        100001 bits
      The size is a property of the VALUE, and it grows on demand.

So: not 64-bit signed, not 64-bit unsigned, and definitely not a float. BigInt is an arbitrary-precision integer — mathematicians call this a bignum — bounded only by memory. It never overflows and it never rounds. Every BigInt operation is exact by construction:

2n ** 128n
// 340282366920938463463374607431768211456n   — 39 digits, exact

let f = 1n;
for (let i = 1n; i <= 21n; i++) f *= i;
f    // 51090942171709440000n  — 21 factorial, exact.
     // As a Number, 21! is 5.109094217170944e19: the low digits are gone.

Choosing arbitrary precision over a fixed 64-bit integer was itself a decision, and worth a sentence. A fixed Int64 would have needed an answer to "what happens on overflow" — wrap around like C, or throw? — and either answer is a new cliff to fall off. It would also have been useless for the cryptography case in Section 6, which needs 2048-bit numbers. Arbitrary precision has no cliff, so there is nothing to specify and nothing to get wrong. Where you genuinely need exact 64-bit wrapping semantics, the language gives you that on top rather than underneath:

BigInt.asIntN(64,  2n ** 63n)   // -9223372036854775808n  — wrapped, signed
BigInt.asUintN(64, -1n)         // 18446744073709551615n  — wrapped, unsigned

new BigInt64Array(1)            // real fixed-width 64-bit storage
new BigUint64Array(1)

That pair is how you talk to something on the other side that really does have an int64 — a database, a binary format, a WebAssembly module.

Section 2 — What it looks like in memory, and the sign-magnitude payoff

You asked for the structure, so here is what V8 actually builds. A BigInt is a heap object — not a machine word, not a tagged Smi:

  a V8 BigInt on the heap:

  +---------------------+
  |  map pointer        |   "I am a BigInt"  (every V8 heap object has this)
  +---------------------+
  |  bitfield:          |
  |    sign   : 1 bit   |   0 = positive, 1 = negative
  |    length : n bits  |   how many digits follow
  +---------------------+
  |  digit[0]           |   64 bits  (a "limb"; least significant first)
  |  digit[1]           |   64 bits
  |  ...                |
  |  digit[length-1]    |   64 bits  (most significant)
  +---------------------+

  So 2n**70n needs two digits. 3n needs one. A 2048-bit RSA modulus
  needs thirty-two.

And now the detail that connects straight back to Resolution 10 Section 1. Notice that the sign is a separate bit, standing outside the magnitude. That is sign-magnitude — the scheme you proposed for integers, which I had to correct because real fixed-width integers use two's complement.

Here it is, vindicated a second time. Two's complement works by giving the top bit a weight of −2n−1, and that requires a fixed n. An arbitrary-precision integer has no fixed width, so there is no "top bit" to assign a negative weight to. Sign-magnitude is therefore not a choice here; it is the only option. Every bignum library ever written — GMP, Java's BigInteger, Python's int, V8's BigInt — stores a sign flag beside a magnitude.

So your instinct has now been correct twice in a row and wrong in exactly one place: sign-magnitude is what floats use and what arbitrary-precision integers use; two's complement is what fixed-width machine integers use. That is the whole rule.

Three consequences of living on the heap:

It has a practical ceiling after all, imposed by the engine rather than the language:

1n << BigInt(2 ** 31)
// RangeError: Maximum BigInt size exceeded
