Plus the practical reason: it gave every platform a free portable NaN test, x !== x, before isnan() was guaranteed to exist.
What does it break, and what was done about it?Section 3: it makes === non-reflexive, so indexOf can never find NaN and sort silently gives up. JavaScript's answer was four equality algorithms, tabulated: ==, ===, SameValueZero (includes, Map, Set — NaN equals itself), and SameValue (Object.is — also separates +0 from −0). includes was added in ES2016 largely because of this. And "SameValueZero" literally means "SameValue, but zero is treated loosely."
What is Number — class, object, array?Section 4: typeof Number === "function", and a function in JavaScript is an object — one with an internal [[Call]]. That is why it can hold isNaN and MAX_SAFE_INTEGER as ordinary properties. It plays three roles at once: converter (Number("42")), constructor (new Number(42) — never write this), and namespace. Not a class in origin (1997 vs 2015) though class X extends Number works. Not an array — the thing you were reaching for, "a bag of named items," is just an object.
Are Math.max and Number.isNaN the same kind of thing?Section 5: no. typeof Math is "object" — a plain namespace, not callable, new Math() throws. Number is a function that also holds functions. The dot behaves identically on both, which is exactly why the difference is invisible.
Standard library, or external?Section 6, and the line is real: ECMA-262 defines Number, Math, JSON, Array, Promise, Map — present in every JavaScript environment on earth. WHATWG specs define document, window, fetch, localStorage — these are not JavaScript; they are host-provided and written in WebIDL. typeof globalThis.document is "undefined" in Node. Almost every environment-specific bug lives on this line.
What is the dot doing at implementation level?Section 7, the algorithm: evaluate the base → throw if null/undefined → box if primitive → call [[Get]], which checks own properties, calls a getter if it finds one, and otherwise walks the [[Prototype]] chain until it hits null and returns undefined. So a missing property is not an error, and [].map is found on Array.prototype two links up.
The thing about methodsSection 7: a method is not a special kind of thing. arr.map(f) is two operations — a lookup that returns a function, then a call. Detach them and const m = [1,2].map; m(x=>x) throws, because the call form is what supplies this. This is the root of every lost-this bug in JavaScript.
How can you dot a primitive with no parts?Section 8: boxing. ToObject builds a temporary wrapper, the lookup runs on it, and the wrapper is discarded — which you can watch: s.foo = 1 then s.foo is undefined. That is the cleanest proof that Resolution 8 was right that primitives have no slots. It also explains what new Number(5) is for, and why you must never use it (if (new Boolean(false)) runs).
What can I put a dot on?Section 10, enumerated — objects, arrays, functions, classes, instances, all five boxable primitives, namespaces, module namespaces, host objects, and any expression's result. Stated as an exclusion it is one line: everything except null and undefined, which have no wrapper type because they represent absence. Hence ?..
Was my dot-vs-bracket model right?Section 9: yes, and here is the sharper version — they are the same operation, differing only in whether the key is literal text in the source or an expression evaluated at runtime. That explains the cases the rule of thumb does not: obj["my-key"], obj[Symbol.iterator], and q[1] being the string key "1".
The consequence worth carryingSection 9: every property key is a string or a Symbol. So two different objects used as keys both become "[object Object]" and silently collide — no error, no warning. Which is exactly why Map exists, and Map compares keys with SameValueZero, tying straight back to Section 3.

You noticed you did not know what Number was, and that was the right thing to notice. It is a function object — because functions are objects — resolved as a property of the global object, defined by the language rather than the browser, and dotted into by the same [[Get]] that reads user.name and borrows a temporary wrapper to read "abc".length. One operation, everywhere.

pieces.title: Resolution 15 — Q16: code units, code points, graphemes, and why strings are UTF-16
pieces.content:
Your follow-up here is short — you asked for the very basics: what a visual character is, what a code unit is, what UTF-16 is, with an example, because this is one of the foundational principles and you want it properly. So this piece assumes nothing and builds the vocabulary from the beginning, because the confusion in this area is almost entirely a vocabulary problem. There are four different things that all get called "a character," they have different counts for the same text, and once you can name them separately the whole subject stops being mysterious.

There is also a historical answer here that closes a loop from Q10. You proposed then that JavaScript's oddities come from decisions made in a hurry that later could not be undone. I argued that this was not the explanation for the single number type. For UTF-16 strings, it is exactly the explanation — and better than that, it was not even a hasty decision. It was a careful, correct decision in 1995 that was invalidated by an outside event in 1996. Section 4 is that story, and it is the cleanest example in the language of your instinct being right.

The asks:

  1. What is a "visual character"? Sections 2 and 7 — it has a technical name, and its count differs from everything else.
  2. What is a "code unit"? Sections 2 and 3 — and why the phrase is always attached to an encoding.
  3. What is UTF-16? Sections 3, 4 and 5 — including why JavaScript uses it and nothing else does any more.
  4. An example, worked properly. Section 6 — the emoji, taken apart bit by bit, plus a Devanagari example that behaves differently again.
  5. Why does this matter? Sections 8 through 10 — where it breaks real code, and how to count what you actually meant.

Section 1 — The problem underneath: text has to be numbers

Start from the substrate, because everything follows from it. A computer stores numbers. Text is not numbers. So every text system in history is a table: a mapping from characters to numbers, agreed in advance by everyone who will read or write the data.

ASCII (1963) was the first widely agreed table: 7 bits, 128 slots. Enough for the uppercase and lowercase English alphabet, digits, punctuation, and some control codes.

  'A' -> 65     'a' -> 97     '0' -> 48     ' ' -> 32

128 slots is enough for English and nothing else. So the 1980s produced dozens of incompatible 8-bit extensions, each using the spare 128 slots differently: Latin-1 for Western Europe, KOI8-R for Russian, Shift-JIS for Japanese, ISCII for Indian scripts. Byte 233 meant é in one table and something else entirely in another.

The result was mojibake — text read with the wrong table, arriving as garbage. Two things were fundamentally wrong: there was no way to mix scripts in one document, and a byte sequence did not carry the identity of the table it was written with.

Section 2 — Unicode's move, and the four words you need

Unicode (work began 1987; version 1.0 published October 1991) fixed this with one decisive separation:

Separate the catalogue of characters from the way they are stored as bytes.

The catalogue assigns every character in every script one permanent number, called a code point, written U+ followed by hexadecimal. That is a pure fact about the character and has nothing to do with storage:

  U+0041   LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A          A
  U+00E9   LATIN SMALL LETTER E WITH ACUTE é
  U+0928   DEVANAGARI LETTER NA            न
  U+1F44B  WAVING HAND SIGN                👋

Then, separately, an encoding says how to turn code points into a sequence of fixed-size chunks. Those chunks are the code units, and their size is the encoding's defining property:

UTF-8code unit = 8 bits. Each code point becomes 1–4 units. ASCII characters are one unit each, identical to their ASCII bytes.
UTF-16code unit = 16 bits. Each code point becomes 1 or 2 units. This is what JavaScript strings are made of.
UTF-32code unit = 32 bits. Every code point is exactly 1 unit. Simple, and wasteful.

So a code unit is not a character. It is a storage chunk, and how many of them a character takes depends entirely on which encoding you chose. That is why the phrase is always "UTF-16 code unit" and never just "code unit" — the number is meaningless without the encoding.

And the fourth word, which is the one you asked about. What a human being points at and calls "a character" is technically a grapheme cluster — formally, "what a user perceives as a single character." It may be several code points that combine into one visible mark. That is the "visual character" the card meant.

Four counts for the same text, and they routinely disagree:

TextGrapheme clusters
(what you see)		Code points
(catalogue entries)		UTF-16 code units
(.length)		UTF-8 bytes
(on disk)
A1111
\u00E9 — é precomposed1112
e\u0301 — é as e + accent1223
नमस्ते36618
👋1124
👍🏽 (thumb + skin tone)1248
🇮🇳 (flag)1248
👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 (family)171125

Every one of those numbers is correct. They are answers to four different questions. .length answers the fourth-from-obvious one, and that is the entire content of the card.

Section 3 — What UTF-16 actually is

UTF-16 encodes a code point in 16-bit units, using one unit when it can and two when it must.

  code points U+0000 .. U+FFFF        ->  ONE 16-bit code unit
     (the "Basic Multilingual Plane" — Latin, Greek, Cyrillic,
      Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, CJK, and most of what most
      people type most of the time)

  code points U+10000 .. U+10FFFF     ->  TWO 16-bit code units,
     (emoji, historic scripts, rare CJK,        called a SURROGATE PAIR
      mathematical alphabets, music notation)

So UTF-16 is a variable-width encoding — which is the thing everyone forgets, because for the first several years of using it you never meet a character that needs two units. Then someone types an emoji.

The two-unit mechanism needed 1,024 × 1,024 = 1,048,576 combinations reserved for the purpose, so Unicode permanently set aside two blocks of 1,024 code points that stand for no character at all:

  U+D800 .. U+DBFF    1024 "high surrogates"   (also called leading)
  U+DC00 .. U+DFFF    1024 "low surrogates"    (also called trailing)

  1024 x 1024 = 1,048,576 pairs
  which is exactly the size of U+10000..U+10FFFF.

Because those code points are permanently unassigned, a decoder can always tell what it is looking at: a unit in the high-surrogate range is the first half of a pair, and everything else stands alone. That is the property that makes the scheme work.

Section 4 — Why JavaScript uses UTF-16, and why nothing designed since does

Here is the history, and it is the Q10 loop closing.

Unicode 1.0, published October 1991, was a 16-bit standard. Not "16 bits for now" — the design claim was that 65,536 code points were enough for all the characters in modern use across all the world's scripts, and that unifying the Han characters used by Chinese, Japanese and Korean would keep it inside that budget. Fixed width, two bytes per character, forever. That encoding was called UCS-2, and it was genuinely attractive: simple, indexable, no variable-width complexity anywhere.

Everything designed in that window bet on it, and it was a reasonable bet:

  • Windows NT (1993) — internal strings are 16-bit.
  • Java (1995) — char is a 16-bit type.
  • JavaScript (1995) — strings are sequences of 16-bit values.
  • Qt, Python 2's unicode type on narrow builds, and others.

Then Unicode 2.0 arrived in July 1996 and broke the assumption. 65,536 was not enough — historic scripts, rare CJK characters, and eventually emoji did not fit. The space was expanded to 17 planes of 65,536, or 1,114,112 code points, and surrogate pairs were introduced so existing 16-bit systems could reach the new space without a redesign. UCS-2 became UTF-16.

Look at the dates. JavaScript shipped in Navigator 2.0 in September 1995. The assumption it was built on was invalidated in July 1996 — ten months later, with the language already deployed on the web and rising fast. Changing what .length counts would have altered the behaviour of every string operation in every script already published.

So this is your Q10 hypothesis, finally correct. Not "written in ten days and nobody thought about it" — Eich made the same decision Sun made for Java and Microsoft made for Windows NT, following the published international standard of the day. The decision was right when it was made and wrong twelve months later, and backwards compatibility froze it. That is a purer example of the phenomenon than anything in the number type, and it is worth holding onto as the shape this class of thing actually takes.

The evidence that it was an accident rather than a preference: nothing designed after 1996 chose UTF-16. Go, Rust, Swift and Python 3 all use UTF-8 or an abstraction over it. The web platform standardised on UTF-8 for transport — HTML, JSON and HTTP are UTF-8 by default. UTF-16 survives only in the runtimes that were built during that five-year window and could not change.

Section 5 — And this is why .length is what it is

Given all of that, the card's fact is now a consequence rather than a rule to memorise:

A JavaScript string is a sequence of 16-bit code units, and .length is the number of units in the sequence. It was defined in 1995, when one unit was one character, and the definition could not be changed when that stopped being true.

The specification is explicit about this rather than embarrassed by it: a String value is defined as a finite ordered sequence of 16-bit unsigned integers, and indexing gives you units. s[0], s.charCodeAt(0), s.slice(), s.padStart(), and every other index-based operation counts units, because the string genuinely is units all the way down.

Section 6 — The example, taken apart

Now the worked example you asked for. Take 👋, WAVING HAND SIGN, code point U+1F44B.

Step 1 — is it above U+FFFF? 0x1F44B is 128,075 in decimal; 0xFFFF is 65,535. So yes: it needs a surrogate pair.

Step 2 — the encoding algorithm. Subtract the 0x10000 offset, split the remaining 20 bits into two halves of 10, and add each half to its surrogate base:

  code point                    0x1F44B
  subtract 0x10000              0x0F44B          (20 bits)

  in binary:   0000 1111 0100 0100 1011
               |-------- 10 --------||-- 10 ---|
               high half             low half
               00 0011 1101 = 0x03D   01 0100 1011 = 0x24B

  high surrogate  = 0xD800 + 0x03D  = 0xD83D
  low  surrogate  = 0xDC00 + 0x24B  = 0xDC4B

  so 👋 is stored as the two 16-bit units:   D83D DC4B

Step 3 — confirm it, and reverse it:

"👋".length                 // 2
"👋".charCodeAt(0).toString(16)   // "d83d"
"👋".charCodeAt(1).toString(16)   // "dc4b"
"👋".codePointAt(0).toString(16)  // "1f44b"  — reads BOTH units

// decoding by hand:
(0xD83D - 0xD800) * 0x400 + (0xDC4B - 0xDC00) + 0x10000
// 0x1F44B — back to where we started

String.fromCharCode(0xD83D, 0xDC4B)   // "👋"
String.fromCodePoint(0x1F44B)         // "👋" — same string

And now a second example that fails differently, which is why one example is not enough. Take नमस्ते:

"नमस्ते".length        // 6
[..."नमस्ते"].length   // 6   — same! no surrogate pairs here

  U+0928  न   NA
  U+092E  म   MA
  U+0938  स   SA
  U+094D  ्   VIRAMA      <- a combining mark, not a standalone letter
  U+0924  त   TA
  U+0947  े   VOWEL SIGN E <- also combining

  but a reader sees THREE clusters:   न  म  स्ते

Every code point here is below U+FFFF, so code units and code points agree at 6. But the visual count is 3, because स + virama + त + vowel sign render as one conjunct. So this string breaks the "one visual character" assumption without involving UTF-16 at all.

That is the important lesson from putting the two examples side by side: surrogate pairs and grapheme clusters are two independent problems. The emoji has 1 code point and 2 units. The Devanagari has 6 code points, 6 units and 3 clusters. Fixing one does not fix the other.

Section 7 — Grapheme clusters, properly

Four separate mechanisms make multiple code points render as one thing. Worth knowing all four, because each one produces a different kind of surprise.

1. Combining marks. A base character followed by a modifier that attaches to it:

"\u00E9"        // "é" — ONE precomposed code point.        length 1
"e\u0301"       // "é" — e + COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT (two).  length 2

"\u00E9" === "e\u0301"     // false — different strings, identical on screen
"\u00E9".normalize("NFD").length   // 2   — decomposes to e + accent
"e\u0301".normalize("NFC").length  // 1   — composes to the single point

2. Zero-width joiner sequences. U+200D glues emoji into a single glyph:

👨‍👩‍👧‍👦  =  👨 + ZWJ + 👩 + ZWJ + 👧 + ZWJ + 👦
        =  7 code points, 11 UTF-16 units, 1 visible glyph

3. Regional indicators. Flags are two letter-shaped code points that the font renders as a flag:

🇮🇳 = U+1F1EE (REGIONAL INDICATOR I) + U+1F1F3 (REGIONAL INDICATOR N)
   = 2 code points, each a surrogate pair, so length 4

4. Modifiers. Skin tones and variation selectors attach to a preceding emoji:

👍🏽 = U+1F44D + U+1F3FD (MEDIUM SKIN TONE)  = length 4

To count what a reader would count, the language finally gained a proper tool in ES2022:

const seg = new Intl.Segmenter("en", { granularity: "grapheme" });
[...seg.segment("👨‍👩‍👧‍👦")].length     // 1
[...seg.segment("नमस्ते")].length      // 3
[...seg.segment("👍🏽")].length        // 1

Note the shape of that API. Grapheme clustering depends on the Unicode text-segmentation rules and, for some scripts, on locale — so it lives in Intl, not on String.prototype. There is no "abc".graphemeLength and there is not going to be one, because the answer is not a property of the string alone.

Section 8 — Counting what you actually meant

Three tiers, three tools. This is the practical core:

const s = "👋नमस्ते";

// TIER 1 — UTF-16 code units. Storage.
s.length                                    // 8

// TIER 2 — code points. Iteration is code-point-aware since ES2015.
[...s].length                               // 7
Array.from(s).length                        // 7
for (const ch of s) { /* ch is a code point */ }

// TIER 3 — grapheme clusters. What a reader sees.
[...new Intl.Segmenter("en", { granularity: "grapheme" })
      .segment(s)].length                   // 4

ES2015 is the dividing line worth remembering: the iteration protocol was defined to walk code points, not code units. So for...of, spread, and Array.from all handle surrogate pairs correctly, while the older index-based API does not. That is why "👋".split("") and [..."👋"] disagree — they are from different eras of the language.

"👋".split("")     // ["\ud83d", "\udc4b"]  — two broken halves
[..."👋"]          // ["👋"]                 — one code point

Section 9 — Where this actually breaks code

The failures are not exotic. They are ordinary string handling.

Truncation splits a pair. The classic:

"👋abc".slice(0, 1)         // "\ud83d" — a lone high surrogate
                            // renders as �, the replacement character

Any "show the first 100 characters" preview, any database column with a character limit, any SMS-length counter will do this eventually.

Padding counts units. Subtle and easy to miss:

"👋".padStart(3, "-")       // "-👋"  — length 3, but only ONE dash,
                            // because the emoji already used two units.

Reversing destroys text. The naive idiom is wrong on two levels:

"👋a".split("").reverse().join("")   // "a" + two swapped surrogates = broken
[..."👋a"].reverse().join("")        // "a👋" — correct for code points,
                                     // still wrong for é as e+accent, and
                                     // still wrong for the family emoji

Regex . matches one code unit without the u flag.

/^.$/.test("👋")     // false — one dot cannot match two units
/^.$/u.test("👋")     // true  — the u flag makes the regex code-point-aware

Use the u flag on any regex that might see non-ASCII text. It also enables \u{1F44B} escapes and \p{...} Unicode property classes.

Comparison fails on normalisation. This one silently breaks search and deduplication:

"caf\u00E9".indexOf("e\u0301")     // -1  — needle decomposed,
                                    //      haystack precomposed
"caf\u00E9" === "cafe\u0301"        // false — identical on screen

// the fix: normalise both sides to a canonical form first
a.normalize("NFC") === b.normalize("NFC")

NFC composes to precomposed characters where they exist; NFD decomposes into base plus marks. Normalise anything that arrives from a user, a file, or an API before comparing or storing it — NFC is the usual choice, and it is what the web platform recommends.

Case conversion is not one-to-one. A related trap in the same family:

"ß".toUpperCase()                 // "SS" — one character becomes two
"i".toLocaleUpperCase("tr")       // "İ"  — Turkish dotted capital I

Section 10 — Two loose ends worth knowing

JavaScript strings are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-16. Because a string is defined as any sequence of 16-bit values, you can build one containing a lone surrogate that encodes nothing:

const bad = "\uD800";           // a high surrogate with no partner
bad.length                       // 1
bad.isWellFormed()               // false   (ES2024)
bad.toWellFormed()               // "�" — replaced with �

This matters at boundaries: such a string cannot be encoded as UTF-8, so sending it to a server, a file, or TextEncoder will either throw or silently substitute. isWellFormed and toWellFormed were added in ES2024 specifically to let you check before crossing that boundary.

What the engine actually stores is not UTF-16. V8 keeps a one-byte (Latin-1) representation for strings whose characters all fit in 8 bits, and only uses two bytes per unit when it must. So "hello" occupies 5 bytes internally, not 10. This is invisible: .length, indexing and every string method behave exactly as if the string were UTF-16, because the specification says so. It is the same pattern as Resolution 9's Smi and Resolution 8's shared string buffers — the specification defines the semantics, the engine optimises the representation, and the optimisation is unobservable.

And one more distinction that trips people at the file boundary: your source files are UTF-8; your string values are UTF-16. The engine decodes the source from UTF-8 and builds UTF-16 strings from it. When you send text out you encode again:

new TextEncoder().encode("👋").length    // 4  — UTF-8 bytes
"👋".length                              // 2  — UTF-16 code units

Which is why a database column declared as 100 bytes, 100 characters, or 100 JavaScript length units are three different limits, and mixing them up is a common source of truncation bugs at the storage layer.

What this resolves

What is a code point?Section 2: the permanent number Unicode assigns to a character, written U+XXXX. A fact about the character, with nothing to do with storage. A is U+0041; 👋 is U+1F44B.
What is a code unit?Section 2: the fixed-size storage chunk an encoding uses — 8 bits in UTF-8, 16 bits in UTF-16, 32 in UTF-32. It is not a character, and the number is meaningless without naming the encoding, which is why the phrase is always "UTF-16 code unit."
What is a "visual character"?Sections 2 and 7: technically a grapheme cluster — "what a user perceives as a single character." Four mechanisms build one from several code points: combining marks (e + accent), ZWJ sequences (the family emoji), regional indicators (flags), and modifiers (skin tones). Counting them needs Intl.Segmenter — and it lives in Intl rather than on String.prototype because the answer depends on locale, not on the string alone.
Four counts, one stringSection 2's table. 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 is 1 grapheme, 7 code points, 11 code units, 25 UTF-8 bytes — all four correct, all four answering different questions. .length answers the third.
What is UTF-16?Section 3: a variable-width encoding in 16-bit units. U+0000–U+FFFF take one unit; U+10000–U+10FFFF take two, called a surrogate pair. Unicode permanently reserved U+D800–U+DBFF and U+DC00–U+DFFF — 1024 × 1024 = exactly the size of the space above U+FFFF — so a decoder can always tell halves from whole characters.
Why does JavaScript use it?Section 4, and this is your Q10 hypothesis finally being right. Unicode 1.0 (October 1991) was a fixed-width 16-bit standard — 65,536 was declared enough for every modern script. Everything built in that window bet on it: Windows NT (1993), Java (1995), JavaScript (1995). Unicode 2.0 (July 1996) expanded to 17 planes and added surrogate pairs. JavaScript had shipped in September 1995, ten months earlier. So this was not a hasty decision — it was a correct decision, invalidated by an outside event, then frozen by compatibility. The proof: nothing designed after 1996 chose UTF-16 — Go, Rust, Swift, Python 3 and the web platform all use UTF-8.
The example, workedSection 6: 👋 is U+1F44B, above U+FFFF, so subtract 0x10000, split the remaining 20 bits into two 10-bit halves, add 0xD800 and 0xDC00 — giving D83D DC4B, two units, .length === 2. Reversed by hand and confirmed.
The second example that fails differentlySection 6: नमस्ते is 6 code points, 6 units (no surrogates at all) and 3 visible clusters. So surrogate pairs and grapheme clusters are two independent problems — fixing one does not fix the other, and one example cannot show both.
How do I count what I meant?Section 8, three tiers: s.length for units; [...s].length / Array.from / for...of for code points — ES2015 defined iteration to walk code points, which is why "👋".split("") and [..."👋"] disagree; and Intl.Segmenter for graphemes.
Where it breaks real codeSection 9: "👋abc".slice(0,1) yields a lone surrogate rendering as �; "👋".padStart(3,"-") adds only one dash; naive reversal destroys text; /^.$/ fails without the u flag; and "caf\u00E9" === "cafe\u0301" can be false across normalisation forms — fix with .normalize("NFC") on both sides. Also "ß".toUpperCase() is "SS".
Two loose endsSection 10: JavaScript strings are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-16 — lone surrogates are legal values, hence isWellFormed/toWellFormed (ES2024) before crossing to UTF-8. And the engine does not actually store UTF-16: V8 keeps Latin-1 strings at one byte per character, unobservably — the same specification-versus-representation split as Smis and shared string buffers.

Four words, four counts: grapheme cluster, code point, code unit, byte. .length counts UTF-16 code units because in 1995 that was the same as counting characters, and Unicode changed the rules ten months after JavaScript shipped.

pieces.title: Resolution 16 — Q17: why strings are the only primitive whose immutability you can notice
pieces.content:
You are right that this is ground Q9 already covered, and you name it yourself. Resolution 8 answered why primitives cannot be mutated in general — the argument was that mutation requires identity, a subject that persists through the change, and primitives have none. That argument stands and is not repeated here.

But your follow-up asks something Resolution 8 did not: is the immutability uniform, or are some primitives mutable and others not? That question has a genuinely interesting answer. All seven are immutable — but the rule is vacuous for six of them and load-bearing for one. Only strings have syntax that looks like a mutation, which is why only strings need the rule stated out loud, and why your card is about strings rather than about numbers.

There is also a distinction hiding in your question that is worth separating out, because "you cannot change it" means three different things in JavaScript and conflating them causes real bugs. Section 4 pulls them apart.

And one correction to the card itself, which matters in practice: s[0] = "x" does not silently do nothing in modern code. It throws. Section 3.

The asks:

  1. Why exactly are strings not mutable? Section 1 — Resolution 8 gave the general argument; here is what is specific to strings, including the mechanism the engine actually relies on.
  2. Are all primitives immutable in the same way? Section 2 — yes, but the rule only has teeth for one of them, and that is why you have never wondered about it for numbers.
  3. Is there a distinction — some mutable, some not? Sections 2 and 4 — not among primitives, but among the three different things people call immutability, and that is almost certainly what you are sensing.
  4. The complete picture. Sections 3, 5 and 6 — what actually happens when you write the assignment, what it costs, and how the engine avoids paying.

Section 1 — What is specific to strings

Resolution 8 Section 3 made the case that for numbers and booleans immutability was not decided at all — it is what "value" means — while for strings it genuinely was a decision, and gave three reasons: safe sharing, hash-key integrity, and interning. Let me make the second and third concrete, because they are the ones that would actually break the language.

Hash-key integrity. Resolution 14 Section 9 established that every property key in JavaScript is a string or a Symbol. That means the property table of every object in your program is keyed by strings. Now suppose strings were mutable:

const key = "name";
const user = { };
user[key] = "Devansh";      // stored under the string "name"

key[0] = "g";               // if this worked, key is now "game"

user.name                   // is the property still findable?
                            // the object's hash table hashed "name".
                            // the string that was hashed is now "game".

The stored hash no longer matches the string it was computed from. Every object that used that string as a key would have a corrupted table, and the corruption would be invisible until the next lookup missed. Engines cache a string's hash inside the string precisely because it can never change — if it could, the cache would have to be invalidated across every table in the heap, which is not a thing that can be done.

So this is not a stylistic preference. Every property access in JavaScript rests on string immutability, and Resolution 14's whole account of the dot depends on it.

Interning. Because strings cannot change, identical strings can safely be the same object in memory. V8 keeps a table of internalized strings, and a literal appearing in a thousand places is stored once:

"a" + "b" === "ab"          // true — and comparison here can be a
                            // pointer comparison, not a character walk

Two consequences. Equality of interned strings becomes O(1) instead of O(n). And a large program with thousands of repeated property names — "length", "name", "type" — pays for each of them once. Mutability would make both impossible: you could not share a buffer if anyone might write to it.

Section 2 — Is it uniform across the seven? Yes — but the rule only bites once

Here is the direct answer to your distinction question. All seven primitives are immutable, and none is more or less so than another. But look at what "immutable" can even mean for each:

PrimitiveIs there syntax that looks like mutating it?
numberNo. There is no way to write "change the 5." x = x + 1 rebinds; it does not alter the 5.
bigintNo. Same.
booleanNo. There are two values and no operation that edits one.
nullNo. One value, no parts.
undefinedNo. Same.
symbolNo. sym.description is read-only; there is no writable field.
stringYes. s[0] = "x" and s.length = 2 are both syntactically valid and look exactly like mutations.

That is the whole asymmetry. Strings are the only primitive with indexed access, so they are the only primitive where you can write something that looks like an in-place edit. For the other six the rule is true but empty — you would have to invent syntax before you could violate it.

This is exactly the point Resolution 8 Section 1 was circling. Strings have parts — that is why "primitives are atomic" was rejected as a definition — but those parts are computed, not stored. s[0] is a question whose answer is a freshly constructed one-character string; it does not name a slot. So there is nothing to assign to, and the assignment has nowhere to land.

The clean comparison is an array, because an array is also an indexed sequence and the syntax is identical:

const arr = ["a", "b", "c"];
arr[0] = "X";      // works. arr is now ["X","b","c"]

const str = "abc";
str[0] = "X";      // does not. str is still "abc"

Same syntax, opposite outcome, and the reason is not that one is "a collection" and the other is not. It is that arr is an object and str is a value. The array has real, addressable, writable slots; the string does not. Resolution 8's whole framework in one pair of lines.

Section 3 — What actually happens when you write s[0] = "x", and the card's correction

Now the mechanism, which is a direct payoff from Resolution 14 Section 8. Two independent things go wrong, and either one alone would be enough.

First, boxing. A property assignment on a primitive triggers ToObject, which builds a temporary String wrapper. The assignment targets the wrapper, and the wrapper is discarded immediately afterwards. Even if the write succeeded, it would be written to an object that no longer exists — which is precisely what Resolution 14 demonstrated with s.foo = 1; s.foo // undefined.

Second, the wrapper's index properties are read-only. A String wrapper is a String exotic object, and the specification gives its index properties fixed attributes. You can inspect them:

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Object("abc"), "0")
// { value: "a", writable: false, enumerable: true, configurable: false }

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Object("abc"), "length")
// { value: 3, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }

writable: false on both. So the write fails on the wrapper as well as being pointless.

And now the correction. Your card says the assignment "silently does nothing." That was true in 1997 and it is not true in the code you are writing today:

// sloppy mode — the ES1..ES3 behaviour, still the default in a bare script
const s = "abc";
s[0] = "X";        // no error
s                  // "abc"

// strict mode
"use strict";
const s = "abc";
s[0] = "X";
// TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property '0' of string 'abc'

Silent failure was the ES1 rule: assignment to a non-writable property just did not happen. ES5 (December 2009) added strict mode partly to fix exactly this class of silent failure, and made it throw. And strict mode is not opt-in any more in most modern code — ES modules and class bodies are strict automatically. So if you are writing import/export, or anything inside a class, this throws without you asking for it.

The card's phrasing describes the legacy behaviour. The accurate version: it fails, and whether it fails loudly or silently depends on strictness, which in modern code is on by default.

Section 4 — The three different things called "immutability"

Your question — "is there some distinction, some immutable and some mutable" — is answered "no" among primitives. But I suspect the distinction you are feeling is real and lives one level up. Three unrelated mechanisms in JavaScript all get described as "you cannot change it," and they are constantly confused:

1. Value immutability
(primitives)		A property of the value itself. The number 5 cannot be edited because there is no "the 5." Applies to all seven primitives, always, with no opt-out and no opt-in. This is Resolution 8's subject.
2. Binding immutability
(const)		A property of the variable, not the value. const means the binding cannot be pointed at something else. It says nothing at all about the value.
3. Object freezing
(Object.freeze)		A runtime property of a particular object, set by you. Not a type-level fact, and — crucially — shallow.

Watch all three fail to be each other:

// const does NOT freeze the value
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.push(4);        // fine. The binding did not change; the object did.
arr = [];           // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

// freeze is SHALLOW
const o = Object.freeze({ a: { b: 1 } });
o.a = 5;            // fails — the outer object is frozen
o.a.b = 2;          // WORKS. The inner object was never frozen.
o                   // { a: { b: 2 } }

// and a primitive needs neither
let s = "abc";      // not const, not frozen
s[0] = "X";         // still cannot be mutated. The value is immutable
                    // regardless of how the binding is declared.

That last one is the sharpest. Immutability of a string has nothing to do with const. A let string is exactly as immutable as a const one; what const stops is you pointing the name somewhere else.

So the distinction you were reaching for exists, and it is: values versus bindings versus objects. Primitives are uniformly immutable as values. Objects are uniformly mutable unless you freeze them one at a time. And const is orthogonal to both.

Section 5 — The consequence: every string operation returns a new string

Because there is no in-place edit, every method on String.prototype is non-mutating. There are no exceptions — not one method modifies the string it was called on:

let s = "hello";

s.toUpperCase();     // "HELLO"  — returned
s;                   // "hello"  — unchanged

s.replace("h", "j"); // "jello"  — returned
s;                   // "hello"  — unchanged

s = s.toUpperCase(); // THIS is how you "change" a string:
                     // rebind the variable to a different string.

Compare Array.prototype, where you have to know which is which, and getting it wrong is a classic bug:

  MUTATE the array          RETURN a new array
  ----------------          ------------------
  push, pop                 map, filter, slice
  shift, unshift            concat, flat
  splice                    join (returns a string)
  sort      <-- mutates!
  reverse   <-- mutates!
  fill, copyWithin

sort and reverse mutating in place is a genuine trap, because they also return the array, so const sorted = arr.sort() looks like it made a copy and did not. The language finally addressed this in ES2023 with non-mutating twins:

const a = [3, 1, 2];
a.toSorted()      // [1, 2, 3]  — a is untouched
a.toReversed()    // [2, 1, 3]
a.with(0, 9)      // [9, 1, 2]  — a copy with one index changed
a.toSpliced(1, 1) // [3, 2]
a                 // [3, 1, 2]  — still

Which is worth noticing as a trend: twenty-eight years after strings were made immutable, the committee added array methods that behave the way strings always have. The immutable style won on merit, not on necessity.

Section 6 — What it costs, and how the engine avoids paying

The obvious objection to immutable strings is performance. If every operation makes a new string, then building one in a loop should be catastrophic:

let s = "";
for (let i = 0; i < 100000; i++) {
  s += "x";        // a new string of length i, 100,000 times?
}                  // that would be ~5 billion characters copied. O(n^2).

On the specification's semantics, that is exactly what happens. In reality it is fast, and the reason is a mechanism worth knowing because it is the same trick as Resolution 8 Section 4 and Resolution 9 Section 6: the engine implements something cheaper and hides it behind identical behaviour.

V8 does not build a new flat string on every concatenation. It builds a ConsString — a small node holding pointers to its two halves, and nothing else:

  s += "x"  does NOT copy. It allocates:

        ConsString
        /        \
    (old s)      "x"

  repeated 100,000 times, you get a tree of 100,000 tiny nodes.
  Total copying so far: zero.

  Then the first time anyone needs the actual characters — an
  index, a comparison, a call into C++ — the engine FLATTENS the
  tree into one contiguous buffer, once, in O(n).

This structure is generally called a rope, and it is why the naive loop is linear in practice rather than quadratic. The same family of tricks includes sliced strings, where s.slice(10, 20) stores an offset and a length into the original buffer instead of copying twenty characters.

You cannot observe any of it, and that is the point — Resolution 8's argument again in a third setting: when a value cannot change, sharing and copying are indistinguishable, so the engine is free to share. Immutability is what makes the optimisation legal. A mutable string could not be a rope, could not be interned, could not have a cached hash, and could not share a buffer with a slice of itself.

So the honest accounting is not "immutability costs performance and we accept it for safety." It is: immutability costs performance in the semantics and buys it back in the implementation, and the implementation wins.

What this resolves

Why exactly are strings not mutable?Section 1 builds on Resolution 8 with the two string-specific reasons made concrete. Hash-key integrity: every property key in JavaScript is a string (Resolution 14 Section 9), engines cache a string's hash inside the string because it can never change, and a mutable key would corrupt every property table that used it — invisibly, until the next lookup missed. Interning: identical strings can share one buffer, making equality a pointer comparison; mutability would make sharing unsafe.
Are all primitives immutable the same way?Section 2: yes — but the rule is vacuous for six of them. Strings are the only primitive with indexed access, so they are the only one where you can write something that looks like a mutation. For numbers, booleans, symbols and the rest you would have to invent syntax before you could violate the rule. That is why the card is about strings.
Why does arr[0] = "X" work when str[0] = "X" does not?Section 2: same syntax, opposite outcome, and the reason is not "collection versus scalar" — it is that arr is an object and str is a value. The array has real writable slots; the string's parts are computed, not stored, exactly as Resolution 8 Section 1 argued.
Correction to the cardSection 3: it does not silently do nothing any more. Silent failure is the ES1 rule; ES5 (2009) strict mode made it throw, and ES modules and class bodies are strict automatically. In modern code you get TypeError: Cannot assign to read only property '0'.
What actually happens mechanically?Section 3: two independent failures. The assignment boxes the primitive into a temporary String wrapper that is discarded immediately (Resolution 14 Section 8) — and that wrapper's index properties are specified as writable: false, configurable: false, which you can inspect directly. Either alone would be enough.
Is there a distinction — some mutable, some not?Section 4: not among primitives, but three unrelated things are all called "immutability" and that is almost certainly what you are sensing. Value immutability (the primitive itself; no opt-out). Binding immutability (const — a property of the variable, which is why const arr = []; arr.push(4) works). Object freezing (per-object, at runtime, and shallow — Object.freeze({a:{b:1}}) does not protect b). And a let string is exactly as immutable as a const one.
The complete pictureSection 5: every String.prototype method returns a new string; none mutates. Contrast arrays, where sort and reverse mutate and return, so const sorted = arr.sort() is a classic bug — addressed in ES2023 with toSorted, toReversed, with and toSpliced. Twenty-eight years on, the committee gave arrays the behaviour strings always had.
What does it cost?Section 6: on the semantics, s += "x" in a loop is O(n²). In reality it is linear, because V8 builds a ConsString — a two-pointer node — and flattens the tree once, lazily, when someone finally needs the characters. Plus sliced strings that store an offset instead of copying. Immutability is what makes all of that legal: a mutable string could not be a rope, could not be interned, could not cache its hash, could not share a buffer. The cost is paid in the specification and refunded in the implementation.

Strings are the only primitive where immutability is a rule you can notice, because they are the only one with parts you can point at. And the parts you point at are answers to questions, not places — which is why the assignment has nowhere to land.

pieces.title: Resolution 17 — Q18: null and undefined, as types and as values
pieces.content:
Buried in the middle of this follow-up is one of the best questions in the whole set, and you almost apologise for it as a digression. It is not a digression — it is the thing that has been making this topic feel unstable:

"JavaScript has seven primitive types... these are types that define the shape of a value. But in many places I have also seen undefined and null being used as values as well. So which is it? Are these types, are these values, are these both? Does it depend on context?"

They are both, the specification is completely unambiguous about it, and the confusion is a fact about English rather than about JavaScript. Section 1 resolves it, and once resolved it stays resolved — the same confusion is sitting inside Q19's follow-up, where you work your way to the right answer yourself.

The rest of the follow-up asks for the undefined/null distinction to be made real rather than recited. Sections 4 through 8 do that, including the historical question — why does the language have two of these at all? — which has a clean answer: one of them was inherited and the other was invented, and a dynamically typed language has no choice but to invent it.

The asks:

  1. Are null and undefined types, or values, or both? Sections 1, 2 and 3 — both, and here is why that is not a contradiction.
  2. Why does the syntax reinforce the confusion? Section 3 — because the two are not even symmetrical: one is a keyword and one is not.
  3. The practical distinction, properly. Sections 4 and 5 — every place each one comes from, exhaustively.
  4. How did this come up in the first place — why two? Section 6 — null was inherited from Java; undefined had to be invented.
  5. Where the difference actually matters in code. Sections 7 and 8 — four places where they behave differently and most people do not know it.

Section 1 — Both. And the word you need is unit type.

Resolution 5 defined what a type is: a set of values, together with the operations that apply to them. Hold onto the first half — a set of values — and count the members of each of JavaScript's types:

TypeHow many values are in itSome of them
Numberabout 18 quintillion (264 bit patterns, minus the NaN collapse)0, 1, -0, 0.5, NaN, Infinity
Stringunbounded"", "a", "hello"
BigIntunbounded0n, 1n, 2n**128n
SymbolunboundedSymbol(), Symbol.iterator
Boolean2true, false
Null1null
Undefined1undefined

Look at the last two rows. The type Null contains exactly one value, and that value is null. The type Undefined contains exactly one value, and that value is undefined.

A type with exactly one member is called a unit type, and it is a perfectly ordinary thing. A set with one element is still a set. There is nothing degenerate about it.

And now the source of your confusion, stated plainly: when a type has exactly one value, there is no practical reason to give the type and the value different names, so nobody does. When someone says "Boolean" you know they mean the type, because there are two values and they are called true and false. When someone says "null," the type and the value are the same word, so which one they mean is determined entirely by the sentence they are in. That is an ambiguity in how we talk, not an ambiguity in the language.

Your instinct — "are these both? does it depend on the context?" — is exactly right. It depends on context, and the context always disambiguates.

This is not JavaScript-specific, which is reassuring. Python has the type NoneType whose single value is None — and note that Python bothered to give the type a distinct name, which is why Python programmers rarely get confused about this. Haskell has (), pronounced "unit," a type with one value also written (). Kotlin has Unit. Same structure everywhere.

Section 2 — How the specification keeps them apart

ECMA-262 is careful about this even though ordinary speech is not, and knowing its convention makes the spec readable:

  the TYPE is written capitalised:      Null,  Undefined,  Number,  String
  the VALUE is written as the literal:  null,  undefined,  5,       "abc"

  "The Null type has exactly one value, called null."
  "The Undefined type has exactly one value, called undefined."

Those are close to the specification's actual sentences, and they say precisely what Section 1 said.

The spec also has an internal operation it writes as Type(v) — "the type of the value v" — which is a specification-level function, not something you can call. It exists so that the standard can write rules like "if Type(x) is Null, then…". That operation is what typeof is a crude, public, partially broken approximation of — which is Q19.

Section 3 — The syntax is asymmetrical, which makes it worse

Here is something that quietly reinforces your confusion, and it is worth knowing because it is genuinely strange: null and undefined are not the same kind of thing syntactically at all.

  null       is a KEYWORD. A reserved word in the grammar, like
             `true`, `false`, `if`, `return`. It is a literal.
             You cannot use it as a variable name.

  undefined  is NOT a keyword. It is an ordinary IDENTIFIER that
             happens to resolve to a property of the global object.

You can verify the second claim directly:

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(globalThis, "undefined")
// { value: undefined, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }

undefined is a property, like Number and Math are properties (Resolution 14 Section 6). It is looked up through the scope chain like any other name.

And in ES1 through ES3 it was writable. You could genuinely do this, and it would break code across the entire page:

undefined = 42;          // legal in 1997. Nightmare.

ES5 (2009) made the global property non-writable and non-configurable, which is why the descriptor above says writable: false. But the deeper problem never went away — undefined is still just a name, so it can still be shadowed by a local binding:

(function (undefined) {
  typeof undefined      // "number"  (!!)
})(5);

This is why older library code is full of void 0, which is an expression that always evaluates to the real undefined no matter what any identifier has been bound to:

void 0            // undefined — the void operator evaluates its operand
                  // and returns undefined, unconditionally.

You will still see it in minified bundles, because void 0 is shorter than undefined.

So the two are not parallel: null is a literal baked into the grammar, and undefined is a global variable that happens to hold the only value of its type. That asymmetry is pure history — Section 6 — and it is one more reason the pair feels less tidy than it should.

Section 4 — Everywhere undefined comes from

You restated the card's answer and said you still do not fully have it. The card says "absence the language supplies by accident," which is evocative but not checkable. Here is the checkable version: these are all the ways the language hands you undefined, and there are no others.

// 1. A declared binding that has not been assigned
let x;
x                            // undefined

// 2. A function parameter that was not passed
function f(a) { return a; }
f()                          // undefined

// 3. A function that returns nothing
function g() { }
g()                          // undefined

// 4. Reading a property that does not exist
({}).nope                    // undefined
// ...including after deleting one
const o = { a: 1 };
delete o.a;
o.a                          // undefined

// 5. Reading past the end of an array, or a hole in it
[1, 2][5]                    // undefined
const holey = [1, , 3];
holey[1]                     // undefined

// 6. A destructuring pattern with nothing to match
const { missing } = {};      // missing is undefined

// 7. The void operator
void 0                       // undefined

Notice the common thread, which is sharper than "by accident": in every case, the language was asked for something that was never there, and had to return something. undefined is the answer to "you asked, and there is nothing here." It is not a decision anybody made about the data; it is a report about a lookup.

Section 5 — Everywhere null comes from

Much shorter, and that is the point:

// 1. You wrote it.
let selectedUser = null;     // "deliberately nothing, for now"

// 2. An API chose it as its "not found" answer.
document.getElementById("nope")   // null
/x/.exec("abc")                   // null
JSON.parse("null")                // null

// 3. The end of a prototype chain.
Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype)   // null

That third one is quietly the most instructive. Resolution 14 Section 7 showed [[Get]] walking the prototype chain until it hits null. It uses null rather than undefined because the end of the chain is a deliberate structural fact — "this object intentionally has no parent" — not a failed lookup. The language is following its own convention.

So the distinction, stated properly:

undefined means "nothing was ever put here." It is produced by the runtime as the result of a lookup that found nothing.

null means "nothing is here, and that is the intended state." It is produced only by a decision — yours, or an API author's.

The difference is not in the absence. It is in whether the absence was chosen.

Section 6 — Why the language has two at all

This is your "how did this thing actually come up in the first place" ask, and it has a real answer.

null was inherited. Resolution 3 covered the Netscape/Sun deal of 1995 and the instruction to make the new language look like Java. Java has null. So JavaScript has null, spelled the same way, meaning roughly the same thing. There is nothing deeper to it than that — and Q19 will show that even the bug in typeof null comes from the same imitation.

undefined had to be invented, because Java's situation does not apply. Here is the argument, and it is the interesting half.

In Java, every variable has a declared type, and the compiler knows it before the program runs:

int    count;     // if it were a field: automatically 0
String name;      // if it were a field: automatically null
                  // and as a LOCAL, the compiler simply refuses to
                  // let you read it before you assign it —
                  // "variable might not have been initialized"

Two mechanisms cover the gap. Fields get a type-appropriate default, and locals are protected by definite assignment analysis at compile time. Neither mechanism is available to JavaScript:

  • There is no declared type, so there is no such thing as a type-appropriate default. What would let x; default to? 0? ""? false? Any choice would be wrong most of the time, and — worse — indistinguishable from a value the programmer had actually assigned.
  • There is no compile step that could reject reading an unassigned variable. JavaScript in 1995 parsed and ran; there was no phase in which to complain.

So the language needed a runtime value meaning "this exists but has never been given anything," and it needed that value to be distinguishable from every value a programmer might deliberately assign — including null. If let x; defaulted to null, then you could never tell "I never set this" apart from "I set this to nothing on purpose," and Section 7's default-parameter behaviour would be impossible.

Hence undefined: a second empty value, whose entire job is to be the one the programmer did not choose.

That is why the criticism you sometimes hear — "JavaScript is badly designed because it has two nulls" — is mostly wrong. Having two is a consequence of being dynamically typed without a compile step. Python solved the same problem differently, by raising NameError when you read an unbound name, which is an option JavaScript did not take because a script that threw on a typo would have been hostile to its 1995 audience. What is fair criticism is the execution: that undefined is a mutable-ish global identifier rather than a keyword (Section 3), and that typeof null lies (Q19).

Section 7 — Where the difference actually bites

Four places where they behave differently, and the first two are the ones people are genuinely surprised by.

1. Default parameters trigger on undefined only.

function f(a = 1) { return a; }

f()             // 1     — nothing passed
f(undefined)    // 1     — explicitly undefined still triggers the default
f(null)         // null  (!!) — null is a VALUE. The default does not fire.

This is the language's own distinction, made operational. A default parameter means "if nothing was supplied" — and null was supplied. It is Section 5's rule enforced by the grammar. Destructuring defaults behave identically:

const { a = 1 } = { a: undefined };   // a is 1
const { a = 1 } = { a: null };        // a is null

2. JSON.stringify treats them completely differently.

JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: null })   // '{"b":null}'
                                            //  the `a` key VANISHED

JSON.stringify([undefined, null])           // '[null,null]'
                                            //  in an array it becomes null,
                                            //  because arrays cannot have holes
                                            //  in JSON

JSON has null in its grammar and has no notion of undefined at all, so undefined object properties are dropped and undefined array elements are coerced. Two different repairs for the same missing concept. If you send { a: undefined } to a server expecting to clear a field, nothing arrives; send { a: null } and the field is explicitly cleared. That is a real API bug that people ship.

3. A property set to undefined still exists.

const o = { a: undefined };
o.a                  // undefined
"a" in o             // true      — the key IS there
Object.keys(o)       // ["a"]

const p = { a: 1 };
delete p.a;
p.a                  // undefined — same reading!
"a" in p             // false     — but the key is gone
Object.keys(p)       // []

Reading the property gives undefined in both cases and they are not the same object. in and Object.keys tell them apart; === against undefined does not. This is why in and Object.hasOwn exist.

4. They coerce differently to numbers.

Number(null)        // 0        null + 1  ->  1
Number(undefined)   // NaN      undefined + 1  ->  NaN

String(null)        // "null"
String(undefined)   // "undefined"

Number(null) being 0 is an ES1 inheritance from the "null is like zero" tradition in C, and it is inconsistent with everything else about null. It is a good reason never to let either value into arithmetic.

Section 8 — The one place the language deliberately merges them

There is exactly one rule in the language that treats null and undefined as interchangeable, and it is deliberate:

null == undefined     // true   — the ONLY == pairing they participate in
null === undefined    // false  — different types

null == 0             // false
null == false         // false
null == ""            // false
undefined == 0        // false

Loose equality has a special rule saying these two, and only these two, are equal to each other and to nothing else. That is not an accident of coercion — it is a written clause. And it produces the one genuinely useful idiom involving ==:

if (x == null) { ... }
// means exactly: x is null OR x is undefined.
// This is the idiomatic "is it absent?" check, and it is the one
// case where == over === is correct rather than sloppy.

ES2020 turned the same idea into two operators, which is the modern way to write it:

x ?? "default"        // "default" only if x is null or undefined
x?.prop               // undefined only if x is null or undefined

And ?? is worth contrasting with ||, because the difference is the entire reason it was added:

0  || "default"       // "default"   — 0 is falsy, so || replaced it
0  ?? "default"       // 0           — 0 is not absent, so ?? kept it

"" || "default"       // "default"
"" ?? "default"       // ""

|| asks "is this falsy," which is a much wider net than "is this absent" — and that net catches 0 and "", which are usually real data. Which is the bridge into your next two follow-ups: Q20 and Q21 are about exactly that falsy list, and ?? exists because ||'s use of it was the wrong question most of the time.

Section 9 — What to actually do

Short, since the mechanism is now clear:

  • Never assign undefined yourself. It is the language's word for "you did not choose." Writing x = undefined is claiming an absence you in fact chose, which is what null is for. (The exception: passing undefined deliberately to trigger a default parameter, per Section 7.)
  • Use null for intentional emptiness — a cleared selection, a field explicitly blanked, a "no result" return.
  • Check for both at once with x == null, ??, or ?., unless you specifically need to tell them apart.
  • Be deliberate at API boundaries. undefined disappears through JSON; null survives. If "clear this field" must reach a server, it has to be null.

What this resolves

Are null and undefined types, or values, or both?Section 1: both, and your instinct that it depends on context is exactly right. The type Null is a set containing exactly one value, and that value is null. Same for Undefined. A type with one member is called a unit type and is perfectly ordinary — a set with one element is still a set. When a type has only one value, nobody bothers giving the type and the value different names, so the same word does both jobs. The ambiguity is in English, not in JavaScript.
Is this a JavaScript oddity?Section 1: no. Python's NoneType/None, Haskell's (), Kotlin's Unit. Python avoids the confusion only by naming the type differently.
How does the spec keep them apart?Section 2: by capitalisation — Null and Undefined are types, null and undefined are values — and by the internal Type(v) operation, of which typeof is a crude and partly broken public approximation (Q19).
Why does it feel inconsistent?Section 3, and this is a real asymmetry: null is a keyword baked into the grammar; undefined is an ordinary identifier resolving to a property of the global object. It was writable in ES1–ES3 (undefined = 42 was legal), and even today it can be shadowed — (function(undefined){ typeof undefined })(5) gives "number". Hence void 0 in older and minified code.
Where does undefined come from?Section 4, exhaustively — seven sources: unassigned binding, missing argument, no return value, missing property, deleted property, past-the-end or hole in an array, unmatched destructuring, and void. The thread: in every case the language was asked for something that was never there. It is a report about a lookup, not a decision about data.
Where does null come from?Section 5, and the list is short because that is the point: you wrote it, or an API author chose it (getElementById, regex.exec, JSON.parse("null")). Plus the end of a prototype chain — which uses null rather than undefined because "no parent" is a deliberate structural fact, not a failed lookup. The difference is not the absence; it is whether the absence was chosen.
Why does the language have two?Section 6: null was inherited from Java (the look-like-Java mandate of 1995). undefined had to be invented, because Java's two coping mechanisms — type-appropriate field defaults and compile-time definite-assignment analysis — both require declared types and a compile step, and JavaScript has neither. So it needed a runtime value for "never assigned" that was distinguishable from anything a programmer might deliberately assign, including null. Having two is a consequence of being dynamically typed without a compiler, not a design failure.
Where does the difference actually bite?Section 7, four places. Default parameters fire on undefined only — f(null) returns null, not the default, because null was supplied. JSON.stringify drops undefined properties entirely but keeps null — so "clear this field" must be null to reach a server. A property set to undefined still exists — "a" in o tells it apart from a deleted one, === undefined does not. And Number(null) is 0 while Number(undefined) is NaN.
Where they are merged on purposeSection 8: null == undefined is true and they are loosely equal to nothing else — a written clause, not a coercion accident. Hence the one idiom where == beats ===: x == null means "absent, either way." ES2020 formalised it as ?? and ?.. And the contrast that bridges to your next follow-ups: 0 || "d" is "d" but 0 ?? "d" is 0 — ?? exists because "is it falsy" was the wrong question most of the time.

A type is a set of values. Some sets have one element. null is the only member of Null and undefined is the only member of Undefined — so the word does double duty, and the sentence tells you which job it is doing. And the language has two of them because a dynamic language must be able to tell "never assigned" from "deliberately empty," and only one of those two was available to borrow from Java.

pieces.title: Resolution 18 — Q19: what typeof actually is, and where the null bug cuts
pieces.content:
You open by saying you asked something similar before, and you did — Q6's follow-up, answered in Resolution 5. That piece established three things this one will not repeat: the mechanism (a tagged-union value representation where the object tag was 000 and null was the machine null pointer, all zero bits, so it answered "object" without being asked); that the fix was proposed and died; and the full anomaly table. If any of that is hazy, Resolution 5 Sections 1 and 6 are the place.

What this follow-up adds is a different question entirely, and it is the one worth the space:

"What exactly is typeof? Is it a function, is it a property, what is it? What is it applicable to — types, values, functions? With whom can I actually use it and it would be valid?"

That has never been answered here, and it is a genuinely good question because typeof is grammatically unlike almost everything else you write. It is also the operator with the strangest single superpower in the language — it is the only construct in JavaScript that can read a variable that does not exist without throwing — and that superpower has a hole in it that was punched in 2015.

And you talked yourself to the correct answer mid-dictation. You wrote, roughly: typeof obviously applies to values only, and typeof null is asking "what is the type of this value," where the value is null, so it should have returned "null." That is right, all of it. Section 3 confirms it against your own words and shows the one place your reasoning stops a step early.

The asks:

  1. What should typeof null have returned? Section 1 — short, since Resolution 5 argued it.
  2. What does typeof return for the other primitives? Section 2 — the complete table, with the anomalies marked.
  3. What is typeof — a function, a property, an operator? Section 4 — an operator, and the proofs matter.
  4. What is it applicable to? With whom is it valid? Sections 5 and 6 — everything, including things that do not exist, which is its whole historical purpose.
  5. Where does this bug actually cut us? Section 7 — three real bug patterns, one demonstrated end to end.
  6. Do we have to hard-code the check? Section 8 — yes, and that is fine.

Section 1 — What it should have returned

"null". That is the whole answer, and Resolution 5 Section 3 makes the case: a value whose type is Null should report "null", exactly as a value whose type is Undefined reports "undefined". There is no coherent reading on which null belongs to the Object type — Resolution 17 just established that the type Null is a set with exactly one member, and Object is a different set that does not contain it.

The strongest evidence is that the engine agrees with you everywhere except in this one operator:

Object.prototype.toString.call(null)   // "[object Null]"
typeof null                            // "object"

Same value, same runtime, two different answers, and only one of them is dispatching on the 1995 tag bits.

Section 2 — The complete typeof table

You asked what the operator returns for the other primitives. All eight possible results, in one place:

Operandtypeof givesIs that the type's name?
undefined"undefined"yes
true"boolean"yes
42, NaN, Infinity, -0"number"yes
42n"bigint"yes
"abc""string"yes
Symbol()"symbol"yes
{}, [], new Date(), /x/, new Map()"object"yes — but uselessly coarse
null"object"NO — the bug
function(){}, class{}, async()=>{}"function"NO — not a type at all

Two things to take from this rather than one.

The six clean rows are genuinely clean. For every primitive except null, typeof is correct, exact, and the right tool. typeof x === "string" is not a workaround; it is the check.

There are two anomalies, not one. null reporting "object" is the bug you asked about. But "function" is an anomaly in the opposite direction: there is no Function type. Resolution 12 Section 7 listed the eight language types and Function is not among them — a function is an Object that additionally has a [[Call]] method (Resolution 14 Section 4). So typeof returns a ninth string for a type that does not exist. That one is deliberate: in 1995, "can I call this?" was a more useful question than "is this an object?", so it got its own answer.

And "object" for everything non-primitive is the third weakness. It cannot distinguish an array from a date from a plain object from a Map. That is not a bug, it is just the operator being coarse — but it is why Array.isArray had to exist.

Section 3 — Your own reasoning, checked

You wrote, working it out as you dictated: what I previously had in my mind was that typeof returns the type of a value — so with x = 5, typeof x should return "number" — but then typeof number should also… and is null here actually a value itself rather than a type, which is the confusion I acknowledged in the other question, and typeof of course obviously applies to values only, so typeof null is asking "what is the type of this value," and that value is null, and it should have returned "null."

Every step of that is correct. Confirming it point by point:

"typeof returns the type of a value." Yes. More precisely: it evaluates its operand to a value, determines which of the eight types that value belongs to, and returns a string naming it.

"typeof obviously applies to values only." Yes, and this is the key move. It cannot apply to types, because types are not values in JavaScript — there is no way to get hold of "the Number type" as a thing you can pass around. Resolution 5 Section 8 made this point: types exist in the specification and in the tag bits, not in the value space.

"but then typeof number should also…" — you trail off here, and it is worth finishing, because you can actually run it:

typeof Number      // "function"

Not "type", not "number". Why? Because Number is not a type — it is an identifier, which evaluates to a value: the constructor function object from Resolution 14 Section 4. typeof did what it always does — took a value, reported its type — and that value happens to be a function. This is the cleanest possible demonstration of your own conclusion. There is no way to hand typeof a type, because there is nothing to hand it.

"is null here actually a value itself and not the type." Yes — and Resolution 17 Section 1 is the full answer: null is the sole value of the type Null, and the word does double duty in English because the type has only one member. In typeof null, the word is unambiguously the value, because typeof's operand position can only hold an expression.

"so it should have returned null." Yes. Section 1.

The one step further your reasoning does not take: you say typeof applies to values only, which is right about its semantics. But grammatically its operand is an expression, not a value — and that distinction is where the interesting behaviour in Sections 5 and 6 comes from. An expression can be a variable that does not exist, and that changes what typeof can do.

Section 4 — What typeof is: an operator

Now the direct question. typeof is a unary prefix operator — the same grammatical category as !, -, void, delete and await. It is part of the grammar, not part of the library.

It is not a function, and it is not a property. Four proofs, because the distinction has consequences:

1. It is a reserved word in the grammar. You cannot name a variable typeof. You could if it were a function, because function names are ordinary identifiers.

2. It has no value of its own. A function is an object you can refer to (Resolution 14 Section 4). typeof is not:

const f = Math.max;    // fine — a function is a value
const g = typeof;      // SyntaxError — there is nothing to refer to
typeof.call(null, 5);  // SyntaxError
[1,2].map(typeof);     // SyntaxError — cannot be passed anywhere

3. The parentheses you sometimes see are not a call. This is the thing that makes it look like a function:

typeof(5)      // "number"
typeof (5)     // "number"  — identical; the space proves it
typeof 5       // "number"  — no parentheses needed at all

Those parentheses are ordinary grouping parentheses around the expression 5. Compare Math.max(5), where removing the parentheses gives you the function itself rather than a call. With typeof there is nothing to remove them from.

4. It has operator precedence, and it can bite you. Unary operators bind tighter than binary ones:

typeof 5 + 1        // "number1"  (!!)  — parsed as (typeof 5) + 1
typeof (5 + 1)      // "number"         — what you probably meant

A function call would have consumed its argument list unambiguously. An operator grabs only as much as precedence allows. This is a real source of bugs in conditions like typeof x === "string" — which happens to work, because === binds looser than typeof, but the reason it works is precedence rather than luck.

And one small pleasure that follows from it being an operator: it composes with itself, because its result is a value like any other.

typeof typeof 5     // "string"  — typeof 5 is "number", and that is a string

Section 5 — What it is applicable to: everything

Your question — "with whom can I use it and it would be valid?" — has an unusually simple answer:

typeof is valid on any expression whatsoever. There is no operand that makes it a syntax error and, with one exception in Section 6, none that makes it throw.

This is worth appreciating against the contrast you have just met. Resolution 14 Section 8 established that the dot throws on null and undefined, because ToObject has no wrapper for them. typeof has no such restriction, because it does not need to build anything — it reads the type tag and returns a string.

typeof undefined         // "undefined"    — the dot would throw here
typeof null              // "object"       — and here
typeof NaN               // "number"
typeof Symbol.iterator   // "symbol"
typeof Math              // "object"
typeof Number            // "function"
typeof (() => {})        // "function"
typeof class {}          // "function"
typeof (1 + 1)           // "number"       — any expression, evaluated first
typeof getUser().name    // whatever that turns out to be

Section 6 — The superpower: reading a variable that does not exist

And here is the thing that makes typeof genuinely special, which follows from the "operand is an expression" point at the end of Section 3.

Reading an undeclared variable is an error in JavaScript:

nope
// ReferenceError: nope is not defined

But:

typeof nope        // "undefined"   — no error at all

typeof is the only operator in the language that can be applied to a variable that was never declared without throwing. The specification does this deliberately: when typeof's operand is a Reference that cannot be resolved, it returns "undefined" instead of propagating the error.

This was, for about fifteen years, the entire mechanism of feature detection on the web. Before there was any way to ask "does this browser support X," you asked typeof:

if (typeof XMLHttpRequest !== "undefined") {
  // this browser has it
} else {
  // fall back to ActiveXObject
}

if (typeof module !== "undefined" && module.exports) {
  // we are in CommonJS
} else if (typeof define === "function" && define.amd) {
  // we are in AMD
} else {
  // attach to the global
}

That second pattern is the UMD wrapper, and it was at the top of essentially every distributed JavaScript library for a decade. It only works because typeof does not throw on a name that is not there.

And the hole in it, punched in 2015. The guarantee "typeof never throws" is no longer strictly true, because of the temporal dead zone:

typeof tdz;        // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'tdz' before initialization
let tdz = 1;

A let or const binding exists from the top of its block but cannot be touched until its declaration runs, and typeof is not exempted. So the rule is now:

typeof is safe on a name that does not exist at all, and unsafe on a name that exists but has not been initialised yet.

Which is arguably the worst of both worlds — the check is safe in exactly the case where you did not need it and throws in the case where a stale reference is most likely. It is a real cost of let, and Node 4's scope questions will come back to it.

Section 7 — Where the bug actually cuts you

This is the ask Resolution 5 did not cover: not what to use instead, but what goes wrong. Three patterns, and they are all common.

Pattern 1 — the "is this an object?" guard, which is the big one.

function isObject(v) {
  return typeof v === "object";     // looks right. is wrong.
}

isObject({})      // true
isObject([])      // true
isObject(null)    // TRUE  (!!)  — and now null flows into object code

Every function written that way accepts null as an object and then dereferences it. The error does not appear at the guard; it appears one or two frames deeper, as Cannot read properties of null, in code that looks unrelated. That indirection is what makes it expensive to debug.

Pattern 2 — recursive traversal, and here it does something worse than throw. This is a real bug shape, demonstrated end to end:

function deepMerge(target, source) {
  for (const key in source) {
    if (typeof source[key] === "object") {       // the bug
      target[key] = target[key] || {};
      deepMerge(target[key], source[key]);
    } else {
      target[key] = source[key];
    }
  }
  return target;
}

deepMerge({}, { a: null })
// { a: {} }     <-- the null became an EMPTY OBJECT

Nothing threw. The function decided null was an object, created {} for it, recursed over nothing, and returned successfully. A deliberate null — which Resolution 17 established means "intentionally empty" — has been silently replaced with a different value with different meaning. If that object is a settings patch, "clear this field" has become "leave an empty object here," and the wrong thing is now in your database. Every deep-merge, deep-clone, and recursive-validator implementation has to guard against this, and plenty of published ones did not.

Pattern 3 — the classifier that misses.

switch (typeof value) {
