  case "string":  return quote(value);
  case "number":  return String(value);
  case "object":  return serialiseObject(value);   // null arrives here
  default:        return "?";
}

Serialisers, form encoders and validators written as a typeof switch all route null into the object branch. And note that the default case — the one you wrote to catch surprises — never fires, because null did not look surprising.

What the three have in common is worth stating: the bug is never a crash at the point of the mistake. It is a wrong branch taken silently, with the consequence surfacing somewhere else, or not at all. That is the expensive kind.

Section 8 — Do you have to hard-code it? Yes, and it is fine

You asked whether we need to hard-code the check. We do, and the good news is that the hard-coded check is exact, cheap and short:

// null — there is exactly one right test, and it is total
x === null

// "is this a non-null object?" — the guard every codebase needs
x !== null && typeof x === "object"

// including functions, if you want "anything non-primitive"
x !== null && (typeof x === "object" || typeof x === "function")

// arrays specifically
Array.isArray(x)

// "is it null or undefined?" — Resolution 17 Section 8
x == null
x ?? fallback
x?.prop

Two notes on that list.

x === null is not a workaround in the way Number.isNaN is. Resolution 14 explained that NaN genuinely cannot be found with ===, so a separate predicate was required. Here, === works perfectly — null is the single member of its type, so identity comparison against the literal is exact and total. The bug is only in the reporting operator, not in equality.

And the ordering in the guard is deliberate: x !== null && typeof x === "object", with the null test first. It reads as "not null, and an object," which is the sentence you mean. Writing it the other way round works too, but the null check is what carries the meaning and belongs in front.

What this resolves

What should typeof null have returned?Section 1: "null". Resolution 5 Section 3 argued it fully. The clinching evidence: Object.prototype.toString.call(null) is "[object Null]" — the engine knows, and only typeof lies, because only typeof dispatches on the 1995 tag bits.
What does it return for the other primitives?Section 2, all eight results tabulated. The six clean primitive rows are genuinely clean — typeof x === "string" is the correct check, not a workaround. And there are two anomalies, not one: null reporting "object", and "function" being returned for a type that does not exist (a function is an Object with [[Call]]). Plus a third weakness: "object" cannot tell an array from a date from a Map.
Was my reasoning right?Section 3: every step. typeof takes a value, reports its type; it cannot apply to types because types are not values in JavaScript; null in typeof null is unambiguously the value; therefore it should say "null". And the sentence you trailed off on has an answer you can run: typeof Number is "function" — because Number is an identifier evaluating to a constructor function object, not a type. That is your own conclusion demonstrated.
What is typeof — function, property, operator?Section 4: a unary prefix operator, the same grammatical category as !, -, void and delete. Four proofs: it is a reserved word; const g = typeof is a SyntaxError because it has no value to refer to; typeof(5)'s parentheses are ordinary grouping, not a call; and it has operator precedence — typeof 5 + 1 is "number1". It also composes: typeof typeof 5 is "string".
What is it applicable to?Section 5: any expression whatsoever. No operand is a syntax error and, with one exception, none throws — notably including null and undefined, where the dot would throw, because typeof reads a tag rather than building a wrapper.
The superpowerSection 6: typeof is the only construct in the language that can read an undeclared variable without throwing — typeof nope is "undefined" while bare nope is a ReferenceError. This was the mechanism of web feature detection for fifteen years and is why the UMD wrapper at the top of every distributed library works. And the hole: since ES2015, typeof on a let/const in its temporal dead zone does throw — safe on names that do not exist, unsafe on names that exist but are uninitialised.
Where does the bug actually cut us?Section 7, three patterns. The isObject guard — typeof v === "object" lets null through, and the crash surfaces two frames deeper as Cannot read properties of null. Recursive merge/clone, demonstrated: deepMerge({}, {a: null}) returns {a: {}} — nothing throws, and a deliberate null meaning "intentionally empty" has been silently replaced with a different value. The typeof switch, where null routes into the object branch and the default case you wrote to catch surprises never fires. What all three share: not a crash at the mistake, but a wrong branch taken silently.
Do we hard-code it?Section 8: yes — x === null, plus x !== null && typeof x === "object" as the guard every codebase needs. And unlike Number.isNaN, this is not a workaround for broken equality: === works perfectly on null, because null is the single member of its type. Only the reporting operator is wrong.

typeof is an operator, not a function; it applies to expressions, evaluates them to values, and reports which of eight sets that value belongs to. It gets six of seven primitives exactly right, invents a ninth answer for functions, and gives the wrong one for null — and the damage from that last one is never a crash where you made the mistake, but a branch quietly taken somewhere else.

pieces.title: Resolution 19 — Q20: what falsy means, the three zeros, and the n suffix
pieces.content:
Four separate questions here, and the third one — "what is this notation of appending a letter to a number, I saw it in the elaboration and honestly didn't care enough at the time" — is worth answering carefully rather than in passing, because the answer connects straight back to Q10. The n in 0n exists for exactly the reason JavaScript has only one number type, and once you see that, the suffix stops looking like decoration.

The largest question is the last one: was there a need for this concept of truthy and falsy in the first place? There is a real answer, it is historical, and it comes with a bill. Sections 6 and 8.

And the first question — "is it dependent on the context?" — deserves a precise answer rather than a yes or no, because the list is not context-dependent but something adjacent to it is, and confusing the two is the source of the single most common surprise in this area. Section 2.

The asks:

  1. What does "falsy" actually mean? Is it just "interpreted as false"? Section 1 — it names the result of one specific operation.
  2. Is it context-dependent? Section 2 — the list is not, but whether the operation runs at all is, and there are neighbouring algorithms that give different answers.
  3. What is the difference between 0, -0 and 0n? Sections 4 and 5 — three zeros, two types, one bit that flips.
  4. What is the n suffix? Section 5 — and why a language without type declarations has no choice but to put the type in the literal.
  5. How was the list fixed? Why these eight? Section 3 — the list is not a list. It is eight rules, one per type, and it is derivable.
  6. Was the concept needed at all? Sections 6, 7 and 8 — inherited from C, kept for the 1995 audience, and eventually regretted enough to add an operator.

Section 1 — What "falsy" names

Start precisely, because the informal phrasing is what makes it feel vague.

The specification has an internal operation called ToBoolean(v). It takes any value and returns true or false. It is total — every value has an answer — and it is deterministic. That is all.

"Falsy" means: ToBoolean(v) is false. "Truthy" means it is true. There is nothing else to the words.

So "interpreted as false" is right, with one refinement worth making: falsiness is not a property the value carries. The number 0 does not have a flag on it saying "I am falsy." It is a fact about what one function returns when handed that value — in the same way that "even" is not a property stored inside the number 4.

You can call the operation yourself. Boolean(x) and !!x are both just ToBoolean exposed:

Boolean(0)        // false
!!0               // false — ! applies ToBoolean and negates; !! negates twice
Boolean("")       // false
Boolean("0")      // true   (!!) — a non-empty string. Section 7.

Section 2 — "Is it context-dependent?" — the precise answer

Your instinct that context is involved is right, but not in the way you fear. Two separate statements:

The list does not change. ToBoolean(0) is false everywhere, always, in every construct, in every engine. There is no context in which 0 is truthy. The falsy set is fixed by the specification and universal.

What is context-dependent is whether ToBoolean gets called at all. Some syntactic positions invoke it; others use a completely different algorithm. Here is the division, and it is worth having in full because it is the practical part:

  CALLS ToBoolean:
    if (x)                 while (x)          do...while (x)
    for (;x;)              x ? a : b          !x
    x && y                 x || y
    [].filter(Boolean)     Boolean(x)         !!x

  DOES NOT call ToBoolean — uses something else entirely:
    x == y        -> loose equality, a different algorithm
    x === y       -> strict equality
    switch (x)    -> strict equality (===) against each case
    x ?? y        -> tests ONLY for null and undefined
    x?.prop       -> tests ONLY for null and undefined

Two of those deserve demonstrations, because both surprise people.

switch uses ===, not truthiness:

switch (0) {
  case false: return "matched";      // never runs
  default:    return "no match";     // this one
}
// 0 === false is false. Truthiness is not consulted anywhere.

And && / || call ToBoolean but do not return a boolean:

0 || "x"      // "x"     — not true/false. The OPERAND is returned.
"a" && "b"    // "b"
null && "b"   // null
1 && 0        // 0

They test truthiness to decide which operand to return, and then return that operand unchanged. This is why const name = input || "Anonymous" works as a default — and Section 8 is why it is often the wrong default.

The genuinely confusing case, which shows that these really are different algorithms rather than one rule applied differently:

[] == false       // true   (!!)  — loose equality says they are equal
if ([]) { ... }   // RUNS         — truthiness says [] is truthy

The same value, apparently "false" by one test and "true" by another. It is not a contradiction because they are not the same test. Q21's follow-up is where this gets taken apart properly; for now the point is only that "is x false-ish" has more than one meaning in JavaScript, and ToBoolean is exactly one of them.

Section 3 — How the list was fixed: it is not a list, it is eight rules

You asked how these eight values came to be the falsy ones. The answer is that nobody sat down and enumerated eight values. ToBoolean is defined by type — one clause per type, seven types plus Object — and the eight values fall out.

Here is the entire definition:

If the value's type is…Result
Undefinedfalse — always
Nullfalse — always
Booleanthe value itself
Numberfalse if it is +0, -0 or NaN; otherwise true
Stringfalse if its length is 0; otherwise true
BigIntfalse if it is 0n; otherwise true
Symboltrue — always
Objecttrue — always, with no exceptions

Count the false outcomes and you get exactly the eight: undefined, null, false, +0, -0, NaN, "", 0n. The list is a consequence, not a decision.

And the shape of the rules is coherent rather than arbitrary. Read them as one sentence:

Absence is false. The two absences are false. For each type that has a natural notion of "empty" or "zero," that value is false and everything else is true. Types with no such notion are always true. And every object is true, because an object's existence is itself the information.

That is why Symbol has no falsy member — there is no "empty symbol." It is why BigInt needed its own clause when it was added in ES2020: 0n is a different type from 0, so the Number clause does not reach it, and a new clause had to be written. This is Resolution 12 Section 8's point in miniature — adding a primitive means adding a row to every table like this one, and here is one of those tables.

The genuine oddity is NaN. It is falsy despite not being zero or empty, and the reason is Resolution 13's: NaN means "there is no valid answer here," which is closer to absence than to a number. Treating it as truthy would have made if (result) pass on a failed computation.

Section 4 — The three zeros

Now your second question directly. Three of the eight falsy values look like zero, and you asked what distinguishes them.

0Number. Positive zero. The ordinary one.
-0Number. Negative zero — a genuinely different bit pattern, equal to 0 under === but distinguishable.
0nBigInt. A different type entirely. Section 5.

On -0: Resolution 10 Section 1 explained where it comes from, and it is the payoff of the correction to your integer model. IEEE 754 floats use sign-magnitude — the sign is a separate bit standing outside the magnitude — so flipping that bit on a zero produces a second, distinct zero. Two's complement integers have no such thing, which is why you have never met a negative zero anywhere else.

It is deliberately hidden by almost every operation:

0 === -0            // true    — === is specified to ignore the sign of zero
(-0).toString()     // "0"     — printing hides it
-0 + 0              // 0

// but it is really there:
Object.is(0, -0)    // false        — SameValue keeps them apart (Resolution 14)
1 / -0              // -Infinity    — and here the sign changes the ANSWER
1 / 0               //  Infinity

You do not have to write it deliberately to get it:

-1 * 0              // -0
0 * -5              // -0
Math.round(-0.4)    // -0     — rounding a small negative toward zero
Math.min(0, -0)     // -0

Where it matters in practice is direction-sensitive maths: an angle, a velocity, a scroll delta that has reached zero from the negative side. Math.atan2(0, -1) and Math.atan2(-0, -1) give π and -π — opposite answers from inputs that === calls equal.

For truthiness it changes nothing: the Number clause in Section 3 names +0 and -0 together. The falsy list mentions both only because they are two distinct values, not because they behave differently here.

Section 5 — The n suffix, and why it has to exist

You said you saw this notation and did not follow it. Here it is properly.

0n, 1n, 42n are BigInt literals. The trailing n is part of the literal syntax, introduced with BigInt in ES2020 (Resolution 12). It is not an operator and not a variable — it is a character in the token, like the 0x in 0xFF or the e in 1e6.

42        // a Number  — typeof "number"
42n       // a BigInt  — typeof "bigint"

0n === 0  // false — different types (Resolution 12 Section 11)
0n == 0   // true  — loose equality converts
Boolean(0n)  // false
Boolean(1n)  // true

Now: why does it need to exist at all? This is the part worth having, and it is a direct consequence of Resolution 9.

Resolution 9 Section 2 argued that multiple numeric types are a feature of declarations, and that JavaScript has no declarations to hang them on. That argument had a corollary that goes unstated until you meet BigInt: if the type cannot be written at the variable, it has to be written at the literal.

// In Java, the declaration carries the type:
long  id = 42;        // the "long" tells the compiler everything

// In JavaScript there is nowhere to put it:
let id = 42;          // let says nothing about type
                      // so 42 alone must decide, and 42 means Number.

let id = 42n;         // therefore the LITERAL has to carry the type.

This is exactly the mechanism other languages use for the same purpose — you have probably seen it without registering it:

  Java:   42L   long          42f   float        42d   double
  C/C++:  42u   unsigned      42L   long         42.0f float
  C#:     42m   decimal       42u   uint
  JS:     42n   BigInt

A suffix on a numeric literal is the standard way to say "this number is of the wider or narrower type" when the surrounding syntax does not say it. JavaScript needed exactly one of them, because it has exactly two numeric types.

Two small notes. There is no suffix for decimals, because there is no decimal type — Resolution 12 Section 9's missing piece; if a Decimal proposal ever lands, it will almost certainly arrive with a suffix of its own for this same reason. And you cannot write a fractional BigInt: 1.5n is a SyntaxError, since BigInt is integers only.

Section 6 — Was the concept needed? Where it came from

Now your largest question: was there a need for truthy and falsy at all?

It was inherited, and the source is C. C — until C99, twenty-seven years after the language appeared — had no boolean type at all. if took an integer, and the rule was simply: zero is false, everything else is true. So all of this is ordinary C:

  if (n)              /* n is not zero */
  if (ptr)            /* ptr is not NULL */
  if (strlen(s))      /* s is not empty */
  while (*p++)        /* not at the terminating zero byte */

Every C programmer in 1995 wrote that way, and Java kept the syntax while removing the coercion — Java's if requires an actual boolean, and if (n) on an int is a compile error.

JavaScript went the other way, and Resolution 9 Section 3's audience argument is why. The language was for page authors writing form validators, and the difference in ceremony is real:

  // with truthiness
  if (name) { ... }

  // without it, you must know the type and its empty value
  if (name !== undefined && name !== null && name !== "") { ... }

And in a dynamically typed language that second line is worse than verbose — you often do not know which of those checks applies, because name could be a missing property (undefined), a cleared field (null), or an untouched input (""), and truthiness handles all three with one word.

So the honest case for it is: in a language with no types at the declaration site, "is there something here?" is a question you ask constantly and cannot phrase precisely, because "here" could hold anything. Truthiness is a single test that gives a usable answer across all seven primitive types at once. That is a real service, and it is why the feature is used so heavily.

Section 7 — And the bill

The cost is stated in one sentence: truthiness cannot distinguish "absent" from "present but empty or zero." Those are different states, and conflating them is a bug generator.

// 1. Zero is real data
function render(count) {
  if (count) show(count);      // 0 items never renders
}

// 2. Empty string is real data
if (user.middleName) { ... }   // someone with no middle name and
                               // someone who typed "" are the same

// 3. The default-value idiom eats valid values
const port    = config.port    || 8080;   // config.port = 0 -> 8080
const label   = config.label   || "none"; // config.label = "" -> "none"
const enabled = config.enabled || true;   // enabled = false -> TRUE (!!)

That last line is the worst of them, and it appears in real configuration code: false || true is true, so the option can never be turned off.

And the trap that catches people specifically:

Boolean(0)      // false
Boolean("0")    // TRUE  (!!) — a non-empty string of length 1

// so a numeric form field is truthy when it holds "0" as text,
// and falsy the moment you convert it:
if (input.value)          { ... }   // runs for "0"
if (Number(input.value))  { ... }   // does not

// and to complete the confusion:
"0" == false    // true   — loose equality converts BOTH to numbers
"0" === false   // false

The string "0" is truthy, and loosely equal to false. Both are correct, by two different algorithms — Section 2's point again.

Section 8 — The eventual admission: ??

The strongest evidence that truthiness was doing too much is that the committee eventually added an operator to stop it.

Nullish coalescing, ??, shipped in ES2020. It does not use ToBoolean at all. It tests for exactly two values — null and undefined, Resolution 17's pair — and nothing else:

0  || "d"     // "d"   — 0 is falsy, so || replaced it
0  ?? "d"     // 0     — 0 is not absent, so ?? kept it

"" || "d"     // "d"
"" ?? "d"     // ""

false || true // true   (!!)
false ?? true // false  — correct

null  ?? "d"  // "d"
undefined ?? "d" // "d"

Read that as a verdict on Section 6: for twenty-five years, || was used to mean "if absent, use a default," and it was answering a wider question — "if falsy" — that was wrong whenever 0, "" or false were legitimate values. ?? asks the question people actually meant.

The same release added ?., which also tests only for null and undefined. Both operators are the language moving away from truthiness toward explicit absence checks — which is the answer to "was this needed": it was needed in 1995, it was overused for two decades, and the language has since supplied the narrower tool.

The practical rule that follows:

  Use ?? or == null   when you mean "is it absent?"
  Use truthiness      when you genuinely mean "is it empty, zero, OR absent"
                      — which is common for strings you are about to display
  Be explicit         when 0, "" or false are legitimate values:
                        if (count > 0)
                        if (name !== "")
                        if (enabled === true)

What this resolves

What does "falsy" actually mean?Section 1: it names the result of one specific spec operation, ToBoolean(v) — total, deterministic, and exposed to you as Boolean(x) and !!x. And the refinement worth having: falsiness is not a property the value carries. The number 0 has no flag on it; it is a fact about what one function returns, like "even" is not stored inside 4.
Is it context-dependent?Section 2, precisely: the list never changes — there is no context in which 0 is truthy. What is context-dependent is whether ToBoolean runs at all. if, while, ?:, !, &&, || call it; ==, ===, switch (which uses ===), ?? and ?. do not. Hence the apparent contradiction [] == false being true while if ([]) runs — two different algorithms, not one rule applied twice.
How was the list of eight fixed?Section 3: it is not a list — it is eight rules, one per type, and the values fall out. Absence is false; each type with a natural "empty" or "zero" has that one value false; types without one are always true; every object is always true. That is why Symbol has no falsy member, and why BigInt needed a brand-new clause in ES2020 — 0n is a different type, so the Number clause could not reach it. The one genuine oddity is NaN, falsy because "no valid answer" is closer to absence than to a number.
0 vs -0 vs 0nSection 4: the first two are both Number; the third is BigInt, a different type. -0 exists because IEEE floats are sign-magnitude (Resolution 10 Section 1) — flip the separate sign bit on a zero and you get a second, distinct zero. It is hidden by === and by printing, but Object.is(0,-0) is false and 1/-0 is -Infinity. You get it without asking: -1*0, Math.round(-0.4). For truthiness it changes nothing — the spec names both together.
What is the n suffix?Section 5: a BigInt literal (ES2020) — part of the token, like the 0x in 0xFF. And why it must exist: Resolution 9 Section 2 argued that multiple numeric types are a feature of declarations and JavaScript has none — the corollary is that if the type cannot be written at the variable, it must be written at the literal. Same mechanism as Java's 42L, C's 42u, C#'s 42m. JavaScript needed exactly one suffix because it has exactly two numeric types — and there is no decimal suffix because there is no decimal type.
Was truthiness needed at all?Section 6: inherited from C, which had no boolean type until C99 and where if (n), if (ptr), if (strlen(s)) were ordinary. Java kept the syntax and removed the coercion; JavaScript kept the coercion, for the 1995 audience reason. And the honest case for it: in a language with no types at the declaration site, "is there something here?" is a question you cannot phrase precisely, because the value could be a missing property, a cleared field, or an untouched input — and truthiness answers all three at once.
What did it cost?Section 7: it cannot distinguish "absent" from "present but empty or zero." if (count) never renders zero items; config.enabled || true can never be turned off. And the specific trap: Boolean("0") is true (a non-empty string) while "0" == false is also true — both correct, by the two different algorithms of Section 2.
The verdictSection 8: the committee eventually added an operator to stop it. ?? (ES2020) does not call ToBoolean at all — it tests only for null and undefined. false ?? true is false; false || true is true. So: needed in 1995, overused for twenty-five years, and now supplied with the narrower tool it should have had.

Falsy is not a property of values; it is the answer ToBoolean gives. The eight are not a list anyone wrote down but the fallout of eight per-type rules. And the n in 0n is there because a language with no type declarations has only one place left to write a type: on the number itself.

pieces.title: Resolution 20 — Q21: what an empty array actually is, and why it is truthy
pieces.content:
You start by confirming the rule and then ask the better question underneath it: what is the differentiator? Why is the language's answer "everything not on the list," rather than something that looks inside the value? Section 1 answers that, and the answer is mechanical rather than philosophical — inspecting an object's contents in an if would mean running arbitrary user code inside a condition, and one very popular language does exactly that and pays for it.

Then the larger half. You laid out your mental model of an array in some detail — a contiguous range of memory blocks, the first element's address held as a pointer, index access as pointer arithmetic — and asked how an empty array or an empty object fits into it, and how something with nothing in it can be a single value at all.

Your model is a correct description of a C array. It is not what a JavaScript array is. That is not a small correction, and getting it right dissolves the puzzle completely: once you know what [] actually is, "why is it truthy" stops needing an answer. Sections 3 and 4.

And then the twist, which is becoming a familiar shape in these pieces: your C model is wrong about the language and substantially right about the machine. V8 really does store most arrays as a contiguous buffer with pointer arithmetic — it just abandons that representation the moment you do something the specification permits and the optimisation does not. Section 5.

The asks:

  1. What is the differentiator — why "everything else is truthy"? Sections 1 and 2, including the language that chose the other way.
  2. How do we interpret an empty array, given that an array is a contiguous block with a base pointer? Sections 3 and 5 — the model is C's, and here is what JavaScript actually has.
  3. How can [] or {} be a single value when there is nothing in them? Section 4 — because the variable does not hold the contents.
  4. They are storing data — how do I actually understand this? Section 5 — the specification's answer and the engine's answer, which are different and both true.
  5. (The thing that will trip you next) Why [] == false is true while if ([]) runs. Section 6.

Section 1 — The differentiator: an object's existence is the information

Resolution 19 Section 3 showed that the falsy list is not a list but eight per-type rules, and that the Object clause reads:

If the value is an Object, ToBoolean returns true. Always. Without looking at it.

Your question is why that clause is written that way. Three reasons, and the second is the decisive one.

1. The truthy set cannot be enumerated. There are eight falsy values and infinitely many truthy ones. A specification can only define the finite side, so the rule has to be stated as an exclusion. That is a presentational point, not a design one, but it is why the card is phrased the way it is.

2. Looking inside would mean running arbitrary code inside an if. This is the real argument. Suppose ToBoolean asked objects whether they were "empty." What would it ask?

  []            -> length 0. Empty, presumably.
  {}            -> no properties. Empty, presumably.
  new Map()     -> size 0.
  function(){}  -> is a function with no body empty?
  new Date()    -> what would an empty date even be?
  Promise       -> empty until it resolves?
  new Proxy(...) -> whatever the trap decides to say.

There is no answer that covers all of them, so the operation would have to consult the object — call a method, read a property, invoke a getter. And that has an unacceptable consequence:

const o = new Proxy({}, {
  get(target, key) { console.log("someone read", key); return undefined; }
});

if (o) { }        // if ToBoolean inspected contents, THIS LINE
                  // would run the trap — arbitrary user code,
                  // possibly throwing, possibly with side effects,
                  // inside the condition of an if.

ToBoolean is invoked constantly — in every if, every loop test, every &&. Making it capable of executing user code, throwing, or taking O(n) time would make the most basic control flow in the language unpredictable. As specified, it is a switch on the type tag: constant time, side-effect free, cannot throw. That is worth a great deal.

3. And the semantic reading, which follows from the other two: for an object, existence is the information. Objects have identity (Resolution 8 Section 2) — an object is a thing, not a quantity — and the question if (x) asks of a thing is "do I have one," not "how full is it." An empty box is still a box.

Section 2 — The road not taken: Python does inspect

Worth knowing, because it shows this was a genuine choice and not a necessity.

  Python:
    bool([])        -> False        an empty list is falsy
    bool({})        -> False
    bool("")        -> False
    bool(set())     -> False
    bool([0])       -> True         non-empty, even though it holds 0

  JavaScript:
    Boolean([])     -> true
    Boolean({})     -> true

Python has a protocol for it: an object may define __bool__, and failing that, __len__ is consulted and zero means false. So if my_list: is the idiomatic Python emptiness test, and it reads beautifully.

And it costs exactly what Section 1 predicted. bool(x) in Python can execute arbitrary user code, can be O(n), and can raise — most famously with NumPy, where if array: raises "The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous", because the protocol has no sensible answer and the library refuses to guess. That error message is Section 1's argument, printed at runtime, in a real library, for millions of users.

So neither choice is wrong. Python bought expressiveness and paid in predictability; JavaScript bought a constant-time, total, side-effect-free operation and paid by making you write arr.length === 0.

Section 3 — Your array model, checked

Now the main event. Here is the model you described:

  C:  int arr[3] = {10, 20, 30};

  memory:   [ 10 ][ 20 ][ 30 ]
            ^
            arr is (decays to) a pointer to this address

  arr[i]  IS  *(arr + i * sizeof(int))    — literally pointer arithmetic
  the array HAS no length stored anywhere
  the array HAS no identity beyond its address
  "empty array" is barely a thing — int arr[0] is not standard C

That is accurate C, and your discomfort with [] comes directly from it: in that model an empty array is a base pointer to nothing, which is hard to call a value.

A JavaScript array is not that. A JavaScript array is an object.

typeof []                    // "object"
Object.getPrototypeOf([]) === Array.prototype   // true
[].hasOwnProperty("length")  // true

And its "elements" are not memory offsets. They are ordinary properties whose keys are the strings "0", "1", "2" — exactly the mechanism from Resolution 14 Section 9, where every property key is a string or a Symbol:

const a = [10, 20];

Object.keys(a)     // ["0", "1"]     <- STRINGS. Not numbers.
a["0"]             // 10             <- same property as a[0]
a[0]               // 10             — the 0 is converted to "0"

Once you see that, the things that make no sense in the C model start making sense:

// 1. You can put non-index properties on an array. It is an object.
const a = [10, 20];
a.foo = 1;
a.length           // 2         — length only counts index-like keys
Object.keys(a)     // ["0", "1", "foo"]
JSON.stringify(a)  // "[10,20]" — foo is not serialised

// 2. Deleting leaves a HOLE. The array does not shrink.
delete a[0];
a.length           // 2         — still
0 in a             // false     — the property is GONE, not zeroed
a                  // [ <1 empty item>, 20, foo: 1 ]

// 3. A hole is not the same as undefined.
[1, , 3].map(x => x * 2)          // [2, <hole>, 6]  — map SKIPS holes
[1, undefined, 3].map(x => x * 2) // [2, NaN, 6]     — undefined is visited

// 4. Assigning a large index just sets length. No memory is reserved.
const b = [];
b[5] = 1;
b.length           // 6
0 in b             // false — indices 0..4 were never created

None of that is expressible in a contiguous-memory model. All of it is obvious once "an array is an object with numeric-string keys and a magic length" is the model.

The one genuinely special thing about an array — the reason it is an "exotic object" in the specification rather than an ordinary one — is that length is linked to the index properties in both directions. Adding index 5 raises length to 6; setting length to 1 deletes every index property at or above 1. That two-way link is the entire specialness. Everything else is object behaviour.

Section 4 — So what is [], and how is it "one value"?

Now your question can be answered directly.

[] is an expression that allocates a new object — with Array.prototype on its chain, a length property of 0, and no index properties — and evaluates to a reference to it.

Two things follow, and between them they answer "how can this be a single value."

First: the variable does not hold the contents. It holds a reference. This is Resolution 8's whole distinction. A primitive is its value; an object variable holds a pointer to a thing that exists independently. So the question "how can it be one value when it has nothing in it" has a slightly deflationary answer: the variable holds exactly one thing either way — one reference — and how much is on the other end of that reference is a separate matter entirely.

Second: each [] makes a new one, and they are distinguishable. This is the proof that an empty array is a real, individual thing rather than an absence:

[] === []                    // false — two different objects
{} === {}                    // false
const x = []; x === x        // true  — the same object

const p = [], q = p;
p.push(1);
q                            // [1] — same object, seen through two names

If [] were "nothing," those two empties would be the same nothing. They are not. Each has its own identity, its own address, its own life in the garbage collector. That identity is precisely what makes it truthy: if (x) on an object is asking "is there an object here," and there demonstrably is.

And {} is the same story with one fewer special feature: a new object with Object.prototype on its chain and an empty property table. No length, no exotic behaviour, just an object with nothing in it yet.

Section 5 — But the engine does use contiguous memory

Here is where your C model comes back and turns out to be right about the layer underneath.

The specification says an array is an object with string keys. If engines implemented that literally — a hash table lookup for every arr[i] — array code would be unusably slow. So they do not. V8 stores array elements in one of two completely different ways, and switches between them at runtime.

  FAST ELEMENTS  ("elements backing store")
    A contiguous buffer. Index i is at offset i.
    This is your C array, exactly.
    Used while the array is dense and its indices are small.

  DICTIONARY ELEMENTS
    An actual hash table from index to value.
    Slow, but handles anything.
    Used when the array becomes sparse or weird.

V8 further tracks what kind of thing is in the fast buffer, because that determines whether values can be stored unboxed:

  PACKED_SMI_ELEMENTS      [1, 2, 3]           — small ints, raw, no boxing
  PACKED_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS   [1.5, 2.5]          — raw doubles, no boxing
  PACKED_ELEMENTS          [1, "a", {}]        — general, boxed pointers

  HOLEY_SMI_ELEMENTS       [1, , 3]            — same, but holes possible,
  HOLEY_DOUBLE_ELEMENTS                          so every read needs a check
  HOLEY_ELEMENTS

The transitions are one-way: once an array goes holey it does not go back, and once it goes to dictionary mode it stays. Which gives concrete advice:

const a = [1, 2, 3];   // PACKED_SMI — the fast path, a real C array

delete a[0];           // -> HOLEY. Every subsequent read needs a hole check.
a[100000] = 1;         // -> DICTIONARY. Now it is a hash table.
a.push("x");           // -> PACKED_ELEMENTS. Values must be boxed.

// so: don't delete from the middle (use splice or filter),
//     don't assign far-out indices,
//     keep the element types uniform.

And notice that this is the fourth time this exact pattern has appeared in these resolutions. It is worth naming as a recurring principle rather than meeting it fresh each time:

The specification says…The engine actually does…
Every number is a 64-bit double (Resolution 9)Small integers are tagged machine words — Smis — with no allocation at all
Every string is a sequence of 16-bit code units (Resolution 15)Latin-1 strings are stored at one byte per character
Every concatenation produces a new string (Resolution 16)A ConsString node is built and flattened lazily
An array is an object with string keys (here)A contiguous buffer, exactly the C array you described

In every case the optimisation is legal because it is unobservable — there is no program that can tell the difference. And in every case the specification describes meaning while the engine chooses representation. So the honest answer to "how do I actually interpret and understand this" is: hold both. Reason about your code with the specification's model, because that is what determines behaviour; know the engine's model, because that is what determines speed.

Section 6 — The thing that will confuse you next: [] == false

Resolution 19 Section 2 flagged this and left it here. It is worth taking apart because it is the single most cited piece of evidence that "JavaScript is broken," and it is not evidence of that at all.

if ([]) { /* RUNS */ }      // [] is truthy
[] == false                 // true                (!!)
[] == 0                     // true
[0] == false                // true
[1] == true                 // true
[2] == true                 // false               (!!)

The resolution is Resolution 19 Section 2's: these are two different algorithms with two different destinations.

Path 1 — if ([]). Calls ToBoolean. The value is an Object. The Object clause returns true without looking inside. One step, done.

Path 2 — [] == false. Never calls ToBoolean at all. Loose equality has a rule that says: if one side is a Boolean, convert it to a number and start again. Then, if one side is an Object and the other a Number, convert the object to a primitive. Follow it:

  []  ==  false
  []  ==  0                    // ToNumber(false) is 0
                               // now: Object == Number
  ""  ==  0                    // ToPrimitive([]) — valueOf returns the
                               // array itself (not a primitive), so
                               // toString runs: [].toString() is ""
  0   ==  0                    // ToNumber("") is 0
  true

Every step is a written rule, and the destination is a number. That is the key sentence:

== converts toward numbers. if converts toward booleans. They are not the same question and there is no reason to expect them to agree.

The [2] == true row is the one that makes it click: true becomes 1, [2] stringifies to "2" which becomes 2, and 2 == 1 is false. Nothing about "truth" was consulted anywhere in that computation. The operator is named == and compares numbers; true is just a value that converts to 1.

This is also the cleanest possible argument for ===: it has none of these steps. [] === false is false immediately, because the types differ.

Section 7 — How to actually test emptiness

Since the language will not do it for you:

// arrays
arr.length === 0

// plain objects
Object.keys(obj).length === 0

// Map and Set have a real answer
map.size === 0

// strings — here truthiness DOES work, because "" is falsy
if (!str) { ... }

// and the check people reach for that does not exist:
// there is no Object.isEmpty, and no [].isEmpty()

Why is there no built-in? For the same reason as Section 1 — "empty" is not a concept the language can define once for all objects. Object.keys works for plain objects and quietly misses Symbol keys and non-enumerable properties; arr.length === 0 works for arrays and says nothing about non-index properties. Each container knows what empty means for itself, and the language declines to guess. That is the same refusal as the ToBoolean rule, applied consistently.

What this resolves

What is the differentiator — why "everything else is truthy"?Section 1, three reasons, and the second is decisive. The truthy set is infinite so only the finite side can be listed. Looking inside an object would mean running arbitrary user code inside an if — a getter, a Proxy trap, something that throws or takes O(n) — and ToBoolean runs in every condition and every loop test. As specified it is a switch on the type tag: constant time, side-effect free, cannot throw. And semantically: objects have identity, so if (x) asks "do I have one," not "how full is it."
Was there another option?Section 2: yes, and Python took it — bool([]) is False, via the __bool__/__len__ protocol. It reads beautifully and costs exactly what Section 1 predicted: NumPy's famous "The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous" is that argument printed at runtime. Neither is wrong; Python bought expressiveness and paid in predictability.
My array model — contiguous memory, base pointer, pointer arithmeticSection 3: an accurate description of a C array, and not what a JavaScript array is. A JavaScript array is an object: typeof [] is "object", and its elements are ordinary properties keyed by the strings "0", "1" — Object.keys([10,20]) returns ["0","1"], exactly the mechanism from Resolution 14 Section 9.
What that explainsSection 3: things that are impossible in the C model. You can set a.foo = 1 without changing length. delete a[0] leaves a hole and does not shrink the array — 0 in a becomes false. A hole is not undefined: [1,,3].map(f) skips the hole while [1,undefined,3].map(f) visits it. And b[5] = 1 on an empty array sets length to 6 without creating indices 0–4. The one genuinely special thing is that length is two-way linked to the index properties.
How can [] be "one value" with nothing in it?Section 4: because the variable does not hold the contents — it holds a reference (Resolution 8). One reference either way; how much is on the other end is a separate matter. And the proof that an empty array is a real individual thing rather than an absence: [] === [] is false. Two empties are two different objects with two identities. That identity is exactly what makes it truthy. An empty box is still a box.
…and my C model?Section 5: wrong about the language, substantially right about the machine. V8 stores dense arrays as fast elements — a contiguous buffer where index i is at offset i, exactly your model — and falls back to a hash table (dictionary elements) when you make it sparse. It also tracks PACKED_SMI/DOUBLE/ELEMENTS and their HOLEY variants, and the transitions are one-way. Hence: don't delete from the middle, don't assign far-out indices, keep element types uniform.
The recurring principleSection 5: this is now the fourth instance of one pattern — Smis (Resolution 9), Latin-1 strings (15), ConsStrings (16), and array backing stores (here). In every case the optimisation is legal because it is unobservable. So the answer to "how do I actually understand this" is hold both models: the specification determines behaviour, the engine determines speed.
Why [] == false is true while if ([]) runsSection 6, traced step by step. if calls ToBoolean, hits the Object clause, returns true in one step. == never calls ToBoolean at all: false → 0, then ToPrimitive([]) → [].toString() → "" → 0, and 0 == 0. == converts toward numbers; if converts toward booleans. The clincher is [2] == true being false — nothing about truth was consulted anywhere in that computation.
How do I test emptiness?Section 7: arr.length === 0, Object.keys(obj).length === 0, map.size === 0. There is no Object.isEmpty and there is not going to be — for the same reason as Section 1: each container knows what empty means for itself, and the language declines to guess.

An empty array is not an absence of an array. It is an object — allocated, with an identity, with Array.prototype on its chain and a length of zero — and if (x) on an object asks whether one is there, not how much is inside it.

pieces.title: Resolution 21 — Q22: the complete coercion algorithm, and where === came from
pieces.content:
You open with an objection from common sense, and it is worth taking seriously and then dismantling, because the intuition behind it is wrong in a way that will keep costing you until it is named. You wrote that if one side of the comparison is false, the whole thing should return false — that there is no point comparing a false value with anything, since it would always be false.

Test it:

false == false     // true
false == 0         // true
false == ""        // true
false == "0"       // true
false == []        // true

Five comparisons with false on the left, and every one is true. Section 1 explains why, and the correction is a single sentence that reorganises the whole topic.

Then the substance. You asked for the exhaustive end-to-end specification — the complete rule set, so that any comparison becomes something you can evaluate by hand rather than guess at. Sections 6, 7 and 8 are that, in full, and they are the centre of this piece. You also asked what these operators are actually called (Section 4), whether JavaScript invented coercion (Section 3 — no, and you correctly suspected as much), whether it is connected to weak versus strong typing (Section 2 — yes, and your hunch about C is right), and where === came from (Section 9 — there is a real story, including a failed attempt to fix == itself that had to be rolled back).

The asks:

  1. Shouldn't a comparison involving false just be false? Section 1.
  2. Is this connected to weak versus strong typing? Section 2 — and the two-axis picture that makes those words mean something.
  3. Did JavaScript invent this, or did it come from somewhere? Section 3 — eighteen years older than JavaScript, and one predecessor solved it better.
  4. What are == and === actually called? Section 4.
  5. How does coercion make the language accessible? Section 5 — the argument is real, concrete, and has expired.
  6. The exhaustive algorithm. Sections 6, 7 and 8 — every step, every conversion table.
  7. Why was === introduced, and what problems forced it? Sections 9 and 10 — including the one that is genuinely fatal.

Section 1 — The correction: false is a value, not a verdict

Your objection treats false as if it were the answer to a question — as though putting it into a comparison poisons the result. But false is not a verdict; it is a value, of type Boolean, sitting there being compared like any other.

Compare two sentences:

  "is this comparison false?"        <- a question about the comparison
  "is x equal to the value false?"   <- what x == false actually asks

x == false is asking the second. It is exactly as much a truth test as x == 5 is a test of fiveness. The operator does not care that one of its operands happens to be the boolean that means "no."

And then the mechanism, which Section 6 gives in full but which is worth previewing here because it explains all five results above: when == sees a Boolean, the first thing it does is convert it to a number. false becomes 0. So x == false is never really a boolean comparison at all — it immediately becomes x == 0, and then the question is whether x converts to zero. And 0, "", "0" and [] all do.

Which produces the rule worth carrying away from this whole piece:

== converts toward numbers. It is a numeric comparison wearing a general-purpose costume.

Resolution 20 Section 6 made the same point from the other side — if converts toward booleans, == converts toward numbers, and they are different destinations. Your objection assumed == was doing something boolean. It never is.

Section 2 — Weak versus strong typing, and why C belongs where you put it

You wondered whether this is connected to weak typing, and said you were not sure whether C counts. It is connected, and your instinct about C is correct. But the words "strong" and "weak" are used so loosely that they are nearly useless unless you split them from a different pair they get confused with.

There are two independent axes:

Static vs dynamicWhen are types checked? Static: before the program runs, by a compiler. Dynamic: while it runs, by the values themselves carrying tags (Resolution 5 Section 1).
Strong vs weakHow much implicit conversion does the language perform? Strong: type boundaries are enforced; mixing types is an error. Weak: the language silently converts to make the operation work.

They are orthogonal, and all four combinations exist:

                   STRONG                      WEAK
              +---------------------+---------------------+
   STATIC     |  Java, Haskell,     |  C, C++             |
              |  Rust, Go           |                     |
              |                     |  int/double convert |
              |  "a" + 1 won't      |  implicitly; arrays |
              |  compile in Haskell |  decay to pointers; |
              |                     |  casts reinterpret  |
              +---------------------+---------------------+
   DYNAMIC    |  Python, Ruby       |  JavaScript, PHP,   |
              |                     |  Perl, AWK          |
              |  1 + "a" raises     |                     |
              |  TypeError AT       |  1 + "a" is "1a"    |
              |  RUNTIME            |                     |
              +---------------------+---------------------+

Python is the important cell, because it destroys the common assumption that dynamic implies weak. Python is fully dynamic — no declarations, types checked at runtime — and yet:

  Python:   1 + "a"    -> TypeError: unsupported operand type(s)
  JS:       1 + "a"    -> "1a"

Same amount of static checking (none). Completely different attitude to mixing types. So JavaScript's coercion is not a consequence of being dynamically typed — it is a separate, additional decision. That matters for your question about whether it was deliberate: it had to be, because dynamic typing alone would not have produced it.

And C. You hesitated, saying "maybe not C, I think C is weakly typed, although I don't really know." You were right the first time. C converts implicitly all over the place — int to double, char to int, signed to unsigned (Resolution 9 Section 2's -1 < 1u being false), arrays decaying to pointers — and a cast lets you reinterpret any bit pattern as anything. C is statically typed and weakly typed, which is exactly why the two words needed separating.

Section 3 — Did JavaScript invent this? No, and you guessed correctly

You said you doubted a concept like this could have been invented in ten days, and that it probably came from somewhere. That is right, and the ancestry is well documented.

AWK (1977) is the closest ancestor. In AWK a value is simultaneously a string and a number — a "strnum" — and comparison decides which to use based on how the value arrived. Input fields that look numeric compare numerically; everything else compares as strings. This is JavaScript's model, eighteen years earlier.

Perl (1987) is the more interesting one, because Perl solved the problem in a better way and JavaScript did not copy the solution. Perl also converts freely between strings and numbers — but it gives you separate operators, so the code says which comparison it wants:

  Perl:
      $a == $b     numeric equality
      $a eq $b     string equality

      $a <  $b     numeric less-than
      $a lt $b     string less-than

      10 == "10"   true     (numeric)
      10 eq "10"   true     (both become "10")
      "10" == "10.0"  true  (numeric: 10 == 10)
      "10" eq "10.0"  FALSE (string: different text)

The ambiguity that makes JavaScript's == hard is "which kind of comparison did you mean?" — and Perl makes you answer it in the operator. There is no guessing, no conversion table, and no surprises. JavaScript has one == and a fifteen-step algorithm to decide what you probably meant.

Also in the lineage: Tcl (1988), where everything is a string converted on use, and HyperTalk (1987), Apple's HyperCard language, where values are untyped text — "3" + 4 is 7 because HyperTalk simply reads the text as a number when arithmetic asks.

So the concept was standard practice in the scripting-language family that Eich was working in. The specific design — one == that guesses — was the choice, and it is the part that has not aged well.

Section 4 — What they are called

You asked for the names, and there are two registers.

OperatorSpecification nameCommon name
==IsLooselyEqual — historically Abstract Equality Comparisonloose equality; abstract equality; "double equals"
===IsStrictlyEqual — historically Strict Equality Comparisonstrict equality; "triple equals"
!=the negation of IsLooselyEqualloose inequality
!==the negation of IsStrictlyEqualstrict inequality

Collectively the grammar calls all four the equality operators, and < > <= >= the relational operators — a distinction that matters, because Section 8 shows they use different conversion rules and disagree about null.

The words "abstract" and "strict" are worth reading literally. Abstract means it compares at an abstracted level, ignoring representation — it wants to know whether the values "amount to the same thing." Strict means it compares exactly, with no conversion permitted. And Resolution 14 Section 3 added two more algorithms beyond these: SameValueZero (used by includes, Map, Set) and SameValue (used by Object.is). Four equality algorithms in total, and knowing which one a given construct uses is most of the practical skill here.

Section 5 — Does coercion actually make the language accessible? The argument, and its expiry date

You asked how this could possibly have made JavaScript easier for non-technical people, since surely errors would give better clarity. It is a fair challenge and the answer is concrete rather than hand-waving. It comes down to one fact about 1995:

Everything that came out of an HTML form was a string. There was no other kind of input.

Here is the actual code a page author was writing in 1996:

<FORM onSubmit="return check(this)">
  <INPUT TYPE="text" NAME="age">
</FORM>

function check(form) {
  // form.age.value is the STRING "21", never the number 21
  if (form.age.value < 18) {
    alert("Too young");
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}

With coercion, "21" < 18 converts and works, and the author never has to know that a form field is a string. Without coercion, the correct version is:

  if (parseInt(form.age.value, 10) < 18)

Now consider who was writing this and with what. The audience was designers and hobbyists, many of whom had never used a compiler. There was no debugger — Netscape 2.0 reported errors in a dialog box or not at all. There was no console, no source maps, no Stack Overflow, no MDN. A type error meant a broken page and no way to find out why.

In that setting, "make it work rather than complain" is a defensible product decision, and it is the same reasoning as Resolution 9 Section 3's integer-division argument: the language repeatedly chose the behaviour that let a non-programmer's near-correct code run.

And now the honest half, because you asked whether it actually helped. The argument has expired, for three reasons:

  • The input is no longer strings. Data arrives as JSON with real types, from APIs with schemas. The problem coercion solved has largely stopped existing.
  • The tooling arrived. Debuggers, consoles, linters and TypeScript all exist. Errors are now cheap to diagnose, which was the entire premise of avoiding them.
  • The failures are silent. This is the decisive one. Coercion does not prevent errors; it converts loud errors into quiet wrong answers. A thrown TypeError tells you the line. "10" + 5 giving "105" tells you nothing until a number appears in your database with a stray digit.

So: a reasonable decision for 1995 that stopped being reasonable somewhere around 2010, which is roughly when "always use ===" became universal advice.

Section 6 — The exhaustive algorithm: ==, every step

This is what you asked for. Here is IsLooselyEqual(x, y) in full. Every rule, in order, and the first one that matches wins. Nothing is omitted.

  IsLooselyEqual(x, y):

   1. If Type(x) is the same as Type(y):
          return IsStrictlyEqual(x, y).        <- no coercion at all!

   2. If x is null and y is undefined:  return true.
   3. If x is undefined and y is null:  return true.

   4. If Type(x) is Number and Type(y) is String:
          return  x == ToNumber(y).
   5. If Type(x) is String and Type(y) is Number:
          return  ToNumber(x) == y.

   6. If Type(x) is BigInt and Type(y) is String:
          let n = StringToBigInt(y);
          if n is undefined, return false;
          return  x == n.
   7. If Type(x) is String and Type(y) is BigInt:
          return  y == x.

   8. If Type(x) is Boolean:  return  ToNumber(x) == y.
   9. If Type(y) is Boolean:  return  x == ToNumber(y).

  10. If Type(x) is Number, BigInt, String or Symbol,
      and Type(y) is Object:
          return  x == ToPrimitive(y).
  11. If Type(x) is Object,
      and Type(y) is Number, BigInt, String or Symbol:
          return  ToPrimitive(x) == y.

  12. If one is BigInt and the other is Number:
          if either is NaN, +Infinity or -Infinity, return false;
          return true iff their mathematical values are equal.

  13. Return false.

Six observations that turn this from a list into a model.

Rule 1 is the most important and the least known. If the two operands are already the same type, == does exactly what === does. No conversion happens. So "a" == "b", 1 == 2, {} == {} are all resolved by strict equality. Coercion only ever happens between different types — which means the entire reputation of == rests on rules 2 through 12.

Rules 2 and 3 are the hand-written exception. null and undefined are equal to each other and — because no later rule mentions them — to nothing else at all. They do not convert to 0, they do not convert to "". This is Resolution 17 Section 8, and it is the basis of Q24's idiom.

Rules 8 and 9 are why Section 1's puzzle happened. A Boolean is converted to a number immediately, before anything else is considered, and then the algorithm restarts. false is 0 and true is 1. There is no rule anywhere that gives true special standing.

Rules 10 and 11 are the only place objects appear, and they always resolve by converting the object to a primitive — never by converting the primitive to an object. So an object is always reduced to a string or a number before comparison.

Rule 13 catches everything else, which is why Symbol() == 1 is simply false rather than an error.

And the algorithm is recursive. Several rules end by comparing again with converted operands, so a single == can take three or four passes. Section 8 traces one.

Section 7 — The conversion tables the algorithm depends on

The rules above call ToNumber and ToPrimitive. Without those the algorithm is not exhaustive, so here they are.

ToNumber(v):

InputResult
undefinedNaN
null0 — the asymmetry from Resolution 17 Section 7
true / false1 / 0
a Numberitself
"" or whitespace only0
a numeric stringthat number — including "0x10" → 16, "1e2" → 100, "0b11" → 3, "Infinity" → ∞, and surrounding whitespace is ignored
any other stringNaN
a Symbolthrows TypeError
a BigIntthrows TypeError (Resolution 12 Section 11)
an ObjectToNumber(ToPrimitive(v, "number"))

ToPrimitive(v, hint) — how an object becomes a primitive:

  1. If the object has a Symbol.toPrimitive method, call it with the
     hint and use the result. (Rare, but it wins outright.)

  2. Otherwise, try two methods in an order set by the hint:

       hint "number" or "default":   valueOf()  then  toString()
       hint "string":                toString() then  valueOf()

     Take the first result that IS a primitive. If neither is,
     throw TypeError.

And the defaults that make everything else fall into place:

  Object.prototype.valueOf   returns THE OBJECT ITSELF — not a primitive.
                             So for a plain object it is always skipped.
  Object.prototype.toString  returns "[object Object]".
  Array.prototype.toString   returns elements joined by commas.

  ({}).valueOf() === "not primitive"  -> falls through
  ({}) + ""      -> "[object Object]"
  [].toString()      -> ""
  [5].toString()     -> "5"
  [1,2].toString()   -> "1,2"

That single fact — that [].toString() is the empty string — is the source of half the famous == puzzles. An empty array becomes "", which becomes 0.

You can watch the priority order directly:

const o = { valueOf() { return 42; }, toString() { return "no"; } };

o == 42        // true       — hint "default" tries valueOf first
`${o}`         // "no"       — template literals use hint "string"
o + ""         // "42"       — + uses hint "default": valueOf wins

And one built-in breaks the pattern deliberately. Date is the only standard object whose "default" hint behaves like "string", which is why:

typeof (new Date() + 1)   // "string"  — concatenation
typeof (new Date() - 1)   // "number"  — subtraction forces hint "number"

Section 8 — Working the rules by hand

Now the algorithm is a tool. Six comparisons, each traced.

"1" == 1

  types String and Number       -> rule 5: ToNumber("1") == 1
  1 == 1                        -> rule 1: strict equality
  true

"" == 0

  rule 5: ToNumber("") is 0     ->  0 == 0
  true

[] == false — the one from Q21, now by the numbered rules:

  y is Boolean                  -> rule 9: [] == ToNumber(false)
  [] == 0
  x is Object, y is Number      -> rule 11: ToPrimitive([]) == 0
      valueOf() returns the array — not primitive — skip
      toString() returns ""
  "" == 0
  rule 5: ToNumber("") is 0     ->  0 == 0
  true                          — four passes.

[2] == true

  rule 9: [2] == ToNumber(true) ->  [2] == 1
  rule 11: ToPrimitive([2]) is "2"  ->  "2" == 1
  rule 5: ToNumber("2") is 2        ->  2 == 1
  FALSE

  — so [] == false and [2] == true are both about NUMBERS.
    Nothing in either computation consulted truthiness.

null == 0 — and this is the sharpest inconsistency in the language:

  rule 2? no (y is not undefined).  rule 3? no.
  rules 4-12 never mention Null.
  rule 13: return false.

  null == 0     // false

  BUT:
  null >= 0     // TRUE   (!!)

Why the disagreement? Because >= is a relational operator, not an equality operator (Section 4), and relational operators have a completely different algorithm: they call ToNumber on both sides with no special case for null. So ToNumber(null) is 0, and 0 >= 0 is true. Meanwhile == has the hand-written rules 2 and 3 that stop null converting at all.

The same value is "not equal to 0" and "greater than or equal to 0" at the same time, because two operator families were specified with different attitudes to null. This is not derivable from any principle; it is two decisions that were never reconciled.

And the fatal one — == is not transitive:

  0  == ""      // true   (ToNumber("") is 0)
  0  == "0"     // true   (ToNumber("0") is 0)
  "" == "0"     // FALSE  (rule 1: same type, so strict — "" !== "0")

If a == b and b == c, then a == c should follow. It does not. That is not a quirk, it is a broken invariant, and it means == cannot be used to reason about equality at all — you cannot substitute equals for equals, cannot safely deduplicate, cannot sort by it. Section 10 is why this matters more than any individual surprise.

Section 9 — Where === came from, and the fix that had to be rolled back

Now your history question, which has a better answer than "they added it later."

=== did not exist in the original language. JavaScript 1.0 in Navigator 2.0 (1995) and JavaScript 1.1 in Navigator 3.0 (1996) had only ==, and ECMAScript 1st edition (June 1997) does not contain === either. For the first two years there was no way to compare without coercion.

The complaints were immediate, and Netscape's first attempt at a fix was the interesting part: rather than adding a new operator, JavaScript 1.2 changed what == did — making it stop coercing between types in at least some cases.

That failed, and it failed in the way Resolution 3 would predict. Changing the meaning of an operator that existed in deployed pages broke those pages, and it also meant the same source code behaved differently depending on the LANGUAGE="JavaScript1.2" attribute on the <SCRIPT> tag — so a page could compare two values differently in two browsers. The change was reverted: == got its coercion back, and the non-coercing comparison was given a new operator instead, so that old code kept working and new code could opt in.

=== and !== were standardised in ECMAScript 3rd edition, December 1999, alongside regular expressions, try/catch and exceptions — the release that made JavaScript a serious language.

Two lessons in that, and both generalise:

The wrong fix was tried first, and it was the obvious one. "Just make == behave correctly" is what everyone proposes, and it is unavailable for exactly the reason Resolution 3 gives about typeof null: you cannot change the meaning of something the deployed web already uses. Every repair in JavaScript's history has taken the same shape — add a new thing beside the old thing: === beside ==, let beside var, "use strict" beside sloppy mode, ?? beside ||, Number.isNaN beside isNaN, toSorted beside sort.

And it is the tell Resolution 9 used. That resolution argued the single number type was a genuine design choice rather than a frozen mistake, and the evidence was that no escape hatch was ever added beside it. == has an escape hatch. That is what a frozen mistake looks like.

Section 10 — How === works, and what it still gets wrong

After Section 6, this is refreshingly short. IsStrictlyEqual(x, y), in full:

  1. If Type(x) is not Type(y), return false.
  2. If Type(x) is Number:
        a. If x is NaN, return false.
        b. If y is NaN, return false.
        c. If x and y are the same value, return true.
        d. If x is +0 and y is -0, return true.
        e. If x is -0 and y is +0, return true.
        f. Return false.
  3. Otherwise: return true iff x and y are the same value.
     (For objects, "the same value" means the same identity —
      the same reference, Resolution 20 Section 4.)

Four lines of substance, no conversion, no recursion, no tables. And it is transitive, which is the property == lacks and the reason the advice is universal.

It has exactly two oddities, both inherited from IEEE 754 rather than invented here:

NaN === NaN     // false   — Resolution 14 Section 1
0 === -0        // true    — Resolution 19 Section 4

Those two are why the language needed Object.is (SameValue) and SameValueZero, and Resolution 14 Section 3 has the four-algorithm table that lays out which does what.

The practical position, then:

  Use  ===  everywhere.

  Use  == null  as the ONE exception — it means "null or undefined"
       and nothing else, guaranteed by rules 2, 3 and 13 (Q24).

  Use  Object.is  when you need NaN or -0 handled correctly.

  Never use == with a Boolean literal. `x == true` is a numeric
  comparison against 1, which is almost never what you mean.
  Write  if (x)  or  if (x === true).

What this resolves

Shouldn't a comparison with false just be false?Section 1: no — and the counter-evidence is five lines long: false == false, == 0, == "", == "0", == [] are all true. false is a value being compared, not a verdict about the comparison. x == false is exactly as much a truth test as x == 5 is a test of fiveness. And mechanically, rule 9 converts the Boolean to a number first, so it is never a boolean comparison at all. == converts toward numbers.
Is this connected to weak typing?Section 2: yes, and the words only mean something once you separate two independent axes — static/dynamic (when types are checked) and strong/weak (how much implicit conversion). All four cells are occupied. Python is the decisive one: fully dynamic, yet 1 + "a" raises a TypeError. So JavaScript's coercion is not a consequence of dynamic typing — it was a separate decision, which answers your "was this deliberate."
Is C weakly typed? (you hesitated)Section 2: you were right the first time. C is statically typed and weakly typed — implicit int/double conversion, array-to-pointer decay, signed/unsigned conversion (why -1 < 1u is false), and casts that reinterpret bits. That combination is exactly why the two words had to be pulled apart.
Did JavaScript invent coercion?Section 3: no, and you correctly guessed it could not have been invented in ten days. AWK (1977) had dual string/number values eighteen years earlier. Tcl and HyperTalk did versions of it. And Perl (1987) solved it better: separate operators — == for numeric, eq for string — so the code states which comparison it means. JavaScript took the coercion and not the disambiguation.
What are they called?Section 4: == is loose or abstract equality (IsLooselyEqual); === is strict equality (IsStrictlyEqual). Together with !=/!== they are the equality operators; < > <= >= are the relational operators — a distinction that turns out to matter in Section 8.
How did coercion make the language accessible?Section 5, concretely: everything out of an HTML form was a string, so form.age.value < 18 had to work or the author needed parseInt — in 1996, with no debugger, no console, no MDN, where a type error meant a broken page and no way to find out why. Real reasoning, same shape as Resolution 9's integer-division argument. And it has expired: input is now typed JSON, tooling exists, and above all coercion does not prevent errors — it converts loud errors into quiet wrong answers.
The exhaustive algorithmSections 6 and 7: all thirteen numbered rules of IsLooselyEqual, plus the ToNumber table and the ToPrimitive procedure it depends on. Key readings: rule 1 means == behaves exactly like === when the types already match — coercion only ever happens between types. Rules 2–3 are a hand-written exception making null/undefined equal to each other and to nothing else. Rules 8–9 convert Booleans to numbers immediately. Rules 10–11 always reduce the object to a primitive. And [].toString() being "" is the source of half the famous puzzles.
Working it by handSection 8 traces six, including [] == false in four passes. Plus the two worst results. null == 0 is false but null >= 0 is true — because relational operators use ToNumber with no null exception while == has rules 2–3; two operator families that were never reconciled. And the fatal one: == is not transitive — 0 == "" and 0 == "0" are both true while "" == "0" is false.
Why was === introduced?Section 9: it did not exist in JavaScript 1.0, 1.1, or even ECMAScript 1st edition (June 1997). Netscape's first attempt was to change == itself in JavaScript 1.2 — and it had to be rolled back, because it broke deployed pages and made the same code compare differently depending on a <SCRIPT LANGUAGE> attribute. === was standardised in ES3, December 1999. Two lessons: the obvious fix is unavailable, and every repair in this language takes the same shape — add a new thing beside the old thing (let, "use strict", ??, Number.isNaN, toSorted). Which is exactly the tell Resolution 9 used to argue the number type was not a frozen mistake: no escape hatch was ever added beside it. == has one.
How does === work?Section 10: four lines — different types is false, NaN is never equal, +0 and -0 are equal, otherwise same value (for objects, same identity). No conversion, no recursion, no tables, and it is transitive. Its only two oddities (NaN !== NaN, 0 === -0) are inherited from IEEE 754, and they are why Object.is and SameValueZero exist.

Your objection assumed == was asking about truth. It never is. It converts toward numbers, in thirteen numbered steps, and the reason to abandon it is not any individual surprise but that it is not transitive — which means it cannot be used to reason about equality at all.

pieces.title: Resolution 22 — Q24: what "idiomatic" means, and why x == null is provably a two-value test
pieces.content:
You are right that this one has never been elaborated. The card is a single sentence, you have met that sentence several times, and nobody has unpacked it — including me. So this starts from the words themselves, including the one you flagged: what does "idiomatic" even mean? It is a genuinely useful word and it is doing real work in the question.

The good news is that Resolution 21 just did the hard part. Having the thirteen numbered rules of IsLooselyEqual on the table means x == null stops being folklore you have to trust and becomes something you can prove. Section 4 proves it: not "it usually catches both," but it catches exactly those two values and no others, and here is the rule that guarantees it.

You also re-ask whether null and undefined are types or values. Resolution 17 answered that in full and Section 3 recaps it in a paragraph rather than repeating it — but it is worth noticing that you have now circled this question three times, which is a signal that it was load-bearing.

The asks:

  1. What does "idiomatic" mean? Section 1 — and why the card's question is phrased as an exception rather than a rule.
  2. What is x here — a variable, an array, what? Section 2 — a small ask with a direct answer.
  3. Are null and undefined types or values? Section 3 — both; Resolution 17 Section 1.
  4. How does x == null cover both? What does it actually mean? Sections 4 and 5 — provably, by the rules.
  5. Why is this acceptable when == generally is not? Sections 6 and 7 — every objection Resolution 21 raised, checked against this one case.

Section 1 — What "idiomatic" means

An idiom in ordinary language is a phrase whose meaning is established by usage rather than by its parts — "spill the beans," "under the weather." You cannot work them out from the words; you know them because you have heard native speakers use them.

In programming the word means something adjacent but sharper:

Idiomatic code is written the way an experienced practitioner of that particular language would write it — following the conventions the community has settled on, using the constructs the language actually provides, and looking familiar to another reader of that language.

The crucial part is "of that particular language." Idiomatic is not a synonym for "correct" or "good." It is language-relative, and code can be perfectly correct while being conspicuously unidiomatic:

// correct, and nobody writes this
let result = [];
for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
  result[result.length] = items[i] * 2;
}

// idiomatic JavaScript
const result = items.map(x => x * 2);

Both produce the same array. The first is what someone writes when they know C and are typing JavaScript; the second is what a JavaScript programmer writes. Neither is wrong. One announces that you have not learned the language's habits.

The opposite failure is worth naming too. Idiomatic is not the same as clever:

~~x          // truncates to an integer. Clever. Not idiomatic — obscure.
Math.trunc(x)// idiomatic — says what it means.

And now why the card asks the question in that shape. The blanket advice in JavaScript is "always use ===, never ==" — which Resolution 21 Section 8 justified with the transitivity failure. Linters enforce it by default. So the question "when is == considered acceptable idiomatic style?" is asking something specific and slightly unusual:

Given that there is a near-universal rule against this operator, is there a case where experienced JavaScript programmers deliberately break the rule — and it reads as fluent rather than sloppy?

There is exactly one. That is the entire content of the card.

Section 2 — What x is

You asked directly, so a direct answer: x is a placeholder. It is not a variable of any particular kind, not an array, not anything specific. In documentation and specifications, x means "whatever expression you are testing." All of these are the same pattern:

if (x == null)                    // a variable
if (user.email == null)           // a property
if (getConfig() == null)          // a function's return value
if (arr[0] == null)               // an array element
if (map.get(key) == null)         // anything at all

The value it holds can be of any type — that is the point of the test. You are asking "did I get nothing?" and you do not know in advance what "something" would have looked like.

Section 3 — null and undefined: both, again

You ask again whether these are primitive types or actual values, and note you asked before. Resolution 17 Section 1 is the full answer; here it is in one paragraph.

Both, and there is no tension. A type is a set of values. The type Null is a set containing exactly one member, and that member is the value null. Same for Undefined. A type with one member is called a unit type. Because there is only one value, nobody bothers giving the type and the value different names — so the same word does both jobs, and which one is meant is settled by the sentence. In x == null the word is unambiguously the value, because only expressions can appear on either side of an operator.

That is why the expression is even possible to write. You cannot compare against a type in JavaScript — there is nothing to compare against. x == null compares x to a specific value, exactly like x == 5.

Section 4 — What x == null actually means, proved

Now the mechanism, and it is worth doing exhaustively rather than by assertion, because the claim "covers both" sounds like an approximation and is not.

Recall Resolution 21 Section 6. The relevant rules of IsLooselyEqual(x, y), with y being null:

   1. If Type(x) is the same as Type(y):
          return IsStrictlyEqual(x, y).
   2. If x is null and y is undefined:  return true.
   3. If x is undefined and y is null:  return true.
   4..12  — none of these rules mention the Null type anywhere.
  13. Return false.

Now take every possible x and see which rule fires. There are only three outcomes:
