x is nullRule 1. Both operands are of type Null, so it defers to strict equality — and null === null is true. No conversion happens.
x is undefinedRule 3. A hand-written clause in the specification, stating that these two are equal. No conversion happens.
x is anything else at allRule 1 does not apply (different types). Rules 2 and 3 do not apply. Rules 4 through 12 never mention Null — there is no rule converting Null to a number, a string, a boolean, or a primitive. So control falls to rule 13: return false.

That third row is the whole proof. null does not participate in coercion at all. Every other primitive has conversion rules — Booleans become numbers, strings become numbers, objects become primitives — and null has none. So the notorious machinery of == is entirely bypassed here.

Which gives the exact statement, replacing the card's informal one:

x == null is true if and only if x is null or x is undefined. For every other value in the language, it is false. This is not a tendency; it is guaranteed by rule 13.

You can check it against the values most likely to worry you — the falsy ones from Q20, which are exactly the values that trip up the naive alternative:

0         == null   // false
-0        == null   // false
""        == null   // false
false     == null   // false
NaN       == null   // false
0n        == null   // false
[]        == null   // false
{}        == null   // false
"null"    == null   // false   — a string, not the value
Symbol()  == null   // false

null      == null   // true
undefined == null   // true

Twelve values, two true. And note that [] == null being false is a nice contrast with Resolution 21 Section 8's [] == false being true: the empty array converts happily to 0 when there is a number to meet, and has nothing to convert toward when the other side is null.

Section 5 — Why you would want it

The test names a concept the language did not have a word for until 2020: nullish — meaning "null or undefined," the two ways of being absent that Resolution 17 distinguished.

You want that test constantly, because in real code you usually do not know which one you will get:

obj.missing          // undefined — the property was never set
JSON.parse('{"a":null}').a   // null — the server sent an explicit null
f()                  // undefined — no return statement
getElementById("x")  // null — the DOM's chosen "not found"
arr[99]              // undefined — past the end

A single object assembled from a form, a database and an API can carry both, for reasons that have nothing to do with your code. Testing for only one of them is a bug waiting for the other to arrive.

And the alternative is long enough that people skip it:

if (x === null || x === undefined)   // 32 characters, says it twice
if (x == null)                       //  9 characters, says it once

Written once, the long form is fine. Written in every guard in a codebase, the short form is why the idiom exists.

Section 6 — Why this is acceptable when == generally is not

Resolution 21 made three arguments against ==. Check each against this specific use:

Objection 1: coercion makes the result unpredictable.Does not apply. Section 4: no conversion occurs on either branch. Rules 1 and 3 return directly, and rule 13 catches everything else. The conversion tables are never consulted.
Objection 2: == is not transitive, so you cannot reason with it.Does not apply. Transitivity is a property you need when using == as general equality — comparing two unknown values. Here the right-hand side is a fixed literal and the expression is being used as a predicate: "is x nullish?" There is no chain of comparisons to break.
Objection 3: the intent is unclear to a reader.Inverted. This is the one case where == is clearer: x == null reads as one concept — absence — while x === null || x === undefined reads as two conditions the reader must notice are related. The idiom is more legible, not less.

Which is precisely why it survived. It is not an exception granted out of laziness — it is a case where none of the reasons for the rule are present.

The tooling agrees, and this is checkable rather than a matter of opinion. ESLint's eqeqeq rule — the one that enforces === — ships with an option for exactly this:

"eqeqeq": ["error", "always", { "null": "ignore" }]

A carve-out written into the standard linter for this single pattern. Some style guides do ban == outright and require the long form; that position is defensible on the grounds that a blanket rule is easier to enforce than a rule with an exception. Both are respectable. But the exception exists in the tooling, which is as close to a community verdict as this gets.

Section 7 — The two things it is not

Two nearby tests that look like this one and are not.

1. if (!x) is a much wider net. This is the mistake the idiom exists to avoid:

  x == null   catches:  null, undefined                      (2 values)
  !x          catches:  null, undefined, 0, -0, "", false,
                        NaN, 0n                              (8 values)

Six extra values, and they are all legitimate data — Resolution 19 Section 7's whole complaint. If x is a count, a price, a name field or a boolean setting, !x will treat a real value as missing. x == null will not.

2. typeof x === "undefined" asks a different question. It looks like a stricter version and is actually a broader one:

x === undefined            // ReferenceError if x was never declared
typeof x === "undefined"   // "undefined" — no error

Resolution 18 Section 6: typeof is the only operator that can read an undeclared name without throwing. So typeof x === "undefined" conflates "declared but unset" with "never declared at all". That was essential for 1990s feature detection and is almost never what you want for your own variables — if you do not know whether your own variable exists, that is a different problem.

Section 8 — The modern form

ES2020 turned the idiom into syntax, which is the strongest possible endorsement of it. Both new operators test for exactly the two nullish values and nothing else:

x ?? fallback          // fallback only if x is null or undefined
x?.prop                // undefined only if x is null or undefined
x?.[key]               // same, for computed access
x?.()                  // same, for calls
obj.a ??= 1            // assign only if currently nullish (ES2021)

Compare the pairs, and note that the second column is the same predicate as the first:

  const port = config.port == null ? 8080 : config.port;
  const port = config.port ?? 8080;                      // identical

  const city = user && user.address && user.address.city;
  const city = user?.address?.city;                      // and safer

So the practical position:

  • Use ?? and ?. where they fit — supplying a default, or reaching through a possibly-absent object.
  • Use x == null when you need the test itself, as a condition rather than a value: if (x == null) throw ..., or filtering, or an early return.
  • Never use !x for absence unless 0, "" and false genuinely mean the same thing as missing in that context.

What this resolves

What does "idiomatic" mean?Section 1: written the way an experienced practitioner of that particular language would write it — and the emphasis matters, because idiomatic is not a synonym for correct. result[result.length] = x in a for loop is perfectly correct and announces that you know C and are typing JavaScript. It is also not a synonym for clever: ~~x is clever and unidiomatic; Math.trunc(x) is idiomatic.
Why is the card's question phrased that way?Section 1: because the blanket advice is "never use ==," enforced by linters. So the question is specifically "is there a case where experienced programmers deliberately break the rule and it still reads as fluent?" There is exactly one.
What is x?Section 2: a placeholder — not a variable of any particular kind. Any expression: a variable, a property, a function's return, an array element. The whole point is that you do not know its type in advance.
Are null/undefined types or values?Section 3: both — Resolution 17 Section 1's unit types. A type with one member; the same word does both jobs. In x == null the word is unambiguously the value, because you cannot compare against a type — there is nothing to compare against.
How does it cover both — provably?Section 4, using Resolution 21's numbered rules. If x is null: rule 1 (same type → strict equality → true). If undefined: rule 3, a hand-written clause. If anything else: rules 4–12 never mention the Null type, so control reaches rule 13 → false. null does not participate in coercion at all — it is the one primitive with no conversion rules — so the notorious machinery of == is entirely bypassed. Checked against all twelve troublesome values: 0, "", false, NaN, [], {}, "null" — all false.
Why is it acceptable?Section 6, checking all three of Resolution 21's objections. Coercion: does not occur. Transitivity: irrelevant — the right side is a fixed literal, so this is a predicate, not general equality; there is no chain to break. Clarity: inverted — x == null reads as one concept while x === null || x === undefined reads as two the reader must connect. And it is checkable, not opinion: ESLint's eqeqeq ships with {"null": "ignore"}, a carve-out for this single pattern.
What it is notSection 7. !x catches eight values, not two — 0, "", false, NaN, 0n as well — all of which are legitimate data. And typeof x === "undefined" is broader, not stricter: it also matches names that were never declared (Resolution 18 Section 6), conflating "unset" with "does not exist."
The modern formSection 8: ES2020 turned the idiom into syntax — ??, ?., and ??= all test for exactly these two values, which is the strongest possible endorsement of it. Use ??/?. where they fit; use x == null when you need the test as a condition.

The card's one sentence is true and it is also provable. null is the only primitive with no coercion rules at all, so x == null falls straight through thirteen steps to a two-value answer — and every objection to == is an objection to machinery this particular comparison never touches.

pieces.title: Resolution 23 — Q25: NaN is a value, not a type — and why typeof being right is worse
pieces.content:
This card sits next to Q19's — typeof null returns "object" — and the adjacency is misleading, so let me put the punchline first: one of those is a bug and the other is correct. typeof null === "object" is a 1995 accident (Resolution 18). typeof NaN === "number" is exactly right, and would be right in any language implementing IEEE 754. If they have felt like two examples of the same weirdness, they are not.

Your first ask — is it concrete that NaN is nothing but a value, and specifically of the primitive type Number? — is the fourth time you have circled the value-versus-type question, after Q18, Q19 and Q24. That is not repetition; it is a question that has not been given a general answer. Section 1 gives one, because the three cases you have met are genuinely different from each other and knowing how is worth more than a fourth individual answer.

Resolution 13 covered NaN's purpose and origin in depth and I will not repeat it. What this adds is the type framing, a precise reading of "invalid," an answer to what it means for NaN to be assigned, and the scenarios organised by where NaN actually arrives in real code rather than by mathematical category.

The asks:

  1. Is it concrete that NaN is a value, of type Number? Sections 1 and 2 — yes, entirely, and here is the general rule behind all four times you have asked this.
  2. What does "invalid numerical value" mean in the language generally? Section 3.
  3. What does it mean for NaN to be assigned? Section 4 — nothing special, and that is the point.
  4. All the scenarios that produce it. Section 5 — by where they arrive, not by what they are.
  5. (The consequence you have not asked about yet) Why typeof NaN === "number" being correct is more dangerous than typeof null being wrong. Section 6.

Section 1 — The general answer to the question you keep asking

Four times now: is this a type, or a value, or both? Here is the rule that settles all of them.

In JavaScript, only values exist at runtime. Types are sets that values belong to — they are not themselves things you can hold, pass, or name in an expression. So anything you can write in an expression position is a value. Always.

That is Resolution 18 Section 3's point — typeof cannot be applied to a type because there is nothing to apply it to. Now the three cases you have met, which differ in an important way:

nullA unit type. The type Null has exactly one member, so the type-name and the value-name are the same word, and English cannot tell them apart without context. This is the confusing case — and it confused you correctly.
undefinedSame structure. Type Undefined, one member.
NaNNot a unit type — not a type at all. There is no type called NaN. It is one member of the Number type, which has around eighteen quintillion members. NaN is only ever a value name. This case is unambiguous.

So the answer to "is it concrete" is: more concrete than for null. With null there was a genuine ambiguity in how we speak. With NaN there is none — nothing in the specification is called NaN except a value.

Confirm it the direct way:

typeof NaN          // "number"
Number.isNaN(NaN)   // true
NaN + 1             // NaN      — arithmetic accepts it as a Number
[1, NaN, 3].length  // 3        — an ordinary array element

And the card's answer is correct as written, which is worth saying because your instinct was to check it: NaN is a special value of the Number type representing an invalid numeric result, not a separate type. There is nothing to amend.

Section 2 — But there is a name-versus-value split, as there was for undefined

One wrinkle worth having, because it parallels something from Resolution 17.

NaN, the thing you type, is not a keyword. It is an ordinary identifier that resolves to a property of the global object — exactly like undefined (Resolution 17 Section 3) and exactly like Number (Resolution 14 Section 6):

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(globalThis, "NaN")
// { value: NaN, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }

globalThis.NaN                    // NaN
Number.NaN                        // NaN — the same value, a second name
Object.is(Number.NaN, NaN)        // true

So there are two spellings of one value, and neither of them is a literal in the grammar. Compare: null is a keyword; true and false are keywords; 5 is a numeric literal. NaN and Infinity and undefined are the three values you reach through a name rather than through syntax.

As with undefined, this was writable before ES5 and is not now. And as with undefined, it can still be shadowed by a local binding — which is one small reason Number.isNaN(x) is safer than x !== x-style hand-rolled checks in code you do not control.

Section 3 — What "invalid" means, precisely

You asked what is meant by an invalid numerical value "in general here in the language." The word is doing three different jobs, and separating them is the answer.

Sense 1 — mathematically indeterminate. The operation is well-defined; the particular inputs have no unique answer. Resolution 13 Section 1's criterion: every number would be equally justified. 0/0 is the canonical case — what times zero gives zero? Everything does.

Sense 2 — outside the domain. The operation has an answer, but not among the real numbers. Math.sqrt(-1), Math.log(-1), Math.asin(2). There is an answer in the complex numbers; JavaScript has no complex type, so within the system being asked, none exists.

Sense 3 — the conversion failed. Nothing mathematical happened at all. Something that was not a number was asked to be one, and there was no sensible reading. Number("hello"), undefined + 1, {} * 2.

Sense 3 is the overwhelming majority of NaNs in real code, and it is the one the word "numerical" obscures. Most NaN you will ever meet is not a mathematical event; it is a plumbing failure.

And the boundary that gives all three their shape — invalid is not the same as unrepresentable:

1 / 0                 // Infinity  — the answer exists and is unbounded,
                      //             in a known direction
1e308 * 10            // Infinity  — too large for the format
Number.MIN_VALUE / 2  // 0         — too small; silently underflows
0 / 0                 // NaN       — there is no answer to be too large for

Infinity says "the answer overflowed the format." NaN says "there is no answer to overflow." That distinction is Resolution 13 Section 1 and it is what makes "invalid" mean something rather than being a synonym for "went wrong."

Section 4 — What it means for NaN to be "assigned"

You asked what it specifically means for NaN to be assigned, and I think the honest answer will be slightly anticlimactic — but the anticlimax is the design.

Nothing special happens. NaN is assigned, stored, copied and passed exactly as the number 5 is.

let x = NaN;          // perfectly ordinary. No error, no warning.
let y = x;            // copied by value, like any primitive (Resolution 8)
const o = { n: NaN }; // stored in a property
[NaN, NaN]            // stored in an array
f(NaN)                // passed to a function
JSON.stringify({a: NaN})  // '{"a":null}' — except here (Resolution 13 §9)

There is no flag, no error state, no exception pending, no bit set anywhere outside the value. The variable holds a Number, and that Number happens to be the one that means "no valid answer."

And this is precisely the design decision Resolution 13 Section 4 identified, seen from your angle. The alternative designs were: raise an exception (an event — it has no place to live inside an array), or return a sentinel like -1 (a number — it will be averaged in as data). NaN is a third thing: a value that is storable like data and distinguishable from data. "What does it mean to be assigned" is exactly the question that separates it from an exception, and the answer — "it means nothing unusual" — is the whole point.

The one place the ordinariness breaks is equality, and only because it has to: if NaN compared equal to itself it would be indistinguishable from data in a lookup. Resolution 14 Sections 1–3 cover that, including the four equality algorithms it forced into existence.

Section 5 — Where NaN actually arrives

Resolution 13 Section 8 catalogued the producers by mathematical category. Here is the more useful cut for writing code: the places NaN enters a real program. In practice there are five, and only the last is mathematics.

1. User input, which is always a string. Resolution 21 Section 5's point: everything from a form is text.

Number(input.value)        // NaN if the user typed anything non-numeric
parseInt(input.value, 10)  // NaN if it does not START with a digit
+input.value               // NaN — the unary plus idiom

// and the pair that differ, which is its own bug source:
Number("12abc")     // NaN   — demands the WHOLE string be numeric
parseInt("12abc")   // 12    — reads a prefix and stops
Number("")          // 0     — the empty string is zero
parseInt("")        // NaN

2. A property that was not there. The single most common cause, and it comes from Resolution 17 Section 4:

const total = order.subtotal + order.tax;
// if the API did not send `tax`, order.tax is undefined
// undefined + 5  ->  NaN
// and `total` is now NaN, silently, and stays NaN forever

This is the shape that costs the most time, because the NaN appears at the addition and the mistake was at the fetch. By the time you see it, the responsible code is out of frame.

3. Dates that failed to parse.

const d = new Date("2026-13-45");
d.getTime()          // NaN
String(d)            // "Invalid Date"
d instanceof Date    // true — an ordinary Date whose time value is NaN

4. An object or array where a number was expected.

({}) * 2        // NaN — "[object Object]" is not numeric
[1, 2] * 2      // NaN — "1,2" is not numeric
[5] * 2         // 10  (!!) — a one-element array stringifies to "5"

That last line is Resolution 21 Section 7's ToPrimitive in action, and it is worth noticing that [5] * 2 quietly works. Coercion producing a plausible number is often worse than producing NaN.

5. Actual mathematics. Math.sqrt of a negative, 0/0, Infinity - Infinity. Real, and rare in web code.

And the archetype worth memorising, from Resolution 13 Section 10, because it belongs to category 1 and looks like a language bug:

["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt)     // [1, NaN, NaN]
// map passes (value, index, array); parseInt takes (string, radix).
// So: parseInt("2", 1) — radix 1 does not exist.
// Fix: .map(Number)

Section 6 — Why the correct answer is more dangerous than the wrong one

Here is the thing your card's fact actually costs you, and it makes a nice pair with Resolution 18 Section 7.

Both typeof null and typeof NaN let a bad value slip through a type guard — but for opposite reasons:

typeof null === "object"The operator lies. null is not an Object. The guard typeof x === "object" is asking the right question and getting a wrong answer. Fixable by asking a better question: x !== null && typeof x === "object".
typeof NaN === "number"The operator is telling the truth. NaN is a Number. The guard typeof x === "number" gets a correct answer — and the correct answer is not enough, because "is it a number" was the wrong question.

Which means the second one cannot be fixed by improving typeof. Watch:

function setPrice(p) {
  if (typeof p !== "number") throw new TypeError("price must be a number");
  this.price = p;                 // NaN sails straight through
}

setPrice(NaN);                    // no error. this.price is now NaN.
this.price + 10                   // NaN
this.price > 0                    // false
this.price < 0                    // false   — and so is every comparison
JSON.stringify({price: this.price})  // '{"price":null}'

The guard did its job correctly. NaN passed because it genuinely is a number. And then every subsequent comparison is false — including the ones you would use to detect the problem — so a validation like if (price < 0) reject() lets it through as well.

The correct guard has to ask two questions:

// "is this a usable number?"
Number.isFinite(x)
// true only for actual finite numbers: excludes NaN, Infinity,
// -Infinity, and does NOT coerce — Number.isFinite("5") is false.

// if you specifically want "a number, but not NaN":
typeof x === "number" && !Number.isNaN(x)

// and note the global versions do the wrong thing, both of them:
isNaN("hello")        // true  — coerces first
isFinite("5")         // true  — coerces first
Number.isNaN("hello") // false — correct
Number.isFinite("5")  // false — correct

Number.isFinite is the check most code actually wants and most code does not use. It is one call, it excludes all three of the values that break arithmetic, and it does not coerce.

What this resolves

Is it concrete that NaN is a value of type Number?Section 1: yes — and more concretely than for null. The card is correct as written, with nothing to amend. And the general rule behind all four times you have asked this: only values exist at runtime; types are sets that values belong to, not things you can hold. null and undefined are unit types — one member each, so type-name and value-name collide (Resolution 17). NaN is not a type at all — it is one member of Number, alongside eighteen quintillion others. There is nothing in the specification called NaN except a value.
The two cards are not the same kind of thingOpening and Section 6: typeof null === "object" is a bug; typeof NaN === "number" is correct and would be correct in any IEEE 754 language. If they have felt like two instances of one weirdness, they are not.
Is there a name/value wrinkle?Section 2: yes, the same one as undefined. NaN is not a keyword — it is an identifier resolving to a global property (writable: false since ES5), and Number.NaN is a second name for the same value. NaN, Infinity and undefined are the three values you reach through a name rather than through grammar.
What does "invalid" mean?Section 3, three distinct senses: mathematically indeterminate (0/0 — every answer equally justified), outside the domain (sqrt(-1) — no answer among the reals), and failed conversion (Number("hello") — nothing mathematical happened at all). The third is the overwhelming majority in real code, and the word "numerical" obscures it. Plus the boundary that gives the word meaning: invalid is not unrepresentable — Infinity means the answer overflowed the format; NaN means there is no answer to overflow.
What does it mean for NaN to be assigned?Section 4, and the anticlimax is the design: nothing special. let x = NaN is ordinary — stored, copied, passed, put in arrays and properties exactly like 5. No flag, no error state, no pending exception. And that is precisely what separates it from the alternatives Resolution 13 rejected: an exception is an event with nowhere to live inside an array; a sentinel like -1 is data and gets averaged in. NaN is storable like data and distinguishable from data — the ordinariness is the feature.
All the scenariosSection 5, cut by where NaN enters a program rather than by mathematical category. (1) User input — always a string; plus the Number("12abc") is NaN / parseInt("12abc") is 12 split. (2) A missing property — order.subtotal + order.tax when the API omitted tax; the single most common cause, and the worst to debug because the NaN appears at the addition and the mistake was at the fetch. (3) Failed date parsing. (4) Objects/arrays where a number was expected — including [5] * 2 quietly giving 10. (5) Actual mathematics — real, and rare in web code.
Why the correct answer is worse than the wrong oneSection 6, paired with Resolution 18. typeof null lies — fixable by asking a better question. typeof NaN tells the truth, and the truth is not enough, so if (typeof p !== "number") throw does its job correctly and lets NaN through. And then every comparison against it is false — including price < 0, so the validation you would use to catch it also passes. The check most code wants is Number.isFinite(x): one call, excludes NaN and both infinities, and does not coerce.

NaN is one value among quintillions in the Number type, reached through a global identifier rather than a literal, stored and copied like any other — and the reason it is dangerous is not that typeof gets it wrong, but that typeof gets it right.

pieces.title: Resolution 24 — Q26: what an object is, the overloaded word, and where prototypes come from
pieces.content:
This is the longest follow-up in the corpus and the most ambitious, and it deserves saying at the outset that you did most of the hard work yourself and got it right. The passage where you reason out what "blueprint" means — that a class specifies structure, what fields exist and how they are laid out, the way int specifies a structure and int x is an instance of it — is a correct and unusually precise account of what a C++ class is. Section 6 confirms it, extends it in the one place it stops short, and then uses it as the bridge to prototypes, because the thing you noticed about C++ methods is exactly the thing prototypes are for.

Your first complaint is the right place to start, though: the word "object" is overloaded across the whole of computer science and you have never had a map of the landscape. That is not a failure of yours. There are at least seven unrelated meanings in common use, most of them are homonyms rather than variants of one idea, and nobody ever says so. Section 1 is the map.

Node 2 has no separate card on prototypes, and you asked for them here explicitly — what a prototype is, what the "normal" kind of inheritance is called, how the syntax was made to look class-based over a different mechanism. So they are answered here in full rather than deferred.

The asks:

  1. The word "object" across computer science — the landscape. Section 1.
  2. Is Object a primitive type? Section 2 — no, and the reason is the sharpest line in the language.
  3. What is an object, in terms of data, type and value? A data structure? A value? A collection? Sections 3 and 4.
  4. How is an array an object — and is it like being a child of an Object class? Section 5 — your instinct is very nearly exactly right.
  5. My blueprint analysis of classes — is it right? Section 6 — yes, and here is what it opens up.
  6. What is prototypal inheritance, and what is the other kind called? Sections 7 and 8.
  7. How does class syntax sit on top of it? Section 9.
  8. The OOP principles — encapsulation, abstraction, polymorphism. Section 10, with an honest caveat.

Section 1 — The word "object," mapped

Here is the landscape. The critical thing to know before reading it is that most of these are not related to each other. The word was reused independently in different fields because it is a convenient word for "a thing." Treating them as one concept with variations is what makes the area feel impossible.

1. OOP object
Simula 67, Smalltalk 1972		An entity bundling state and behaviour, usually an instance of a class. This is the meaning in "object-oriented programming," in C++, Java, Python. Related to meaning 2 — genuinely, historically.
2. JavaScript objectA keyed collection of properties with an identity and a prototype link (Section 3). It can be used as an OOP object, and often is — but { x: 1, y: 2 } holds no behaviour and is not an instance of anything. A superset of meaning 1's role.
3. JSON object
ECMA-404 / RFC 8259		A piece of text. Not a runtime thing at all. JSON is a data interchange format whose syntax was borrowed from JavaScript's object literal in 2001 by Douglas Crockford. Related to meaning 2 only by syntax — see below.
4. Object, the JavaScript globalA function object (Resolution 14 Section 4) that acts as constructor, converter, and namespace for Object.keys, Object.freeze, Object.create. A specific value, not a concept.
5. The Object typeOne of the eight language types (Resolution 12 Section 7) — the set of all objects. A set, not a thing.
6. Object storage
S3, Azure Blob, GCS		An infrastructure term. Storage where data is an opaque blob plus metadata plus a key, as opposed to file storage (hierarchical paths) or block storage (raw disk blocks). Completely unrelated to any of the above. The word means "a unit of stored stuff."
7. Object file / object code
.o, .obj		The output of a compiler before linking — machine code plus a symbol table. Also completely unrelated, and older than OOP. Here "object" means "the objective/product of compilation."

Meanings 6 and 7 share nothing with the others but the letters. Meanings 1 and 2 are genuinely related. Meanings 3, 4 and 5 are all about JavaScript but are a text format, a value, and a set respectively — three different categories.

And the JSON confusion is worth killing properly, because it causes real bugs. A JSON object is text. A JavaScript object is a runtime thing. They look alike because one was copied from the other, and they differ in ways that matter:

  JavaScript object literal        JSON text
  ------------------------         ---------
  { a: 1 }                         {"a": 1}      keys MUST be double-quoted
  { 'a': 1 }                       —             single quotes are invalid
  { a: 1, }                        —             no trailing commas
  { a: undefined }                 —             no undefined
  { a: () => 1 }                   —             no functions
  { a: NaN }                       —             no NaN or Infinity
  { a: 1n }                        —             no BigInt
  { a: new Date() }                —             no Date; becomes a string
  // a comment                     —             no comments

JSON.parse("{a:1}")        // SyntaxError — valid JS, invalid JSON
JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: NaN })
// '{"c":null}'  — a and b VANISH, c becomes null

So: "JSON object" and "JavaScript object" are two different things that share a punctuation style. The name JSON — JavaScript Object Notation — is honest about being a notation, and everyone ignores that word.

Section 2 — Is Object a primitive type? No, and here is the line

You said you keep forgetting. Here is the fact plus a reason to remember it, which should help more than the fact alone.

  The seven PRIMITIVE types:
      number, bigint, string, boolean, symbol, null, undefined

  Plus one more, making eight LANGUAGE types:
      Object

  Object is NOT a primitive. It is the other side of the fundamental
  division in the entire language.

And the reason it is the other side — this is the payoff of Resolution 8, and it is the answer to your "what is an object in terms of the fundamentals" question:

PrimitivesObjects
IdentityNone. There is no "the 5." Two 5s are the same 5.Yes. Every object is a distinct thing. {} === {} is false.
MutabilityImmutable, always (Resolution 16)Mutable, unless frozen one at a time
Assignment copiesthe valuea reference to the same object
Has parts you can write toNo slots (Resolution 8)Slots. That is what it is for.
Compared bycontentidentity

So the memorable version: primitives are values; objects are things. A value has no location and no history — 5 is 5 wherever it appears. A thing occupies a place, can change over time, and remains itself while changing. That distinction is not JavaScript's invention; it is the difference between a number and a box.

Section 3 — What a JavaScript object actually is

Now the definition, in the terms we have built. The card says "a bag of key-value pairs," which is true and is roughly a third of it.

A JavaScript object is three things at once: a mutable table of properties, an identity, and a link to another object called its prototype.

Part 1 — the property table, which is not quite key-value pairs. Each entry is not a value but a property record with attributes. You can look at one:

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor({ a: 1 }, "a")
// { value: 1, writable: true, enumerable: true, configurable: true }

Four fields, only one of which is the value:

  • writable — can it be assigned to? Resolution 16 Section 3 showed a String wrapper's indices are writable: false, which is half of why s[0] = "x" fails.
  • enumerable — does it show up in Object.keys and for...in? Built-in methods are all non-enumerable, which is why Object.keys([1,2]) gives ["0","1"] and not every method on Array.prototype.
  • configurable — can the property be deleted or its attributes changed?

And a property may instead be an accessor, holding functions rather than a value:

Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor({ get b() { return 1; } }, "b")
// { get: [Function], set: undefined, enumerable: true, configurable: true }

So "key-value pairs" understates it: a property maps a key to a record, and the record may compute its value on demand. That is why Resolution 14 Section 7 had to say the dot "invokes [[Get]]" rather than "reads a stored value."

Keys are strings or Symbols and nothing else — Resolution 14 Section 9, and the reason two objects used as keys silently collide on "[object Object]".

Part 2 — identity. Every object has one, it is unique, permanent, and cannot be forged or inspected. This is what Section 2's table means by "things":

{} === {}                     // false — two objects
const o = {}; o === o         // true  — one object, two mentions
const a = {}, b = a;
a.x = 1; b.x                  // 1 — the same object seen through two names

Part 3 — the prototype link. An internal slot, written [[Prototype]], holding either another object or null. Sections 7 and 8.

And one more layer that explains the exceptions: internal methods. Every object supports a fixed set of internal operations — [[Get]], [[Set]], [[Delete]], [[OwnPropertyKeys]], and others. Objects using the default implementations are called ordinary; objects that override them are exotic:

  Array              — overrides [[DefineOwnProperty]] to keep `length`
                       in sync with index properties (Resolution 20 §3)
  Proxy              — every internal method is user-supplied
  String wrapper     — index properties are synthesised, non-writable
  arguments (sloppy) — indices are aliased to the parameter variables
  Module namespace   — live, read-only bindings
  Function           — has [[Call]], which is what makes ( ) legal

That list is the complete inventory of "magic" in JavaScript objects. Everything else — arrays aside from length, dates, maps, your own classes — is an ordinary object with ordinary properties.

Section 4 — Answering your three framings directly

You asked whether an object is a data structure, a primitive type, a value in itself, or a collection of values. Each deserves a direct answer.

"Is it a data structure?" Yes, and more than that: it is the only compound data structure the language has. Everything else is built from it or on it. An array is an object (Section 5). A function is an object with [[Call]]. Map, Set, Date, RegExp, Promise, Error — all objects. If you want to store more than one thing in JavaScript, you are using an object, whether or not it looks like one.

"Is it a value in itself?" This is the sharpest of your questions and the answer is no, and this matters. An object is not a value in the sense a primitive is. What a variable holds is a reference to the object; the object itself lives elsewhere and independently. Resolution 20 Section 4 made this point for [] and it generalises:

let a = 5;        // the variable CONTAINS the value 5
let b = {};       // the variable contains a REFERENCE to an object

let c = a;        // c contains its own 5
let d = b;        // d contains a reference to the SAME object
d.x = 1;
b.x               // 1 — one object, two references

Which is why "assignment copies" means two different things in the two rows of Section 2's table — Q30's card, and this is the mechanism behind it.

"Is it a collection of values?" Yes — a collection with an identity. That qualifier is the whole difference between a JavaScript object and a "record" or "tuple" in languages that have them. Resolution 12 Section 10's Records and Tuples proposal was precisely an attempt to add a compound thing without identity, so that #{x:1} === #{x:1} would be true. It stalled. Objects remain the only compound, and objects have identity.

Section 5 — Arrays are objects, and your "child of Object" instinct

Resolution 20 Section 3 covered the mechanics: an array is an object whose element keys are the strings "0", "1", "2", with a length property that is two-way linked to them, and Array.prototype on its chain. I will not repeat that. What is new here is your specific hypothesis, which deserves a direct verdict.

You asked whether "an array is an object" is like a class-based world where Array is a child of the Object class, inheriting some properties and overriding others.

That is very nearly exactly right, and both halves check out mechanically:

// "inherits from Object" — literally true, and you can see the chain:
Object.getPrototypeOf([])              === Array.prototype   // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype  // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype)                      // null

  [1,2,3]
    |  (own: "0","1","2","length")
    v
  Array.prototype     map, filter, push, join, slice...
    |
    v
  Object.prototype    toString, hasOwnProperty, valueOf...
    |
    v
  null

So an array genuinely does inherit from the object world — [].hasOwnProperty works, and it is found two links up on Object.prototype.

And "overrides some" is true too, in two distinct ways:

// 1. Ordinary override: Array.prototype.toString shadows
//    Object.prototype.toString.
[1,2].toString()          // "1,2"          — Array's version
({}).toString()           // "[object Object]" — Object's version

// 2. Exotic override: Array overrides an INTERNAL method, which no
//    amount of ordinary inheritance could express.
const a = [1,2,3];
a.length = 1;
a                          // [1] — setting length DELETED elements

The only refinement: JavaScript has no "Object class" that Array is a subclass of, in the C++ sense — there are no classes underneath at all. What there is instead is a chain of objects, and Array.prototype is an object whose prototype happens to be Object.prototype. Your model is right about the structure and one word off about the machinery, and Sections 7 and 8 are that word.

Section 6 — Your blueprint analysis, checked and extended

Now the passage you worked out for yourself. Your account was: the word "blueprint" is overused to the point of meaninglessness, but it becomes precise once you see that a class specifies structure — what members exist, of what types and sizes, how the contents are organised — and that this is the same relationship int has to int x = 5: the type defines the structure, the variable is an instance of it.

That is correct, and it is a better account than most textbooks give. Three confirmations, then one extension that turns out to matter enormously.

Confirmation 1 — a C++ class really is a memory layout. This is not a metaphor; the compiler computes an actual size and actual offsets:

class Point {
    int x;        // offset 0, 4 bytes
    int y;        // offset 4, 4 bytes
    double z;     // offset 8, 8 bytes
};

sizeof(Point);    // 16 — a real number, known at compile time

Point p;          // reserves 16 bytes. p.y is at address (&p + 4).

Access to p.y compiles to an addition, exactly like the array indexing in your Q21 model. There is no lookup, no table, no name at runtime — the member name disappears during compilation.

Confirmation 2 — your int analogy is stronger than you claimed. You hedged that it "might not be appropriate." It is appropriate, and here is the precise reason: in C++, int and Point are both types, and a type's job is to determine layout and permitted operations. The only difference is that int is built into the language and Point is one you defined. In fact C++ makes this explicit — a struct and a class differ only in default member access, and a struct is plainly just "a layout." So a class is a user-defined type, and "blueprint" is the informal word for "layout specification."

Confirmation 3 — your instinct that the class is not the thing that runs. You wrote that a class in itself is just a definition, not something stored in memory, and that the object is the class "in action" with the actual state. Right. In a compiled language the class exists at compile time and is largely gone at runtime; what remains is instances.

And now the extension, which is the hinge of this whole piece. Your model covers data layout. But a class also carries behaviour — member functions — and here is the question worth asking:

If a class defines the layout and every instance gets its own copy of that layout, does every instance get its own copy of the methods?

No. And that fact is the entire bridge to prototypes.

class Point {
    int x, y;
    void move(int dx) { x += dx; }
};

sizeof(Point);    // 8, not 8-plus-the-size-of-move.
                  // The method is NOT in the object.

// There is ONE copy of move() in the program's code segment.
// It is compiled roughly as:
//      void Point_move(Point* this, int dx) { this->x += dx; }
// and  p.move(3)  is compiled as  Point_move(&p, 3).

A million Point objects share one move. The object carries state; the shared behaviour lives elsewhere and receives the object as a hidden this argument. (For virtual functions, the object carries a single pointer — the vptr — to a shared table.)

Hold that sentence: state per object, behaviour shared, connected by a hidden link and an implicit this. That is what a prototype is. C++ implements the arrangement at compile time and hides it; JavaScript implements the same arrangement at runtime and exposes it. Section 8.

The one place your model does not carry over is the part that forced JavaScript to do something different. In C++ the layout is fixed before the program runs. In JavaScript:

const p = { x: 1 };
p.y = 2;          // add a property. To an existing object. At runtime.
delete p.x;       // remove one.
p.greet = () => "hi";   // add behaviour to one individual object.

There is no size, no offsets, no fixed set of members. A blueprint is meaningless when the building can grow rooms while you are standing in it. That is the fact that makes classes the wrong mechanism for JavaScript, and it is why the language reached for a different one.

Section 7 — The two kinds of inheritance, and the name you asked for

You asked what the "normal" kind is called. It has two names, used interchangeably:

Class-based inheritance, also called classical inheritance — a pun that has caused some confusion, since "classical" here means class-based, not merely traditional. C++, Java, C#, Python and Ruby all use it.

The structural difference from JavaScript's is best seen as a difference in how many kinds of thing exist:

Class-basedPrototypal
Kinds of thingTwo. Classes and instances are different categories.One. There are only objects.
A class isa description; not itself an instance— there are none —
Inheritance isclass inherits from class, fixed at compile timeobject links to object, changeable at runtime
To share behaviourdefine it in a base classput it on an object others link to
To make a new thinginstantiate a classclone or link an existing object

Where prototypes came from: a language called Self, built by David Ungar and Randall Smith starting in 1986 at Xerox PARC and continued at Sun. Self was a descendant of Smalltalk, and its central experiment was to remove classes entirely and see whether anything was lost. The argument was that a class is a static description of objects — and if you already have live objects, you can make new ones by cloning, and share behaviour by linking, without a second category of thing existing at all. Brendan Eich has cited Self as a direct influence on JavaScript's object model.

And the punchline, which is the thing to take away from this section:

JavaScript has no inheritance mechanism. There is no code in the engine that "performs inheritance." There is only property lookup that does not stop at the first object — the [[Get]] walk from Resolution 14 Section 7. "Inheritance" is a name for what that walk looks like from outside.

Section 8 — What a prototype is, mechanically

Every object has an internal slot, [[Prototype]], holding either another object or null. That is the entire mechanism. Property lookup follows it:

const animal = { eats: true, describe() { return "I eat: " + this.eats; } };

const rabbit = Object.create(animal);   // rabbit's [[Prototype]] is animal
rabbit.jumps = true;

rabbit.jumps            // true  — own property
rabbit.eats             // true  — NOT own. Found on animal.
rabbit.describe()       // "I eat: true"
                        //   the function lives on `animal`,
                        //   but `this` is `rabbit` — the call site decides.
rabbit.toString         // found on Object.prototype, two links up
rabbit.nonsense         // undefined — chain ended at null

Look at describe again. One function object, stored on animal, called with this bound to rabbit. That is Section 6's C++ arrangement — state per object, behaviour shared, an implicit this — with the hidden link made explicit and mutable.

Three rules that make the rest predictable.

1. Own properties shadow inherited ones.

const parent = { a: 1 };
const child = Object.create(parent);
child.a = 2;
child.a                            // 2
parent.a                           // 1  — unchanged
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(child)  // ["a"] — a NEW own property was created

2. Writing never modifies the prototype. Assignment creates an own property on the object you assigned to (unless the prototype has a setter). Reads go up the chain; writes stay put. This is what keeps shared prototypes safe.

3. The chain ends at null, and you can start there.

Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype)   // null
const dict = Object.create(null);
dict.toString                              // undefined — no chain at all

That is how you make a dictionary that cannot collide with inherited names, and it is why Resolution 17 Section 5 noted that the chain terminates in null rather than undefined — "deliberately no parent" is a choice, not a failed lookup.

And now the naming trap, which is the single largest source of prototype confusion and which nobody warns you about:

[[Prototype]] and .prototype are two different things with nearly the same name.

[[Prototype]] is the internal link every object has. You read it with Object.getPrototypeOf(x).

.prototype is an ordinary property that only functions have. It is not the function's own prototype. It is the object that will be installed as the [[Prototype]] of instances created by calling that function with new.

Object.getPrototypeOf([]) === Array.prototype       // true
                          // arrays' prototype IS Array.prototype

Object.getPrototypeOf(Array) === Array.prototype    // FALSE (!!)
Object.getPrototypeOf(Array) === Function.prototype // true
                          // Array is a FUNCTION, so its own prototype
                          // is Function.prototype.

So Array.prototype is not Array's prototype. It is the prototype Array hands out. Read .prototype as "the prototype for instances of this," and the confusion goes away permanently.

Section 9 — class is syntax over all of this

You said you understood the syntax was made to feel class-based while being prototypal underneath, without knowing what that meant. Here it is, side by side. ES2015 added class; this is what it does:

class Point {
  constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
  move(dx)          { this.x += dx; }
}

// and here is essentially the same thing written by hand,
// the way everyone wrote it before 2015:

function Point(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
Point.prototype.move = function (dx) { this.x += dx; };

Both create a function whose .prototype object holds the methods. new Point(1,2) creates an object, sets its [[Prototype]] to Point.prototype, runs the constructor with this bound to it, and returns it.

typeof Point                                  // "function"  — not "class"
Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Point.prototype)   // ["constructor", "move"]
Object.getPrototypeOf(new Point(1,2)) === Point.prototype   // true

extends sets up two chains, which is the part hand-written code usually got wrong:

class Base { m() {} static s() {} }
class Derived extends Base { }

Object.getPrototypeOf(Derived.prototype) === Base.prototype  // true
    // the INSTANCE chain: instance -> Derived.prototype -> Base.prototype

Object.getPrototypeOf(Derived) === Base                      // true
    // the STATIC chain: so Derived.s() works too

But it is not purely sugar, and the differences are worth knowing:

  • Class bodies are always strict mode (Resolution 16 Section 3's point about s[0] = "x" throwing).
  • Classes are not hoisted-callable. They sit in the temporal dead zone until their declaration runs — Resolution 18 Section 6's typeof hole.
  • They must be called with new. Point(1,2) without new throws "Class constructor Point cannot be invoked without 'new'". The old function form silently did the wrong thing instead.
  • Methods are non-enumerable. Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(Point.prototype, "move").enumerable is false, whereas a method written in an object literal is enumerable. This is why for...in does not list class methods.
  • Private fields (#x) are genuinely new and cannot be expressed with prototypes at all. They are the one part of class that is not sugar for anything.

Section 10 — The OOP principles, and an honest caveat

You listed the four. Briefly, and mapped to what JavaScript actually offers:

EncapsulationBundling state with the behaviour that manages it, and hiding the internals. JavaScript had no privacy mechanism for twenty-four years — the convention was a leading underscore, this._name, which is documentation rather than enforcement. Real privacy arrived three ways: closures (Node 4's material, and the classic answer), WeakMap, and #private fields in ES2022.
AbstractionExposing an interface and hiding how it works. Not a language feature anywhere — it is a design practice. JavaScript supports it the same way every language does, by you choosing what to export.
InheritanceSections 7 and 8. The prototype chain, which is a runtime link between objects rather than a compile-time relationship between classes.
PolymorphismThe same call working on different kinds of thing. JavaScript gets this for free and does not need any of the machinery — no interfaces, no virtual keyword, no base class. x.draw() looks up draw on whatever x is; if it is there, it runs. This is called duck typing, and it is a consequence of dynamic property lookup, not a feature anyone added.

And the caveat, because you have just come from C++ and it would be easy to over-index. JavaScript is not primarily an object-oriented language and a great deal of excellent JavaScript uses almost none of the above. It is a language in which functions are the main tool — Node 3 and Node 4 are about that — and the dominant modern styles (React, most Node code, most utility code) use plain objects for data and functions for behaviour, with class appearing rarely.

The prototype chain matters enormously for understanding the language — it is how [].map is found, how class works, how every built-in is organised. It matters much less as something you write by hand.

What this resolves

The word "object" across computer scienceSection 1, seven meanings mapped — and the key point is that most are homonyms, not variants of one idea. OOP object and JavaScript object are genuinely related; Object the global is a value, the Object type is a set; and object storage (S3) and object files (.o) share nothing but the letters. Treating them as one concept is what makes the area feel impossible.
JSON objects vs JavaScript objectsSection 1: a JSON object is text. JSON is a data format whose syntax Crockford borrowed from the JS object literal in 2001. Keys must be double-quoted, no trailing commas, no comments, no undefined/functions/NaN/BigInt/Date. JSON.parse("{a:1}") is a SyntaxError — valid JS, invalid JSON.
Is Object a primitive type?Section 2: no — seven primitives plus Object makes eight language types. And the reason to remember it: primitives are values, objects are things. No identity vs identity; immutable vs mutable; copied by value vs by reference; no slots vs slots; compared by content vs by identity.
What is an object?Section 3: three things at once — a property table, an identity, and a prototype link. And the card's "key-value pairs" understates the first: each property is a record with writable, enumerable, configurable, or a getter/setter pair. Which is why the dot "invokes [[Get]]" rather than "reads a stored value." Plus the complete inventory of magic: the exotic objects that override internal methods — Array, Proxy, String wrapper, arguments, module namespaces, functions.
Data structure? Value? Collection?Section 4, each answered. Data structure: yes — the only compound one the language has; arrays, functions, Map, Set, Date, Promise are all objects. A value: no — a variable holds a reference; the object lives independently. A collection: yes, with an identity — and that qualifier is exactly what Records & Tuples (Resolution 12 Section 10) tried and failed to remove.
Is "array is an object" like being a child of an Object class?Section 5: very nearly exactly right. The inheritance is literal — [] → Array.prototype → Object.prototype → null, which is why [].hasOwnProperty works. And "overrides some" is true twice: ordinarily (Array.prototype.toString shadows Object.prototype.toString) and exotically (a.length = 1 deletes elements — an internal-method override no ordinary inheritance could express). One word off: there are no classes underneath, only a chain of objects.
Is my blueprint analysis right?Section 6: yes, and better than most textbook accounts. A C++ class is a memory layout — sizeof(Point) is a real compile-time number and p.y compiles to an address offset. Your int analogy is stronger than you hedged: in C++ int and Point are both types, and a type's job is to determine layout and operations; the only difference is one is built in. C++ makes this explicit — struct and class differ only in default access.
…and the extension that mattersSection 6: your model covers data. Ask the next question — does every instance get its own copy of the methods? No. sizeof(Point) does not include move; there is one copy, and p.move(3) compiles to roughly Point_move(&p, 3). State per object, behaviour shared, connected by an implicit this — that is exactly what a prototype is. C++ does it at compile time and hides it; JavaScript does it at runtime and exposes it. And the reason JavaScript could not use blueprints: p.y = 2 adds a property to a live object. A blueprint is meaningless when the building can grow rooms while you stand in it.
What is the other kind called?Section 7: class-based or classical inheritance — and "classical" is a pun meaning class-based, not merely traditional. The structural difference: class-based has two kinds of thing (classes and instances); prototypal has one (objects). Prototypes come from Self (Ungar and Smith, 1986), a Smalltalk descendant whose experiment was removing classes entirely — a direct influence on JavaScript.
What is a prototype?Section 8: an internal [[Prototype]] slot holding another object or null, and that is the entire mechanism. Three rules: own properties shadow inherited ones; writing never modifies the prototype (which is what keeps sharing safe); the chain ends at null and you can start there with Object.create(null). Plus the payoff sentence: JavaScript has no inheritance mechanism — there is only property lookup that does not stop at the first object.
The naming trap nobody warns you aboutSection 8: [[Prototype]] and .prototype are different things with nearly the same name. .prototype is an ordinary property that only functions have, and it is not that function's prototype — it is the prototype handed to instances. Hence Object.getPrototypeOf(Array) === Array.prototype is false; it is Function.prototype. Read .prototype as "the prototype for instances of this."
How does class sit on top?Section 9, shown side by side with the pre-2015 hand-written form. typeof Point is "function"; methods live on Point.prototype; extends sets up two chains (instance and static). Not purely sugar: class bodies are always strict, they sit in the TDZ, they throw if called without new, their methods are non-enumerable, and #private fields cannot be expressed with prototypes at all.
The OOP principlesSection 10. Encapsulation: JavaScript had none for 24 years (the _name convention); real privacy came from closures, WeakMap, and # fields in ES2022. Abstraction: a design practice, not a feature, anywhere. Inheritance: the prototype chain. Polymorphism: free — x.draw() needs no interface, no virtual, no base class, because lookup is dynamic. And the caveat: JavaScript is not primarily an OOP language; prototypes matter enormously for understanding it and much less as something you write by hand.

You had the pieces. A C++ class is a layout plus shared behaviour reached through an implicit this; JavaScript kept the second half and threw away the first, because a language where objects grow properties at runtime has no layout to specify. What is left is one kind of thing — objects — linked to each other, and a property lookup that keeps walking.

pieces.title: Resolution 25 — Q27: dot versus bracket, worked all the way through
pieces.content:
This follow-up is different from the others in a useful way: you are not confused about the rule, you say you could apply it, and what you want is a proper worked example so that the distinction becomes solid rather than remembered. That is a specific request and this piece answers it in kind — it is built around one realistic example carried all the way through, rather than around mechanism.

Resolution 14 Section 9 gave the mechanism, and one sentence from it is the seed for everything here: dot and bracket are the same operation, differing only in whether the key is literal text you typed or an expression evaluated at runtime. The rest of this piece is that sentence turned into code you could have written.

The asks:

  1. A proper elaborate example that makes dot-versus-bracket click. Sections 2 through 5 — one scenario, developed.
  2. (Implied, and the thing that actually creates confidence) The cases where the rule of thumb runs out, and the test you can apply in a second. Sections 6 and 7.

Section 1 — The one sentence, before the example

The card says: dot when you know the key at authoring time, brackets when the key is in a variable. True, and here is the version that makes it mechanical rather than a judgement call:

user.name and user["name"] are identical. Both look up a property whose key is the string "name".

After a dot, what you type is the key. Inside brackets, what you type is an expression that is evaluated, and its result becomes the key.

const user = { name: "Devansh" };

user.name          // key is the literal text "name"
user["name"]       // key is the string "name" — identical
user["na" + "me"]  // the expression evaluates to "name" — identical

const k = "name";
user[k]            // the expression `k` evaluates to "name" — identical
user.k             // key is the literal text "k" — DIFFERENT. undefined.

That last pair is the whole thing. user.k does not look inside k; it looks for a property literally called "k". The dot cannot see variables — it only sees the letters you typed.

Section 2 — The example: a settings screen

Here is a realistic object. Everything from here on works with it.

const settings = {
  theme: "dark",
  fontSize: 14,
  autoSave: true,
  "user-name": "Devansh",        // note the hyphen
  "2fa": false,                  // note the leading digit
  notifications: {
    email: true,
    push: false
  }
};

Case A — you are writing the code and you know the key. Use the dot.

settings.theme              // "dark"
settings.fontSize           // 14
settings.notifications.push // false

You typed theme because you, the author, decided this line is about the theme. The key is fixed in the source. Nothing about it can vary at runtime. This is the overwhelming majority of property access you will ever write, and the dot is right because it is shorter and reads as a name rather than a lookup.

Case B — the key is decided at runtime. You must use brackets.

Here is where the distinction stops being style and becomes necessity. Suppose the settings screen is generic — one function handles every toggle, and which setting it changes depends on which control the user touched:

function updateSetting(key, value) {
  settings[key] = value;      // brackets — REQUIRED
  // settings.key = value;    // would create a property literally named "key"
}

updateSetting("theme", "light");      // settings.theme is now "light"
updateSetting("fontSize", 16);        // settings.fontSize is now 16

The function does not know, and must not know, which setting it is handling. The key arrives as data. There is no way to write this with a dot — not "it would be worse," but the dot literally cannot express it.

And notice what the mistake does. settings.key = value does not fail; it succeeds at doing the wrong thing:

settings.key = "light";
settings                 // { theme: "dark", ..., key: "light" }
                         //                        ^^^^^^^^^^^^
                         // a new property called "key". No error.
                         // The real theme was never touched.

Silent, plausible, wrong — the shape Resolution 18 Section 7 kept finding. Objects accept any key you give them, so a typo becomes a new property rather than an error.

Section 3 — The four situations that force brackets

Beyond "the key is in a variable," there are three more, and knowing all four is what makes the rule feel complete instead of partial.

1. The key is in a variable — Case B above.

2. The key is not shaped like an identifier. The dot only accepts text that could be a variable name: letters, digits, _, $, not starting with a digit. Our object has two keys that fail that test:

settings["user-name"]    // "Devansh"
settings.user-name       // parses as: settings.user MINUS name
                         // ReferenceError: name is not defined

settings["2fa"]          // false
settings.2fa             // SyntaxError — a name cannot start with a digit

The first one is worth staring at. settings.user-name is not a syntax error — it is valid JavaScript that means something completely different. The parser sees a property access followed by a subtraction. Keys with hyphens are common in real data (HTTP headers, CSS properties, API fields), so this comes up.

3. The key is a number. Arrays are the everyday case, and Resolution 20 Section 3 explained why this is the same mechanism:

const arr = ["a", "b", "c"];
arr[0]        // "a"     — the number 0 is converted to the string "0"
arr["0"]      // "a"     — identical
arr.0         // SyntaxError
arr[i]        // the whole point of a loop

4. The key is a Symbol. Symbols are not text at all, so there is nothing a dot could hold:

const id = Symbol("id");
const u = { [id]: 123 };
u[id]         // 123
u.id          // undefined — a different, string-keyed property

Section 4 — Computed keys when creating an object

The same distinction appears at creation time, and this is a piece people often miss. Inside an object literal, a bare key is literal text, exactly as after a dot:

const key = "theme";

const a = { key: "dark" };      // { key: "dark" }    — the literal text "key"
const b = { [key]: "dark" };    // { theme: "dark" }  — the VALUE of key

The square brackets in a literal are called a computed property name, added in ES2015. Same rule as before: brackets mean "evaluate this expression and use the result as the key."

Where it earns its place:

// building an object whose keys come from data
function indexById(items) {
  const out = {};
  for (const item of items) {
    out[item.id] = item;        // bracket ASSIGNMENT
  }
  return out;
}

// or in one expression, with computed keys
const field = "email";
const patch = { [field]: "a@b.com", [`${field}Verified`]: false };
// { email: "a@b.com", emailVerified: false }

Before ES2015 you could not do this in a literal at all — you had to create the object and then assign, which is why older code has a lot of const o = {}; o[k] = v;.

Section 5 — The same example, both notations, side by side

Pulling it together on one screen:

const settings = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 14, "user-name": "Devansh" };
const key = "theme";

// ---- reading ----
settings.theme          "dark"   dot: key is fixed in the source
settings["theme"]       "dark"   identical, just noisier
settings[key]           "dark"   bracket: key comes from a variable
settings.key            undefined  looks for a property named "key"
settings["user-name"]   "Devansh"  bracket: not identifier-shaped
settings.user-name      ERROR      parsed as subtraction

// ---- writing ----
settings.theme = "light"        sets theme
settings[key]  = "light"        sets theme  (key is "theme")
settings.key   = "light"        creates a NEW property "key"  <-- the bug

// ---- creating ----
{ theme: 1 }                    key is the text "theme"
{ [key]: 1 }                    key is the VALUE of key
{ "user-name": 1 }              quoted: any string is allowed as a key

Section 6 — Two things that look like exceptions and are not

Reserved words are fine after a dot. You may see old code doing this and assume it was necessary:

obj["class"]     // this was REQUIRED before ES5
obj.class        // legal since ES5 (2009). So is obj.new, obj.for, obj.delete.

ES3 forbade reserved words as property names after a dot; ES5 allowed them. So if you see obj["default"] in a codebase, it is either very old or written by someone being cautious.

Quotes in object literals are optional, not meaningful. These three are the same object:

{ theme: "dark" }
{ "theme": "dark" }
{ ['the' + 'me']: "dark" }

Because — Resolution 14 Section 9 — every property key is a string or a Symbol anyway. Writing theme unquoted does not make it "not a string"; it is a shorthand the grammar allows when the text happens to be identifier-shaped. The quotes only become necessary when it is not.

Section 7 — The test, in one second

Here is the check to run when you are unsure, which is what turns the rule into confidence:

Ask: "Am I naming a property, or am I looking one up by a value?"

If the answer is fixed while you type — dot.
If the answer will be decided while the program runs — brackets.

Or the mechanical version, which never fails: if putting the key in quotes would change the meaning, you need brackets.

user.name    -> user["name"]   same thing -> dot is fine
user[k]      -> user["k"]      DIFFERENT  -> brackets are required

And the style guidance, which is not controversial: prefer the dot whenever it works. Not for performance — they compile to the same operation — but because user.name reads as a name while user["name"] reads as a lookup, and the difference matters when a reader is scanning. Reserve brackets for the four cases in Section 3, and their presence then signals that something dynamic is happening.

Section 8 — Where it goes wrong in real code

Three failures, all of them versions of the same confusion, so that you recognise the shape:

// 1. The dot that should have been brackets
function get(obj, prop) { return obj.prop; }
get(user, "name")            // undefined — always. For every input.

// 2. The bracket that should have been a dot
const theme = settings["theme"];    // works, but noise
                                    // — a reader pauses to check
                                    //   whether "theme" is dynamic

// 3. Object keys that are not strings — the collision from
//    Resolution 14 Section 9
const a = { id: 1 }, b = { id: 2 };
const seen = {};
seen[a] = "first";
seen[b] = "second";
seen[a]                       // "second"  (!!)
Object.keys(seen)             // ["[object Object]"]
// both objects converted to the SAME string key.
// Fix: use a Map, which keeps real keys.

The first is the one you will actually write at some point, and it fails silently and universally — the function returns undefined for every call, and nothing anywhere reports an error.

Section 9 — Both notations have an optional form

Worth knowing because it is the same distinction one level up. Optional chaining (ES2020, Resolution 17 Section 8) comes in a bracket flavour, and the syntax surprises people the first time:

user?.name           // dot form
user?.["name"]       // bracket form — note the DOT before the bracket
user?.[key]          // the dynamic case
user?.()             // and the call form

// why the extra dot: without it, `user?[key]` would be ambiguous
// with the conditional operator  cond ? a : b.

All three guard against exactly the two nullish values and nothing else — Resolution 22's proof applies unchanged. So the dynamic lookup that would otherwise need a guard becomes one expression:

// before
const v = settings && settings.notifications && settings.notifications[key];

// after
const v = settings?.notifications?.[key];

And the distinction that matters when a key may be absent: obj[key] returning undefined does not tell you whether the property is missing or present-and-undefined — Resolution 17 Section 7. If you need to know, ask properly:

Object.hasOwn(settings, key)   // ES2022 — own properties only
key in settings                // includes inherited ones:
                               // "toString" in {}  ->  true  (!!)

Section 10 — The one place bracket notation is dangerous

This belongs here rather than in a security topic, because it is caused entirely by the thing this card is about: with brackets, the key is data — and data can come from a user.

Objects accept any string as a key, and three of those strings are not ordinary. The important one is "__proto__", which on a normal object is not a property at all but an accessor inherited from Object.prototype that reads and writes the internal [[Prototype]] link (Resolution 24 Section 8):

const o = {};
o["__proto__"] = { hacked: true };
Object.getPrototypeOf(o).hacked        // true — you changed o's PROTOTYPE,
                                       // not a property called "__proto__"

On its own that only affects o. The damage comes when a path is walked, which is what every "set a nested value from a config string" helper does:

function setDeep(obj, path, val) {
  let cur = obj;
  const keys = path.split(".");
  for (let i = 0; i < keys.length - 1; i++) {
    cur[keys[i]] = cur[keys[i]] || {};
    cur = cur[keys[i]];                  // walks INTO __proto__
  }
  cur[keys.at(-1)] = val;
  return obj;
}

setDeep({}, "__proto__.isAdmin", true);

({}).isAdmin        // true   — every object in the program now has it
someUser.isAdmin    // true
if (user.isAdmin) { /* runs for everyone */ }

That is a real and named vulnerability class — prototype pollution — and it has produced CVEs in widely used libraries (deep-merge utilities, query-string parsers, configuration loaders). The mechanism is exactly Resolution 24 Section 8's chain: writing to Object.prototype gives every object in the realm a property, because lookup walks up until it finds one.

Three defences, in order of preference:

// 1. Use a Map when keys are user data. Map keys are not property
//    keys at all, so none of this applies.
const store = new Map();
store.set(userKey, value);

// 2. Use a null-prototype object as a dictionary (Resolution 24 §8).
const dict = Object.create(null);
dict["__proto__"] = "x";        // an ORDINARY property now
Object.getPrototypeOf(dict);    // null — nothing to pollute

// 3. If you must use a plain object, reject the three dangerous keys.
if (key === "__proto__" || key === "constructor" || key === "prototype") {
  throw new Error("invalid key");
}

None of this arises with dot notation, because a key you typed cannot be attacker-controlled. The moment the key becomes a value, it becomes input — and that is the deepest practical consequence of the distinction this card is about.

What this resolves

The one sentenceSection 1: user.name and user["name"] are identical. The difference is only that after a dot, what you type is the key, while inside brackets, what you type is an expression that gets evaluated. Hence user[k] uses the value of k, and user.k looks for a property literally named "k".
The worked exampleSections 2–5: one settings object carried through reading, writing and creating, with both notations side by side. The decisive case is a generic updateSetting(key, value) — the dot cannot express it at all, and the mistake does not fail: settings.key = value quietly creates a new property called "key" and leaves the real one untouched.
The four situations that force bracketsSection 3: (1) the key is in a variable; (2) the key is not identifier-shaped — and note settings.user-name is not a syntax error, it parses as a subtraction, which is why hyphenated keys (HTTP headers, CSS properties, API fields) bite; (3) the key is a number, which is the array case from Resolution 20; (4) the key is a Symbol, which is not text at all.
The creation sideSection 4: the same rule applies inside object literals. { key: 1 } uses the literal text; { [key]: 1 } uses the value — a computed property name, added in ES2015. Before that you had to create the object and then assign, which is why older code is full of const o = {}; o[k] = v;.
Two non-exceptionsSection 6: reserved words have been legal after a dot since ES5 — obj.class and obj.default are fine, so obj["default"] in a codebase is old habit rather than necessity. And quotes in a literal are optional, not meaningful: every key is a string anyway, and the unquoted form is just shorthand for identifier-shaped text.
The one-second testSection 7: am I naming a property, or looking one up by a value? Fixed while you type → dot. Decided while it runs → brackets. Or mechanically: if putting the key in quotes would change the meaning, you need brackets. And prefer the dot wherever it works — not for speed (identical operation) but because brackets then signal that something dynamic is happening.
Where it goes wrongSection 8: function get(obj, prop) { return obj.prop; } returns undefined for every input, silently, forever — the one you will eventually write. Plus the object-as-key collision from Resolution 14, where two different objects both become "[object Object]" and overwrite each other.
Optional formsSection 9: both notations have one — user?.name and user?.[key], and the extra dot before the bracket is required to disambiguate from the conditional operator. Plus: obj[key] returning undefined does not distinguish missing from present-and-undefined — use Object.hasOwn, or in if inherited keys should count ("toString" in {} is true).
Where brackets get dangerousSection 10, and it belongs to this card: with brackets the key is data, and data can come from a user. "__proto__" is not an ordinary key — it is an inherited accessor for the [[Prototype]] link, so a path-walking helper given "__proto__.isAdmin" writes onto Object.prototype and every object in the program gains the property. Demonstrated: ({}).isAdmin becomes true. This is prototype pollution, a named CVE class in deep-merge and config libraries. Defences: a Map, an Object.create(null) dictionary, or rejecting __proto__/constructor/prototype.

The dot cannot see variables. It only sees the letters you typed. Everything else in this topic follows from that.
